pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Store separately verified anonymized outputs under data_extra/anonymized/pdf; preserve every original file.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift from tightening general CNN verification through both S-shaped and MaxPool bounds to a MaxPool-focused contribution. The first neuron-wise-tightest MaxPool claim persists, while integration across backsubstitution, multi-neuron, and branch-and-bound frameworks becomes central. The separate S-shaped superiority contribution is withdrawn.

C2.justification: v1's discussion of Newise's advantage on non-negative networks is removed. v2 explains the conditional advantages and complementarity of MaxLin and Ti-Lin, attributes transformation overhead to deeper MaxPool2ReLU networks, and discusses framework-dependent runtime differences. Table 3 additionally warns that model-format conversion affects robustness and prevents direct accuracy comparisons across tables.

D1.justification: v2 adds per-network sources, node counts, property counts, and perturbation radii in Table 4, plus integration and model-conversion information. It provides a different Ti-Lin-Hybrid-Lin repository link and changes reported hardware from 8 cores/15 GB RAM to 48 cores/125 GB. Conversely, v1's explicit software versions and model-training recipe are no longer supplied.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates image classification on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny ImageNet. v2 retains these datasets and adds ModelNet40 point-cloud classification using PointNets (Tables 1 and 4), substantially extending the represented data and application domain.

E2.justification: DeepCert, VeriNet, and Newise evaluations disappear. v2 adds evaluated comparisons with 3DCertify, MN-BaB, ERAN, α, β-CROWN, MaxLin, and MaxPool2ReLU. DeepPoly is removed from the CNN-Cert radius comparison but retained in separate accuracy comparisons. Appendix 7.5.2 clarifies that MaxPool2ReLU substitutes for unavailable OSIP code; OSIP itself was not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2's main evaluation uses fixed-radius certified accuracy on correctly classified properties selected from the first 100 inputs, versus v1's average bounds on 10 random images. It adds PGD reference bounds, timeout rates, and verifier-specific protocols. The retained 10-input CNN-Cert experiment changes its stated initial search radius from 0.05 to 0.005. The general 180-second timeout statement conflicts with the 3,600-second BaB setting.

E4.justification: v2 adds output-bound comparisons across 100 inputs, a MaxLin-versus-Ti-Lin trajectory over BaB rounds, and Hybrid-Lin comparisons under CROWN and α-CROWN (Appendix 7.5.3–7.5.4, Figures 3–6). These new analyses investigate when neuron-wise bounds help and how the two bounding approaches complement each other; they are absent from v1.

E5.justification: v1 Section 4.6 and Table 10 report Wilcoxon/Mann–Whitney testing at significance level 0.05 with dataset-specific comparator p-values. v2 removes this statistical validation without replacement significance tests or confidence intervals. Neither version documents repeated-run or seed-based uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: S-shaped comparison tables disappear, while certified-accuracy, PointNet, timeout, and Hybrid-Lin results are added. For the four-layer CIFAR-10 CNN under l1 perturbation, v1 Table 8 reports Ti-Lin's bound as 0.07137, whereas v2 Table 5 reports 0.03029 under revised settings. New Table 3 reports 85.7% versus 7.1% accuracy against α, β-CROWN on CIFAR-10's six-layer CNN: a 78.6 percentage-point gap, not a cross-version gain.

M1.justification: v2 removes v1's dedicated S-shaped activation bounding construction and introduces Hybrid-Lin, which selects Ti-Lin or MaxLin according to the ReLU bound form (Appendix 7.5.4). The underlying MaxPool coefficients are largely retained through reorganized cases, while selecting the three largest upper bounds replaces sorting all interval endpoints.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methodological narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before preliminaries, research-question-based experiments become verifier-family-based sections, and the standalone threats-to-validity section disappears. The appendix is reorganized into numbered proofs, experimental settings, and additional analyses.

P2.justification: The original S-shaped illustration and network-propagation diagram are replaced by MaxPool geometry and four-case illustrations. v2 adds four analytical figures and restructures tables around certified accuracy, runtime, timeouts, and verifier families. CNN-Cert results are consolidated into appendix Table 5; the notation and p-value tables disappear. Headers, typography, and table styling also change substantially.

R1.justification: The activation-by-activation positioning is replaced by a broader discussion of MaxPool verification, attacks, and certified defenses. New substantive comparisons address OSIP, MN-BaB, modern CROWN frameworks, and especially MaxLin's block-wise tightness. Previously described as unsuitable for image perturbations, 3DCertify becomes a central comparator for both image and point-cloud evaluations.

T1.justification: v1's S-shaped bounds theorem and proof, standalone ReLU theorem, and layer-wise/network-wise formal treatment are removed. v2 retains the central MaxPool midpoint and diagonal-endpoint arguments, but expands case-coverage reasoning in Appendix 7.1 and adds explicit computational-complexity analysis. The theoretical scope changes substantially despite preservation of the core MaxPool guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the retained MaxPool contribution beyond v1's single-framework evaluation. Public image and point-cloud benchmarks across several verifier families, detailed experimental settings, and analyses explaining Ti-Lin/MaxLin complementarity address important gaps in generality and mechanism evidence. The narrower contribution and removal of significance testing are tradeoffs; conflicting timeout descriptions and OSIP claims based on a substitute remain weaknesses. Nevertheless, the broader controlled validation and substantive explanatory analyses provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Ti-Lin and share the central MaxPool bounding construction, despite substantial changes in title and scope. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original verification experiments across multiple frameworks and four datasets, including new PointNet evaluations and appendix analyses of Hybrid-Lin.

before.justification: v1 reports original certified robustness bounds, runtimes, and statistical comparisons on CNNs evaluated using MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny ImageNet.

results.title:
Tightening Robustness Verification of MaxPool-based Neural Networks via
  Minimizing the Over-Approximation Zone

C1.justification: v2 explicitly limits its stated research scope to implicit representations, distinguishing the contribution from Gaussian-splatting approaches. The central claims of image-only, three-stage glossy-object reconstruction and superior geometry/material reconstruction remain. Its stronger emphasis on joint surface and volume rendering describes a component already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 proposes model complexity and training instability as explanations for specular-albedo-related lighting degradation, clarifies that Stage 1 colors are not a physical BRDF, and discusses Fresnel-versus-texture tradeoffs. Appendix G explains limited DTU97 gains through the small proportion of glossy regions, replacing v1's broader smooth-surface restriction while retaining fine-detail limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices B and E newly disclose grayscale Stage 1 specular radiance, NeRF++ background modeling, the default Fresnel value, the Glossy loss weight, and 32 visibility-sampling directions. Architecture, schedules, hardware, and training-time information largely remain. Conversely, v1's explicit image resolutions and several view/train/test counts are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds the 13-scene Glossy benchmark, covering real and synthetic reflective objects, and extends DTU evaluation from four glossy scenes to 15 scenes including regular objects. Figure 22 additionally evaluates relighting under changed illumination. The original four datasets remain represented.

E2.justification: NeRO is added to existing geometry comparisons and IndiSG material comparisons. Ref-NeuS, previously only discussed, is evaluated in Figure 7. Figures 9 and 25 introduce UniSDF and Ref-NeRF/S3-NeRF-based architectural comparisons. Original principal baselines remain; Figure 18's inconsistent replacement labels do not establish additional material-baseline evaluations.

E3.justification: Added controlled experiments introduce auxiliary SfM point-cloud/image-pair supervision and a Fresnel comparison of 0.02 versus 0.75, alongside an indirect-illumination removal condition. The retained evaluations preserve Chamfer distance, foreground PSNR, and the reported 300K/40K training budgets. Newly disclosed default settings are distinguished from these experimental interventions.

E4.justification: v2 adds indirect-light removal tests, auxiliary-supervision comparisons, rendering-architecture alternatives, and Fresnel sensitivity analysis (Table 3, Table 7, Figures 9 and 24–26). Figure 13 extends surface-reconstruction ablations to additional objects. The original specular-albedo, visibility, and surface-component ablations remain, including relocated or renamed presentations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Reported means aggregate scene results rather than repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: Many quantitative and qualitative results are added, while matched entries from v1 Tables 2–4 remain unchanged in v2 Tables 1, 3, and 4. New results include a 15-scene DTU mean Chamfer distance of 0.76 versus NeuS's 0.83, and a Glossy mean of 0.0044 versus NeRO's 0.0033. Additional results document indirect-light, supervision, architecture, and Fresnel effects.

M1.justification: The core three-stage pipeline and principal losses remain. Appendix F.2 adds an evaluated adaptation incorporating Geo-NeuS point-cloud and image-pair supervision. Stage 3 also describes the BRDF as Ward rather than Disney; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects an implementation change or a corrected description.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are substantially condensed and revised. Preliminaries, implementation details, detailed training equations, Stage 2 explanations, and limitations move into organized appendices, while the main method and experimental narrative are restructured. Ablation terminology and author/header information also change.

P2.justification: The opening figures are merged, the pipeline diagram gains Stage 2, existing comparison grids are split or relocated, and numerous new figures and tables are introduced. Table ordering, highlighting, and page layout change extensively. Some edits introduce errors: Figure 3's caption reverses dataset sides, and Figure 18 assigns inconsistent method labels to retained material panels.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates the research context through discussion of Gaussian-splatting reconstruction and inverse rendering, explicitly motivating continued work on implicit representations. It adds NeRO, UniSDF, S3-NeRF, Ward, and other references with substantive connections to the method and comparisons. The earlier capabilities survey table is removed.

T1.justification: Appendix E, Equation 27, newly specifies the visibility–Spherical Gaussian approximation through illumination-weighted visibility scaling of the lobe amplitude, previously left implicit in the product notation. Most earlier rendering and loss equations are retained or relocated. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central glossy-reconstruction claims through relevant reflective-object baselines, the Glossy benchmark, regular DTU scenes, and targeted component and sensitivity tests. The new evidence also exposes a boundary: NeRO performs better on Glossy overall. These gains address important comparison and generalization gaps in v1 and outweigh the loss of some dataset details and newly introduced figure-label/reference errors, although those errors reduce clarity and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Factored-NeuS and contain readable text, equations, tables, and figures. The shared methods and experiments can be matched despite extensive reorganization. v1 has no separate appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–G, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F retain original experiments and add Glossy evaluations, broader DTU results, additional baseline comparisons, and controlled ablations.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original reconstruction and inverse-rendering experiments on DTU, SK3D, Shiny, and IndiSG, including quantitative results and component ablations.

results.title:
Factored-NeuS: Reconstructing Surfaces, Illumination, and Materials of
  Possibly Glossy Objects

C1.justification: The original four-photon resolution and approximately 3–4 dB improvement claims remain. v3 adds prominent claims of approximately fourfold frame reduction and CRB matching over a wider flux range, and broadens the contribution toward low-latency, high-resolution inverse imaging and other multiplexed detector models.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations connecting negative bias and CRB departures to omitted coincidence events and spatial flux patterns, explains the deliberate omission of spatial priors, and discusses blockwise processing and computational limits. Its revised large-array experiment is interpreted as showing increasing benefit, whereas v1 discussed declining MSE-reduction factors over smaller arrays; the experimental settings differ.

D1.justification: v3 documents fixed sensor area, fixed maximum flux, and computation-scaling considerations for the resolution study. Conversely, it omits the explicit source flux of 10 PPF stated in v1 Section 4.2. Neither version supplies implementation code, simulation hardware specifications, or measured runtimes.

E1.justification: The simulated row–column intensity-imaging task remains unchanged. v3 replaces BU-logo examples with a moon image, applies the rotation test to the flower, and adds controlled one-, two-, and three-bright-pixel ground truths in supplementary Figure 10.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates the naive and single-photon estimators alongside multiphoton variants. v3 adds random assignments, a multiphoton-unambiguous estimator that retains unambiguous multiphoton detections, and full readout in supplementary Figure 11. Fully addressed readout also participates in the new frame-budget comparison.

E3.justification: The array-size evaluation changes from 2–32 rows in v1 Figure 7 to 4–512 rows in v3 Figure 8, where fixed sensor area and maximum flux are specified. v3 also introduces a frame-count sweep targeting MSE 0.01 and detection-probability evaluations against the CRB. The main image comparisons retain 32×32 images and 100,000 frames.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained photon-count truncation, flux, and rotation analyses, v3 adds explicit bias–variance decomposition, frame-efficiency analysis, and CRB comparisons examining sensitivity to spatial flux patterns. The array-scaling analysis is substantially revised and extended. These test important questions absent from v1's reported analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 Monte Carlo trials for the main image-reconstruction comparisons. v3 adds no seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or explicit change in repetition counts. Its variance and CRB curves are additional analyses of estimator behavior.

E6.justification: Shared flower and coins PSNR values in Figure 3 are retained, while logo results are replaced and new results are added. Reported optimal PPF values change, including SPE 0.9 to 0.83 and the two-photon estimator 0.7 to 1; these are revised operating points, not established same-setting gains. New Figure 6 reports 25,000 ME versus 100,000 SPE frames for MSE 0.01, and Figure 11 shows full readout outperforming ME.

M1.justification: The operational estimator is retained: single-photon estimates determine conditional weights for allocating ambiguous detections, with coincidence modeling truncated at four photons. v1's Eq. (19) matches v3's Eq. (15) after notation changes; the supplementary general formulation documents the same procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and estimator exposition are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces a standalone Related Work section, reorganizes the measurement model, restructures the results narrative, and places expanded derivations and analyses in a separate supplement.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document to a two-column layout, substantially redraws Figure 1, and revises the event schematic. It consolidates earlier flux-comparison plots, reorganizes reconstruction panels, and adds figures for frame requirements, CRB comparisons, bias–variance behavior, and additional baselines.

R1.justification: v3 adds a substantial Related Work section covering multiplexed reconstruction in PET, ultrasound, and gamma-ray imaging, and identifies van den Berg et al.'s deterministic group-testing approach as closely related. The introduction also positions temporal histogram and sketching methods as complementary. v1 mainly situated the contribution among SNSPD hardware developments.

T1.justification: v1's approximate 2×2 naive-bias calculation and Taylor-based SPE argument are replaced by a general naive-bias expression and a conditional unbiasedness proof. v3 also adds a formal general estimator formulation and Fisher-information/CRB derivations. The new derivation contains an error: supplementary Eq. (34) incorrectly squares M9 when differentiating Eq. (33).

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for practical usefulness through more informative baselines, frame-efficiency tests, and larger-array evaluations, addressing important limitations of v1's validation. General bias results and clearer exposition also improve understanding. These gains outweigh the added shortcomings, although supplementary Eq. (34) needs correction and the claim of highest PSNR across all baselines contradicts Figure 11's superior full-readout results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, authors, measurement model, and multiphoton estimator despite the changed title. All 13 pages of v1 and 14 pages of v3, including v3's supplementary material, support reliable comparison. v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: Section 5 and the supplement report original simulation results, including image reconstruction, frame-budget experiments, larger-array evaluations, bias–variance analyses, and additional baseline comparisons.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figures 3–7 report original Monte Carlo image-reconstruction experiments, photon-flux sweeps, estimator comparisons, and array-size analyses.

results.title: Image Reconstruction from Readout-Multiplexed Single-Photon Detector Arrays

C1.justification: The introduction expands the claimed use to regularization during training and explicitly claims superiority over eikonal regularization strategies. The central high-frequency-noise diagnosis, polynomial-fitting approach, and self-supervised fine-tuning contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets GAD's comparable accuracy as evidence for neighborhood aggregation, explains warm-start dependence through initial field quality, and expands training-versus-query cost discussion. Existing limitations involving smoothing-scale selection and low-frequency SIREN errors remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 newly specifies 2^18 surface samples and barycentric interpolation of mesh normals and curvatures. v2 also supplies eikonal weights and search ranges, SIREN architecture parameters, and fine-tuning time estimates. These supplement substantial implementation information already present in v1.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds rendering evaluations on a large-scale scene and specular Lucy. The original FamousShape, image, collision, and advection coverage remains; the restored Serapis table row does not establish a new evaluated shape.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Gaussian-averaged autodiff (GAD), stochastic finite differences (SFD), and its 256-sample variant. Table 2 adds Eikonal and FD-Eikonal regularization comparisons. These substantially broaden the central comparisons beyond the original autodiff, finite-difference, and unmodified-network controls.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a 500-step Armadillo study with 0, 50, 100, or 200 warm-start steps and an 800-step fine-tuning control, plus additional SIREN frequencies and widths. Original benchmark settings remain. Appendix A.5 newly documents evaluation-point construction without establishing a change to the original protocol.

E4.justification: Appendix F and Figure 14 add a substantive study of warm-start duration, optimization failure without warm-starting, and training-budget tradeoffs. Appendix E adds SIREN parameter sensitivity checks, and Appendix B.3 expands training-cost analysis. Earlier neighborhood-size, smoothing-scale, and Marching Cubes analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same runtime means and standard deviations from seven runs of 1,000 calls, and collision averages over one million trials. No new seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance-testing practice is introduced.

E6.justification: Original numerical entries are retained, while v2 adds baseline scores, the missing Serapis row, training-cost findings, and Figures 14–15. GAD has lower angular error than the proposed operator on Dense Grid and Tri-plane. Figure 14 reports 90.19° without warm-starting versus 1.83° with 200 warm-start steps. Section 4.1 also introduces an incorrect fourfold-over-FD statement.

M1.justification: The polynomial-fitting operators and consistency-plus-gradient fine-tuning loss remain unchanged. The training-from-scratch discussion uses the existing pretrain, freeze, and fine-tune sequence with different stage budgets; the new experiments examine this allocation rather than introduce a different operator or loss.

P1.justification: The introduction and closing discussion are substantially rewritten, with additional revisions to method and experimental explanations. Experiments gain numbered subsections, limitations and conclusions become separate sections, and Appendix B is organized into named subsections.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, relocates figures and detailed tables, expands Tables 1–2, and adds Figures 14–15. Existing displays also change, including Figure 2's axis labels and Figure 12's panel arrangement; these exceed simple renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through a new discussion of numerical differentiation of noisy signals, differentiable graphics estimators, and point-cloud regularization. It also relates fine-tuning to Sobolev training and adds the corresponding references and distinctions from prior approaches.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations and reasoning are retained, with no new proofs or substantive derivations. Describing the symmetric Hessian through its lower triangle and identifying least squares as a closed-form convex problem explain equivalent existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens comparative validation by adding closely related smoothing and regularization alternatives and acknowledging GAD's competitive performance. The warm-start failure study and explicit ground-truth construction also improve scientific interpretation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh a localized new reporting error: Section 4.1 claims a fourfold normal-error reduction over FD, although Table 1's unchanged 4.20° and 2.80° values support only 1.5-fold.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, core methods, and experiments. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, warm-start experiments, and rendering examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original normal and curvature evaluations, rendering experiments, collision and PDE simulations, and additional image and runtime results in its appendices.

results.title: Accurate Differential Operators for Hybrid Neural Fields

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a room-scale system and dataset combining body, finger, and articulated-object motion. v2 replaces the stated contribution of introducing future research tasks with presenting two example generative applications, and softens v1's categorical uniqueness language. The core research objective remains stable.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations about blending locomotion and manipulation, coordinate-representation tradeoffs, and reconstruction failures attributed to occlusion and articulation. Synthetic RGB generation substantially extends the applicability discussion beyond v1's warning about biased captured images. Appendix B.1 also explicitly acknowledges that markers can influence natural human motion.

D1.justification: v2 adds FABRIK/autoencoder fitting details, image-generation inputs, and object-motion training settings, including AdamW, learning rate 0.0001, 1500 epochs, and batch size 32. Data availability changes from promised to reported public availability. Conversely, the full action list, scenario-construction details, and detailed contact-computation documentation from v1 are removed.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates capture accuracy and home-interaction data. v2 additionally uses HumanML3D for motion-generation training and AMASS for body-model fitting, and evaluates text-conditioned motion, object-guided motion, and hand/object reconstruction from synthetic images. These substantially expand actual training and task coverage beyond the retained room and 22 objects.

E2.justification: The original capture-system comparators remain. v2 adds comparisons of single-dataset versus mixed-data motion models and models with versus without relative spatial cues (Tables 2-3). Tables 7-8 add IST-Net/GenPose++ and Pose2Mesh/HaMeR comparison rows; IST-Net and Pose2Mesh appear only on reference datasets, not ParaHome.

E3.justification: v2 introduces balanced HumanML3D/ParaHome training, evaluation on a mixed test set, 30/60/90-frame motion windows, and new generation/reconstruction metrics. Collection increases from 30 participants and 440 minutes to 38 and 486. The virtual-marker criterion is also rephrased from four markers tracked throughout a window to four tracked in every frame; whether its implementation changed is unstated.

E4.justification: New analyses test training-data mixture, relative spatial conditioning, body representation, temporal window length, and text conditioning for image synthesis (Tables 2-3 and 9; Figure 13). Figures 14-15 add occlusion failure cases. Original capture robustness tests remain, while v1's per-object contact-frequency analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's additional tables retain point-estimate reporting; diffusion noise definitions do not constitute experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original measurements, including reprojection errors of 1.021/1.016 pixels and 11 mm hand-alignment error, remain unchanged. New Tables 2-3 and 7-9 report generation and reconstruction outcomes, including mixed-training FID 0.85 and lower position errors but greater foot skating with spatial conditioning. These are new experiments, not v1-to-v2 performance gains. v1's contact-ratio table is removed.

M1.justification: v2 adds implemented generative procedures beyond v1's prospective task formulations: MDM-based text-conditioned motion generation with latent interpolation, an object-conditioned transformer, and ControlNet-based RGB synthesis. It also introduces learned SMPL-X fitting using an autoencoder and latent optimization (Sections 3.5 and 5; Appendix C.5).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related work are extensively rewritten. Capture and acquisition material is consolidated into Section 3, validation precedes the expanded generative-modeling section, and dataset documentation is reorganized in the appendix. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 merges setup/marker, object/articulation, and body/hand-calibration figures, and rearranges the retained system plots. It adds fitting, generation, architecture, and failure-case displays. The dataset comparison changes from frame counts to hours and revises its rows; original action/contact tables and extensive contact visualizations are removed.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially into hybrid capture and recent motion/interaction synthesis, including MDM, DiffH2O, Text2HOI, and InterTrack. The dataset comparison replaces several older hand-focused datasets with Chairs, NeuralDome, OAKINK2, TACO, and TRUMANS. v1's first-dataset and frame-count superiority positioning is also softened.

T1.justification: Formal content expands from generic HOI mappings and capture-calibration objectives to conditional diffusion distributions, denoising losses, latent interpolation, object-conditioned motion mappings, and SMPL-X latent-fitting optimization. Existing articulation derivations largely remain. The substantial addition concerns mathematical formulations; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1's generative-modeling motivation is largely prospective. v2 supplies implemented tasks, quantitative evaluations, and targeted ablations (Section 5; Tables 2-3 and 9), substantially strengthening evidence for downstream utility. Added fitting and synthetic-image evaluations further support usability. Removed scenario/contact documentation and the inconsistent 207 versus 208 capture counts weaken reproducibility, but do not outweigh the substantial evidentiary gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ParaHome system and dataset. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, added, and removed material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains capture-system experiments and adds original motion-generation results, ablations, and pose-reconstruction evaluations on synthesized images.

before.justification: v1 reports original capture-system experiments, including marker tracking, reprojection errors, hand alignment, tracking recovery, and dataset contact statistics.

results.title:
ParaHome: Parameterizing Everyday Home Activities Towards 3D Generative
  Modeling of Human-Object Interactions

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes hardware-friendly sparse large-kernel replacement, computational savings, and ImageNet superiority. v2 reframes the contribution around separating feature-extraction granularity from multi-path dependency modeling, explicitly claims successful replacement with 3×3 convolutions, and broadens its superiority claims to classification, segmentation, and detection.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting shuffled paths to feature utilization, reparameterization effects to sparsity initialization, and pruning patterns to stage transitions. Appendices A–E explicitly acknowledge slower throughput than optimized competitors, an unoptimized operator, unresolved hyperparameter interactions, and resource-limited scaling. These substantially qualify v1's emphasis on efficiency and future optimization.

D1.justification: v2 adds extensive training disclosures covering optimizer, learning rate, augmentation, batch size, pruning settings, architecture dimensions, and eight 4090D GPUs (Table 8). Appendices A–B document inference precision, software versions, and the atomicAdd-based implementation. The repository link is retained. Unlike v1's throughput caption, v2 does not specify the inference batch size.

E1.justification: ImageNet-1K classification is retained. v2 additionally evaluates COCO object detection and instance segmentation, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and nuScenes monocular 3D detection (Section 4, Tables 4–6). These substantially extend the tasks and represented domains.

E2.justification: The ImageNet comparison adds FastViT, PVTv2, CoAtNet, DeiT III, SwinV2, HorNet, and ConvNeXt-S, while removing Swin-T, CSwin-T, and InternImage-T from that comparison (Table 3 in both versions). v2 also separately compares standard, reparameterized, and optimized SLaK implementations in its throughput evaluation.

E3.justification: Both versions use 120- and 300-epoch ImageNet experiments, but v2 changes the default padding from N−1 to N//2 and adds explicitly retuned final training configurations and small-model evaluations. New downstream protocols use Cascade Mask R-CNN for 36 epochs, UPerNet for 160,000 iterations, and FCOS3D with a 1x schedule.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's padding/reparameterization experiments and first-layer pruning analysis, v2 tests kernel granularity, shuffled paths, branch counts, mask synchronization, depth versus width, SE, ghost channels, and sparsity (Tables 1, 2, 9). It also adds feature-utilization analysis, pruning profiles across layers, COCO case studies, and effective-receptive-field comparisons.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for performance. v2's pruning distributions characterize trained model structure rather than estimate experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: The 81.36% and 81.26% padding results are retained, but v2 adds 300-epoch SW-tiny/small accuracies of 83.4%/83.9%, downstream results, and numerous ablation findings. SW-small ties UniRepLKNet-S on ImageNet and trails it on COCO and ADE20K. v1's single-operator timings disappear, while v2 reports full-model throughput. These are largely new results under revised conditions, not same-setting gains.

M1.justification: v1 already includes shifting, coarse pruning, ghost channels, and reparameterization. v2 introduces multiple shuffled feature-fusion paths and altered sparsity initialization/mask-sharing procedures. Its final architecture uses 3×3 instead of 5×5 kernels, incorporates SE, deepens the tiny backbone, and replaces the stride-4 stem with two stride-2 convolutions (Sections 3.5–3.9).

P1.justification: The title changes from Shift-ConvNets to ShiftwiseConv, and the abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The original method/theory organization becomes a nine-part architecture-development narrative, followed by separate results and analysis sections and Appendices A–F.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column presentation. Background schematics are removed, retained module concepts are redrawn, and tables are substantially reorganized. New displays include the retinal analogy, feature-utilization plots, pruning profiles, downstream comparisons, training configurations, COCO predictions, and receptive-field visualizations.

R1.justification: The literature discussion is substantially refocused: many earlier multiscale, segmentation, and deformable-kernel references disappear, while PeLK, ShiftViT, receptive-field research, retinal organization, and new evaluation methods are added. v2 develops a substantive contrast between its data-driven connections and PeLK's manually designed peripheral structure, emphasizing granularity and connectivity over hardware compatibility.

T1.justification: v1's generalized focus-length/focus-width operator definition and Equation 3 are removed, alongside the explicit cost-ratio derivations and approximation assumptions in Section 3.4. v2 retains basic decomposition reasoning and tabulated cost expressions, and adds relations such as R(1−G)=1 and the 2E+1 movement bound, but substantially reduces the original formal treatment.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation and reproducibility: it directly tests major design choices, demonstrates transfer beyond ImageNet, supplies detailed training settings, and candidly documents throughput and scaling limitations. These substantially strengthen the paper. The gains are tempered by lost formal derivations, omitted classification comparators, and overly broad superiority claims; notably, SW-small trails UniRepLKNet-S in Tables 4–5.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Shiftwise convolution research. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison despite extensive revision. v1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A–F.

after.justification: v2 reports original architecture ablations, classification and downstream-task results, throughput measurements, and qualitative analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet experiments, pruning measurements, computational comparisons, and operator timings in Section 4 and Tables 1–5.

results.title: $ShiftwiseConv:$ Small Convolutional Kernel with Large Kernel Effect

C1.justification: The central contribution remains continuous, subject-specific, compositional control through text-embedding directions without modifying the diffusion model. V2 drops v1's separate introductory contribution about extracting transferable semantic changes from a single image using reconstruction loss, foregrounding the two attribute-direction identification methods instead.

C2.justification: V2 adds specific qualifications about persistent color and animal-attribute leakage, rare success with spatial relations, and possible benefits of nonlinear modulations. Appendix A.2 explains leakage through inherited model behavior and attention interactions. V1 already discussed inherited limitations and global correlations, so these refine an existing interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C add training pseudocode, integration recipes, comparator implementations, detailed metric aggregation and timing procedures, and figure-by-figure prompts and image sources. V1's single-image delta-training recipe and explicit own-code availability statement are removed. Shared settings such as 1,000 training steps, batch size 10, and optimizer hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds inversion-based real-image editing and explicit color, spatial-relation, dog/cat, and postfix-attribute tests. V1 instead used real photographs for its now-removed single-image semantic-delta learning experiments. Human, vehicle, furniture, and most noun-transfer and compositional coverage remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated AdapEdit and MasaCtrl comparisons and quantitative benchmarking against adjectives, Concept Sliders, and Prompt-to-Prompt in Table 1. V1 primarily compared its own variants quantitatively and demonstrated competitors qualitatively. Appendix A.1 also adds direct-guidance and noise-direction approximation alternatives; v1's capability table does not constitute equivalent evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: V1 reports 100 images per attribute and scale; v2 specifies 50-portrait disentanglement evaluations and 50 two-person samples for specificity. New protocols include clipped bounding-box specificity ratios, normalized change slopes, 20-by-20 attribute-coverage grids, and measured runtime. PixArt-α/T5 and SDXL Turbo introduce additional model settings; SD1.5 and aMUSEd transfer already appeared in v1.

E4.justification: V2 adds ablations of scale variation, direct CLIP embeddings, direct guidance, and noise-direction averaging, plus challenging-attribute and embedding-perturbation analyses. It removes the single-image learning/transfer case study and two age–makeup composition grids. Most noun-transfer, multi-subject, and continuous-modulation appendix analyses are retained and reorganized.

E5.justification: V2 adds an explicitly documented statistical density analysis: Figure 6 and Appendix B.3 use 20 samples per scale, matched generation seeds, and Gaussian kernel density estimation with Scott's rule. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty across repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and A add substantial numerical results, including standalone specificity of 3.35 and runtime of 12.0 seconds, and normalized LPIPS of 0.31 for the no-scale ablation versus 0.10 for the full method. V1's DINOv2 curves and several qualitative results disappear. These are added or replaced evaluations, not established same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The specified training target changes substantively: v1 Eqs. 4–5 use the neutral model prediction plus a contrastive prediction difference; v2 Eq. 4 and Algorithm 1 use sampled noise plus a predicted noise difference. V2 also permits positive-versus-neutral contrasts and adds AdapEdit and ReNoise integration procedures. The two underlying direction-identification approaches remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method motivation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around specificity, disentanglement, continuity, and generalization; appendices are restructured into additional results, implementation details, and visualization documentation.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, replaces the capability table with quantitative comparisons, adds diagrams and evaluation plots, and merges earlier figures. Most appendix grids are retained but repacked, captions are revised, and unmodified-image highlighting changes from orange to green.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work around direction-based control, attention editing, and inversion. It adds discussion and citations for methods such as AdapEdit, MasaCtrl, ReNoise, and newer token-embedding studies, while removing the personalization discussion and references to Textual Inversion, DreamBooth, and Custom Diffusion.

T1.justification: V2 revises the mathematical training target and introduces a formal subject-specificity ratio in Eq. 6. Its identity-change and normalized-disentanglement definitions also change the evaluation formulation. Neither version develops theorems or proofs; much of the remaining mathematical rewriting is notation or explanation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central control claims: quantitative competitor and runtime comparisons replace reliance on largely qualitative competitive demonstrations, while new ablations, explicit failure cases, and detailed evaluation recipes improve validation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed single-image case study and DINOv2 plots. Mixed model backbones still limit some comparisons, and the revised protocols do not establish direct performance gains over v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite extensive restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original quantitative comparisons, ablations, runtime measurements, real-image editing examples, and additional model and attribute evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation experiments, quantitative LPIPS/DINOv2/identity comparisons, and appendix evaluations of transferability and compositional control.

results.title:
Continuous, Subject-Specific Attribute Control in T2I Models by
  Identifying Semantic Directions

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same central contributions: gyro-error-aware deblurring, refinement and deblurring blocks, a camera-motion embedding, curriculum training and synthetic/real datasets. Additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 explains the blocks through global versus spatial error correction and discusses why kernel-error-tolerant baselines struggle with large gyro errors. Its replacement moving-object case claims sharper backgrounds but comparable object quality, qualifying v1's stronger statement about sharpening both. The concluding limitations remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds Huawei dataset specifications, the inference timing resolution and details of metric configuration and baseline adaptation. It removes the explicit synchronization assumption, OpenCamera-Sensors access reference, metadata listing and PSNR-loss stabilizer specification. These are changes in documented reproducibility information, not evidence that the underlying collection or loss changed.

E1.justification: v3 adds GyroBlur-Real-H, containing 17 Huawei P30 Pro images, to test transfer beyond the Samsung Galaxy S22 used for synthetic-data construction. The original 100 Samsung images are retained as GyroBlur-Real-S. This is a limited expansion in device coverage within the same deblurring task.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds AdaRevD-B (NAFNet), INformer, Vasu et al. and Nan et al., while retaining the original comparators. The two non-blind methods substantially broaden comparison to approaches explicitly addressing kernel errors. The replacement moving-object comparison also omits EggNet, which appeared in v1 Figure 10.

E3.justification: v3 introduces quantitative real-image evaluation using NIQE and TOPIQ, where v1 used qualitative comparisons, and evaluates transfer to Huawei images after Samsung-based synthetic training. Newly evaluated non-blind baselines use patch-wise kernels to accommodate spatially varying blur. The original synthetic split and stated training budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a control removing image-guided refinement from both blocks, expands real-image component analysis and tests generalization across devices. It also replaces the moving-object example. The error-free training comparison and motion-field resolution sweep already existed; their consolidation or relocation is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: Neither supplied version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, performance uncertainty intervals or significance tests. v3 continues the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds baseline results and extensive real-image scores: the full model obtains NIQE/TOPIQ of 4.47/0.548 on Real-S and 4.94/0.521 on Real-H. Two matched ablation rows change from 26.64/0.7584 and 26.68/0.7588 in v1 Table 4 to 26.17/0.7465 and 26.32/0.7542 in v3 Table 2. Their cause is unspecified. The full model's original synthetic result remains 27.28 PSNR and 0.7803 SSIM.

M1.justification: The embedding and curriculum are retained, but block descriptions differ: v1 Section 3.2/Figure 3 includes a NAFBlock after spatial attention, whereas v3 Section 3.2/Figure 4 describes convolution and concatenation instead. Unchanged model-size figures do not resolve whether this reflects an architectural modification or revised documentation. Detailed supplementary architectures are unavailable.

P1.justification: Substantial rewriting and condensation affect the introduction, block explanations and dataset-generation narrative. The experiments are reorganized, with the separate noisy-training study incorporated into the ablations. Author and affiliation text changes, and acknowledgements are added. These edits extend beyond formatting or new experimental content.

P2.justification: The paper changes to a two-column layout, redraws the network and block diagrams, and expands tables to combine synthetic and real-image metrics. The dataset montage is removed; the real gyro-error illustration is adapted into the opening figure. Ablation displays are consolidated, the moving-object illustration is replaced, and a Huawei example is added.

R1.justification: v3 updates coverage with INformer, AdaRevD and image-quality assessment references. Section 2 replaces the earlier broad discussion of deconvolution priors with specific accounts of Vasu et al. and Nan et al., emphasizing their treatment of kernel errors. This refines the retained positioning around robust use of erroneous gyro data.

T1.justification: The homography construction, camera-motion-field definition, motion assumptions and clean/noisy field interpolation are retained. Neither supplied PDF presents theoretical propositions or proofs. Omitting v1's explicit formula for the retained PSNR loss reduces exposition without establishing changed mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central robustness claim through relevant kernel-error baselines, quantitative real-image evaluation and testing on an unseen device. v1's real-world evidence was qualitative and limited to the phone used for data synthesis. The more cautious moving-object interpretation also improves calibration. The Huawei test remains small and uses no-reference metrics; some reproducibility details are lost and block descriptions remain ambiguous. Nevertheless, the broader, more relevant empirical evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GyroDeblurNet, and their readable text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. All 18 pages of v1 and 10 pages of v3 were inspected. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix or the separately referenced supplementary material; that material cannot be assessed.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional real-image metrics, component ablations and evaluation on a second phone.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic benchmark results, real-image qualitative evaluations and ablations, including Tables 1–4.

results.title: Gyro-based Neural Single Image Deblurring

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list add MC++ as a primary benchmark contribution covering two to four concepts. This expands the paper's claimed contributions beyond the generation method. The principal claims about heterogeneous model integration, fidelity, and compositional generation remain.

C2.justification: v3 explains how poorly localized attention limits MCG and explicitly identifies identity mixing between similar subjects, with refinement proposed as mitigation. It also expands explanations involving feature leakage and embedding capacity. The original memory-use and shared-base-model limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the latent-update learning-rate schedule, gradient-step count, Cones 2 adaptation and regularization, benchmark prompt construction, and refinement pseudocode. However, it removes v1's hardware/precision disclosure and computational-cost Table 5. It also replaces the explicit ten-composition ablation description with an unspecified MC++ subset; this does not establish that the subset actually changed.

E1.justification: v1 quantitatively evaluates two-concept customization and includes isolated three-concept examples. v3's MC++ retains the original concepts and pairs while adding systematic evaluation of 57 three-concept and 14 four-concept compositions. The separate 276-prompt compositional-generation benchmark remains unchanged.

E2.justification: The customization comparison adds Textual Inversion and removes the separately reported Custom Diffusion Optimization variant. Custom Diffusion joint training, Mix-of-Show, and Cones 2 remain. The compositional-generation comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: Customization evaluation expands from 19,392 to 33,024 generated images, and new experiments introduce mask preprocessing, attention-grounding controls, and qualitative hyperparameter sweeps. Stable Diffusion 1.5, the evaluation metrics, 30 sampling steps, and 16 samples per prompt remain. The newly documented Cones 2 settings do not establish a change from v1's unspecified settings.

E4.justification: v3 adds attention-grounding ablation, guidance-weight and loss-weight sensitivity tests, Cones 2 regularization analysis, and identity-mixing/refinement case studies. It removes the first-model and prompt-prefix ablations and reworks the loss comparison. The final loss-ablation setting is ambiguously labeled: Table 4 indicates removal of Linter, while Figure 7 indicates removal of both losses.

E5.justification: Both versions report 16 samples per prompt with matched random seeds and present point estimates. Neither introduces confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or additional repeated-training-run reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds three-concept, four-concept, and overall results. Its two-concept MC2 scores change from 0.767/0.686/0.406 to 0.780/0.692/0.416 alongside the training augmentation. New four-concept results place Mix-of-Show above MC2 on DINO, 0.288 versus 0.268. Customization ablation and qualitative results also change, while Tables 2–3 retain the compositional-generation and user-study scores.

M1.justification: Although the original MCG framework remains, v3 Section 3.4 adds attention-grounding training using SAM-generated masks and two auxiliary losses adapted from TokenCompose. Supplementary Section 8 also introduces an optional mask-based refinement procedure that changes output merging; it is explicitly excluded from the default method.

P1.justification: The abstract and customization-results discussion are rewritten, the ablation discussion is shortened, and implementation material moves into the reorganized supplement. Authorship and affiliations also change. Much of the introduction, related work, core method explanation, and overall section sequence is retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column formatting to a two-column main paper and supplement. Figure 2 is redrawn, Table 1 gains concept-count groups, qualitative comparisons are rearranged and revised, and grounding, sensitivity, and refinement figures are added. The computational-cost table is removed.

R1.justification: Related work adds a limited discussion of extracting multiple concepts or attributes from one image, including Break-a-Scene. New methodological citations include TokenCompose and SAM/Grounded SAM, while Gen4Gen and Prompt-to-Prompt disappear. The broader research positioning remains.

T1.justification: v3 adds formal definitions of the attention-grounding losses in Equations 12–13 and mask-weighted merging in Equation 14. The original diffusion and MCG mathematics remains, with no new theorem, proof, or substantial revision of its derivation.

improvement.justification: MC++ addresses v1's explicitly acknowledged lack of systematic evaluation beyond two concepts. The added grounding ablation, sensitivity tests, and identity-mixing failures substantially strengthen evidence about when the method works and why it fails. These gains outweigh the lost computational-cost reporting and weaker ablation documentation, although the unspecified subset and inconsistent loss-ablation labels remain material weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MC2 and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and supplementary material. The comparison includes v1's Appendices A–E and v3's supplementary Sections 6–11; retained content can be matched across substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds MC++ evaluations, attention-grounding ablations, sensitivity analyses, and refinement examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original customized and compositional generation experiments, ablations, computational measurements, and a 28-participant user study.

results.title: MC$^2$: Multi-concept Guidance for Customized Multi-concept Generation

C1.justification: The compiler remains the central contribution, but the claimed joint-optimization contribution changes from MCTS to genetic search. V2 adds a distinct third contribution: procedural Gaussian modeling for recovering appearance and fine detail while supporting editing and sharing information between repeated parts.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of GeoCode's synthetic-to-real failure, coordinate descent's local minima, and occlusion recovery through shared Gaussians. Supplementary Section 1.1 explains why hidden cabinet structure and noisy bookshelf segmentation prevent meaningful quantitative evaluation. Section 1.3 qualifies the Gaussian study's sample selection. Existing small-detail and hand-designed-expressiveness limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 supplies detailed graph implementation, parameter ranges, genetic population/mutation/refinement settings, and Gaussian initialization, learning rates and 1000-iteration optimization. It also documents baseline architecture and 10,000 synthetic training instances. V1 promises future code release; v2 states public availability. The referenced but unavailable v1 supplement cannot be checked for earlier disclosures.

E1.justification: V2 adds procedural appearance reconstruction/editing and semantic point-cloud part segmentation. Its table evaluations include integrated cabinets, explicitly excluded in v1 Section 5.4 and Figure 6. Synthetic furniture coverage remains; cabinets also retain a qualitative ScanNet example despite no longer receiving quantitative real-data evaluation.

E2.justification: The reported comparisons change from Random SP and MCTS variants in v1 Tables 1–2 to GeoCode and coordinate descent, each with and without refinement, alongside genetic variants in v2. GeoCode was previously discussed but not evaluated in the available v1 results. Supplementary Figure 4 adds a qualitative vanilla Gaussian-splatting comparison.

E3.justification: The principal real-data evaluation changes from 276 objects across four categories to 176 across three, adding continuous-parameter annotations and errors. Chamfer evaluation changes from SCANnotate CAD annotations to ground-truth program-generated shapes. Synthetic validation changes from 100 rendered scenes per category to 300 complete-point-cloud scenes. Gaussian evaluation introduces 10 selected samples with 20 training and 10 validation views each.

E4.justification: V1's MCTS exploitation-term ablation disappears. V2 evaluates refinement across genetic search, GeoCode and coordinate descent, and adds Gaussian initialization-versus-optimization analysis, qualitative occlusion comparisons with vanilla Gaussian splatting, and a semantic-part segmentation case study in the supplement.

E5.justification: The available contents of both PDFs report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. V2's mutation-noise standard deviation specifies the algorithm rather than experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: V1's MCTS result tables are replaced by genetic-search and baseline results. V2 Table 1 reports refined Chamfer distances of 0.11 m for genetic search, 0.16 m for coordinate descent and 0.21 m for GeoCode. New Gaussian results show initialization-to-final PSNR of 31.1 to 36.74 and LPIPS of 0.06 to 0.03. Changed methods, samples and references prevent interpreting these as comparable v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: V1's MCTS search becomes a genetic algorithm with crossover, mutation and gradient refinement. The depth/normal render-and-compare objective becomes point-cloud, occlusion-grid and floor losses. V2 also introduces shared, trainable Gaussian primitives and staged appearance optimization while retaining the core Blender-to-PyTorch compiler.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, search description and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Compiler subsections are consolidated, synthetic validation moves into the supplement, and main-text validation is reorganized around baseline implementations and real-object parameters. V2 adds a separately structured implementation and evaluation supplement.

P2.justification: The document switches from single-column to two-column layout, replaces overview/search graphics, and adds tables with six method/variant columns plus extensive Gaussian and segmentation displays. Existing illustrations are matched: v1 Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 2, and v1 Figure 2 becomes Supplementary Figure 8. Supplementary Table 4 contains duplicated discrete-parameter rows.

R1.justification: The CAD-retrieval and shape-program literature review largely retains its framing. V2 adds neurosymbolic-graphics and Gaussian-splatting references, including SuGaR and depth regularization, removes MCTS-focused references, and sharpens its positioning against GeoCode's real-data generalization.

T1.justification: The mathematical specification is substantially replaced: v1's standard and shared-score UCB formulations disappear, while v2 defines occlusion-grid and floor penalties, discrete/continuous mutation rules, and Gaussian consistency and regularization objectives in Equations 1–8. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of parameter recovery: v1 relies on discrete real-data annotations, CAD-shape proxies and mostly internal comparisons, whereas v2 adds continuous ground truth, GeoCode/coordinate-descent comparisons and refinement controls. The included supplement also substantially improves implementation transparency, and the Gaussian extension receives concrete evaluation. The smaller real-data study, selected ten-sample Gaussian evaluation, and conflicting duplicate cabinet results in Supplementary Table 4 limit confidence, but the validation and documentation gains remain substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PyTorchGeoNodes, and their supplied text, equations, figures and tables are readable. However, v1 repeatedly references supplementary results and implementation details without including that supplement. V2 includes a ten-page supplement, so comparison of the earlier supplementary material is limited.

after.justification: V2 reports original reconstruction comparisons in main Table 1 and Supplementary Tables 2–5, plus Gaussian appearance experiments in Supplementary Table 1.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic cabinet reconstruction experiments in Table 1 and ScanNet sofa/chair parameter accuracy and Chamfer-distance results in Table 2.

results.title:
PyTorchGeoNodes: Enabling Differentiable Shape Programs for 3D Shape
  Reconstruction

C1.justification: Both versions claim a large, consistent object-addition dataset built by reversing inpainting, strong object-addition performance and benefits for general editing. v2 foregrounds general editing in its abstract and contribution list, but that claim already appears in v1's introduction, Section 6 and discussion.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific limitations involving distant shadows, reflections and object interactions, linking them to restricted changes during dataset construction. It also explains latent chaining and interprets the new trade-off and subgroup analyses. The earlier caveats about human-like instruction generation and unsuccessful reproduction of MagicBrush results disappear without an explicit resolution.

D1.justification: v2 documents filter-threshold calibration, stage-by-stage retention counts, guidance-sweep settings and implementation sources for new baselines. Conversely, it removes the specific Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 checkpoint link and explicit guidance equation. The principal hardware, optimization and fine-tuning details are retained.

E1.justification: The training datasets and principal evaluation benchmarks are retained. v2 adds a demonstrated sequential, multi-instruction editing scenario in Appendix C/Figure S10. Separately reporting addition and non-addition subsets does not introduce a new dataset or previously unrepresented task.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 3, v2 Table 2 adds Null-Text-Inversion, Pix2PixZero and Edit-Friendly DDPM to the MagicBrush comparison. Figure S20 additionally evaluates FLUX-based FlowEdit. Table S12 adds Hive as a human-survey comparator, whereas v1's survey compares only IP2P.

E3.justification: v2 adds CMMD, VQAScore and guidance-sweep evaluations. Object-addition CLIP-T reporting changes from instruction-derived local descriptions to target captions, with CLIP-T removed for PIPE and OPA. New evaluation designs include 500 manually classified inpainting outputs and separate addition/non-addition analyses; the main training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds filter-threshold sensitivity studies, consistency-versus-instruction trade-off curves, general-editing subgroup analysis, output-diversity examples and concrete failure cases. The instruction ablation is retained but revised: v1 Table 8 evaluates MagicBrush and OPA, while v2 Table S11 drops OPA and expands the MagicBrush metrics.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix A/Figure S9 newly reports three qualitative outputs generated using different seeds. Numerical benchmark comparisons retain the fixed-seed protocol, including seed 0. Neither version reports repeated-run means, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Numerous scores change: proposed-model PIPE CLIP-I is 0.962 in v1 Table 2 and 0.945 in v2 Table 3. Added Null-Text-Inversion leads MagicBrush L2 at 0.017 versus PIPE's 0.025, changing the comparator ranking. New metric, filtering, subgroup and Hive-survey results substantially expand the evidence. Metric changes prevent treating every numerical revision as a same-setting performance change.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix C introduces sequential object addition entirely in latent space, encoding before the first edit and decoding after the last to avoid repeated VAE degradation. The underlying dataset-generation pipeline, model architecture and training procedure remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Substantial portions of the introduction, related work, dataset explanation and evaluation narrative are rewritten and condensed. The appendices are reorganized, including moving general editing earlier and introducing dedicated multiple-object and limitations sections. This extends beyond renumbering or adding experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, merges v1's separate dataset-generation and training diagrams, and redraws the filtering illustration as panels. Qualitative examples move between the main text and appendices. New plots, tables and metric columns substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds related work including EraseDraw, Thinking Outside the BBox and video-based editing, plus references supporting new baselines, metrics and instruction-generation motivation. These update the research context and acknowledge later related approaches without substantially redefining the central positioning.

T1.justification: v1 Section 4 explicitly defines the combined text/image classifier-free-guidance score in Equation (1). v2 omits this mathematical expression rather than relocating it, while retaining the conditioning explanation. Neither version presents theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 Table S7 directly supports benefits on non-addition tasks, which v1 demonstrated through aggregate results and examples. Together with filter validation, broader baseline comparisons and specific failure analyses, this substantially strengthens the empirical case and clarifies applicability. Lost implementation details, unexplained score revisions and inconsistent CMMD direction labels are drawbacks, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Paint by Inpaint framework and PIPE dataset. Their main text, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and human-evaluation results and adds filtering analyses, further comparisons, subgroup results and qualitative experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on PIPE, MagicBrush and OPA, a human survey, general-editing experiments and an instruction ablation.

results.title: Paint by Inpaint: Learning to Add Image Objects by Removing Them First

C1.justification: The central claim that pretrained LMM contact knowledge improves pose refinement remains. v2 explicitly adds framework/failure analysis as a contribution and proposes contact-dataset annotation as an application. It drops v1's claim of applicability in principle to arbitrarily many people and reduces the abstract's emphasis on rivaling supervised state-of-the-art approaches.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's hallucination and chirality discussion, v2 interprets low raw-contact F1 alongside useful optimized poses, identifies improvement potential through the oracle, and discusses coarse-region limitations and prompt-dependent failures. Camera sensitivity receives an occlusion-based explanation. The earlier cultural-bias caveat is removed, while existing failure examples are retained.

D1.justification: v2 supplies alternative prompts, a GPT-4o version identifier, LLaVA temperature/top-p settings, runtime measurements, and an explicit code-access statement. It newly specifies that MOYO PCC uses 67 self-contact examples. Most optimizer and split details are relocated unchanged, while the slash-delimited region-parsing explanation and explicit loss-ablation controls are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four datasets and the same two-person interaction and single-person yoga self-contact settings. v2 quantifies viewpoint sensitivity already discussed in v1 and adds analyses within these settings. Harmony4D is newly cited but is not evaluated.

E2.justification: The original BEV, Heuristic, BUDDI, HMR2, and HMR2+opt comparisons are retained. v2 substantially expands the controls with BUDDI+ProsePose, a ground-truth coarse-contact Oracle, and two random-contact baselines using empirical contact frequencies, with and without left/right labels (Tables 1, 2, and 5).

E3.justification: v2 introduces direct contact-F1 evaluation with overlap matching and mesh-derived ground-truth thresholds, plus a five-sample validation protocol for prompt/model comparisons. It also revises reported Hi4D and CHI3D counts from approximately 247 and 504 to 241 and 431, and explicitly excludes keypoint-detection failures alongside BEV failures. These reporting revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic tests of explicit chirality, person labels, caption-based prompting, GPT-4o, and direct LLaVA prompting, together with oracle/random-contact controls, runtime analysis, quantified camera sensitivity, and additional failure cases. The original sampling study remains, and v1's loss-ablation Table 3 is retained numerically in v2's prose rather than removed.

E5.justification: Neither version provides repeated-experiment seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-to-run uncertainty estimates. LMM sample counts describe inference and ablation settings; the new camera-score range describes viewpoint variation, not uncertainty across repeated runs.

E6.justification: Most original ProsePose pose scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results for F1, hybrid/oracle methods, random-contact controls, prompt/model variants, camera views, and runtime. Table 1 newly reports ProsePose F1 values of 24, 13, and 23 on the two-person datasets. BUDDI's reported CHI3D average PCC changes from 78.6 to 78.0, and the 20/25 mm PCC result columns are removed.

M1.justification: The core ProsePose pipeline, contact losses, and two-stage optimization remain intact. v2 adds an evaluated BUDDI+ProsePose adaptation that incorporates the LMM loss into BUDDI (Section 4.1). Expanded explanations of canonicalization, chirality, and fallback handling do not independently establish changes to the default implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conclusion, and limitations are substantially rewritten around evaluating LMMs as contact-prediction tools. Related work is compressed, method subsections are reorganized, optimizer/MOYO details move to the appendix, and the appendix gains a reorganized analysis structure. The loss-ablation table becomes prose.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, replaces the opening illustration, combines the original method and notation figures, and rearranges qualitative panels. Tables gain F1 and new comparison rows while losing selected PCC columns; new prompt and failure illustrations appear. The final fifteen pages retain the same qualitative image assets with renumbering and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion covering CloseInt, language-based human-object reconstruction, Harmony4D, LLaVA-NeXT, and social-touch research. These broaden context and comparisons with prior approaches, while retaining the central positioning around using pretrained LMM knowledge without contact-supervised training.

T1.justification: The existing pose and optimization mathematics is retained without new proofs or theorems. v2 adds a task-specific definition for coarse-contact F1: region-overlap matching for precision/recall, ignoring chirality, and maximizing over the two person orderings (Section 4).

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrated final pose gains but left the accuracy and specificity of the LMM's contact predictions weakly tested. v2 addresses this important gap through direct F1 scoring, ground-truth and random-contact controls, and systematic prompt/model/viewpoint analyses. These substantially strengthen assessment of the central contribution and its limitations despite unchanged headline ProsePose scores. The gains outweigh lost per-radius results and weaker documentation of the retained loss ablation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ProsePose in 'Pose Priors from Language Models.' Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds contact-prediction scores, additional comparison methods, prompt/model analyses, camera-view analysis, and timing measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative and qualitative pose-reconstruction experiments on Hi4D, FlickrCI3D, CHI3D, and MOYO, including loss ablations, sampling analysis, and LLaVA experiments.

results.title: Pose Priors from Language Models

C1.justification: The central claims of an effective, imperceptible SSL attack based on disentangling trigger and augmentation distributions remain. V2 explicitly claims independence from matching pre-training and downstream distributions, while narrowing the claimed demonstrated coverage from seven SSL frameworks to six.

C2.justification: V2 extends the retained entanglement explanation through learned augmentation-space relaxation and interprets resistance to adaptive HSV defenses. It acknowledges CTRL's better LPIPS despite other disadvantages. The human-inspection discussion newly qualifies imperceptibility by admitting detectable color artifacts in Section A5.4.2 and Figure A9.

D1.justification: V2 supplies actual reference-input images in Figures A7–A8 and human-study preparation, randomization, and response-checking details. Most architecture, loss-weight, dataset-size, and training-budget information is retained. However, v1's explicit description of feature extractor M, with ResNet34 as an example, disappears from the stealth-loss explanation.

E1.justification: The five image datasets and existing classification tasks remain. V2 adds human discrimination between clean and backdoored ImageNet images and evaluation under HSV noise during downstream training and inference. These are bounded extensions of the evaluated population and input conditions; DINO's removal concerns model configuration.

E2.justification: V2 adds DRUPE to Table 1's retained BadEncoder-trigger comparisons. New Table 2 compares against POIENC, SSLBKD, SSLBKD-fixed, BLTO, and CTRL using their default attacks on matched CIFAR10 datasets. Stealthiness comparisons also expand substantially in Tables 3 and A9–A11; earlier citations to some methods did not constitute these evaluations.

E3.justification: V2 introduces matched CIFAR10 pre-training/downstream comparisons, FSIM and FID metrics, ASSET evaluation, and HSV perturbations during downstream training and inference. Its human study uses five trained participants and 50 clean plus 50 backdoored images per method. DINO's experimental configuration and augmentation column are removed. Most stated settings for retained experiments remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original component ablations, sensitivity plots, conventional noise tests, and feature visualizations are retained. V2 adds ASSET detection evaluation, adaptive HSV defenses in Table A7, quantitative feature-distribution trajectories using KL divergence in Table A8, and human inspection in Table A11. These substantially extend robustness and supporting analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-to-run variability. V2's participant count describes its new study design, without adding uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes the method's CIFAR10-to-STL10 BA/ASR from 74.48/95.00 to 74.02/99.68. V2 also revises several BYOL/SimSiam and stealthiness scores, corrects Beatrix counts, supplies previously absent CLIP baseline image-quality scores, and removes DINO results. Substantial new results include the additional comparisons, ASSET detection rates, adaptive-defense scores, KL trajectories, and a 49.5% overall human fooling rate. These reported revisions do not establish a changed attack method.

M1.justification: The renamed method retains the U-Net injector, disentanglement/alignment/stealth losses, injector pre-training, and alternating encoder/injector updates. V2's additional encoder minimization notation makes joint optimization explicit, but Algorithm 1 already performs these updates in v1.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, and analysis narrative, changes the title and method name, and reorganizes the appendices into Sections A1–A6. Background and settings move into the supplement, injector pre-training pseudocode moves into the main text, and standalone ethics, limitations, and broader-impact sections disappear.
