P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is redrawn and expanded, Table 1 gains comparator columns and averages, and the combined DECREE/Neural Cleanse table is split. New comparison and analysis tables, reference-input figures, and ImageNet examples are added. Existing noise, sensitivity, and feature plots are largely retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Sections 1–2 substantially recast positioning around training-controlled versus data-poisoning attacks and the claimed distribution restrictions of CTRL and BLTO. V2 adds works including BLTO and REFINE and prunes earlier references. DRUPE and ASSET were already cited in v1, but receive substantially greater comparative and explanatory attention.

T1.justification: V2 introduces predefined and learned augmentation spaces, a perfectly-trained encoder condition, Theorem 3.1, and its Appendix A4 proof concerning impossibility of backdoors with triggers inside the augmentation space. V1 has empirical motivation but no corresponding theorem or proof. Existing loss, color-space, and Wasserstein mathematics are largely retained.

improvement.justification: V1 supports imperceptibility mainly through image metrics and examples, with limited comparative evidence. V2 adds direct human inspection and systematic baseline stealthiness measurements in Tables 3 and A9–A11, broader attack/defense comparisons, and acknowledgment of visible artifacts. These substantially improve the testing and qualification of the central claims. The five-person study, differing threat models in Table 2, narrower framework coverage, and unexplained revisions to some existing scores limit confidence, but the added direct validation provides a clear overall gain.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same research, despite the changed title and renaming of IMPERATIVE to INACTIVE. Both provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices that support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original attack experiments and reports additional comparisons, defense evaluations, distribution analyses, and human-inspection results.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack-effectiveness, stealthiness, defense, and ablation results, including Tables 1–10 and appendix experiments.

results.title: Invisible Backdoor Attack against Self-supervised Learning

C1.justification: v2 reframes the contribution around robust, high-capacity message embedding and makes ITF an explicit principal contribution. It drops v1's explicit security-superiority claim and changes the QR-transition contribution from improving decoding accuracy to maintaining it while improving image quality.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the interpretation that QR transition improves both quality and decoding with an information-loss tradeoff. It adds explanations involving token mixing, artifact distribution and redundancy under tampering, discusses mismatches between module error and recognizability, and identifies failures on homogeneous images and limits on large payloads (Appendices B-C).

D1.justification: Appendices A-B supply previously unavailable tokenizer/detokenizer specifications, QR-scanning kernel and threshold details, distortion parameters, metric implementation and training time. They also document the printer, phone, print dimensions, shooting geometry and cropping workflow. These substantially improve reproducibility; newly disclosed details alone do not establish implementation changes.

E1.justification: COCO and generated QR-code data remain central. v2 removes the IStego100K-based steganalysis evaluation and adds evaluation under mixed distortions, image tampering and screen photography, substantially changing task and environmental coverage.

E2.justification: The principal comparisons replace RIIS and RIIS† with StegaStamp and StegaStamp†, while retaining ISN† and HiNet†. v1 reports reproducing RIIS; v2 explicitly declines that comparison because its code and pretrained model are unavailable.

E3.justification: Reported image resolution changes from 144×144 to 224×224, training from 45K to 50K iterations, and batching from 64 to eight per GPU. Table 1 changes noise/JPEG settings, and ablation evaluation switches to mixed distortions. v2 also introduces controlled shooting conditions, QR versions 5-8 and tampering-rate protocols, while removing security metrics.

E4.justification: v2 adds ITF ablation and CNN replacement controls, distortion-severity sweeps, shooting-condition and capacity analyses, and tampering and screen-photography tests. Appendices also investigate QR-decoding errors and homogeneous-image failures. The earlier QR-transition, cross-attention and block-count ablations remain in revised form.

E5.justification: v1 Tables 1 and 3 state error intervals of ±0.003 for TRA and ±0.005 for EMR; v2 omits these without replacement uncertainty estimates. Neither version specifies training-seed counts. Selecting the best of five photographs remains, so this is not evidence of increased repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the proposed method's PSNR/LPIPS values of 23.826/0.1852 with 32.883/0.0707 under revised methods and resolution, preventing a same-setting performance comparison. v2 adds shooting, capacity, tampering and expanded ablation results, removes security results, and reports that omitting QR transition slightly improves decoding under its new ablation setting.

M1.justification: v2 adds learnable invertible token fusion before AttnFlow and a simulated QR-scanning constraint on the transition network. Its training objective also replaces v1's PatchGAN adversarial losses with LPIPS supervision and the transition loss (v1 Section 3.4; v2 Sections 3.3-3.6). These change the procedure beyond renaming.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial method and experimental passages are rewritten around RMSteg and message embedding. Method exposition gains a separate overview, training details move into organized appendices, and the experimental narrative replaces the security section with capacity analysis. This exceeds a terminology-only revision.

P2.justification: v2 switches to a two-column layout, adds an introductory demonstration, redraws the pipeline for ITF, and reworks comparison and ablation displays. New distortion curves, shooting/capacity tables, explanatory diagrams and appendix galleries substantially expand the visual presentation; the security table disappears.

R1.justification: Most related-work coverage remains. v2 adds supporting references such as ArtCoder, Art-up and matrix inversion, explicitly distinguishes ITF's token mixing from GLOW's channel mixing, and removes references associated with the discarded security evaluation. The positioning increasingly emphasizes capacity alongside quality and robustness.

T1.justification: v2 adds the mathematical definition and inverse of token fusion, T′=MT and T=M⁻¹T′, and formalizes the scanning-error transition loss in Equation S1. The underlying normalizing-flow coupling equations remain essentially unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves substantial reproducibility gaps through Appendices A-B and strengthens architectural and robustness evidence with targeted ablations, controlled shooting tests, tampering analysis and explicit failure cases. These gains outweigh the loss of RIIS/security comparisons and the earlier, unexplained error intervals, although those removals reduce evidential breadth and uncertainty reporting. The improvement rests on stronger documentation and analysis, not on treating changed-setting scores as controlled performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QR-based attention-flow steganography work, renamed from PPRSteg to RMSteg. Their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends with references despite mentioning supplementary material; v2 includes Appendices A-C. Later disclosures can be distinguished from explicitly documented method changes.

after.justification: v2 reports original comparative experiments, shooting-condition and payload tests, ablations, and appendix tampering and screen-photography results.

before.justification: v1 reports original steganography experiments, printing-and-photography tests, security evaluations and component ablations in Tables 1-3.

results.title: Robust Message Embedding via Attention Flow-Based Steganography

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on inexpensive in-distribution preference construction and artifact suppression. V2 redefines the central contribution around real-image realism through a three-stage curriculum, adds GAN-inspired positioning, and emphasizes improvements in fine visual details. AI feedback and transfer to personalized generation remain central claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds domain-gap explanations for naive training failure, tentatively attributes hard-stage FID deterioration to reduced diversity, and explains alignment losses and recovery through preference selection and text-encoder training. It also discusses SFT forgetting earlier stages. Finger failures and the quality–diversity tradeoff already existed in v1; their discussion is revised rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix F newly specifies stage update counts of 300k/20k/20k, reconstruction and winner-selection timesteps, text-encoder LoRA rank 64, and timestep/block restrictions on inference adapters. It also supplies model-estimated dataset demographics. These substantially expand implementation information; the reported step counts do not establish an increase over v1's undisclosed training duration.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates on the people subset of PartiPrompts; v2 replaces this with held-out captions and reference photographs from its internal human-image collection. Preference training also introduces intermediate and near-real image domains beyond v1's generated preference pairs. Human image generation and InstantBooth personalization remain the underlying tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated NCP-DPO, MAPO and Curriculum-DPO comparisons in Table 1, plus DPOK and D3PO in Appendix Table 5. AlignProp and unfiltered HPD/Pick-a-Pic comparisons remain, while v1's human-only HPD/Pick-a-Pic comparator rows disappear. V2 also evaluates Diffusion-DPO in a new naive real-versus-generated training setting.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a 5,000-image held-out evaluation split with Qwen2-VL test captions. It adds FID, CLIP-IQA quality/sharpness and ATHEC metrics, and reports absolute scores alongside win rates. Color evaluation changes from percentage differences in mean HSV channels to circular-mean hue distance. These substantially revise the evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: V2 adds curriculum-stage, omitted-stage, joint-training and stage-wise SFT ablations (Table 2), real-versus-reconstructed hard-target comparisons (Table 9), and a normal-versus-hard user study (Figure 22). V1's quantitative dataset-size and losing-rank ablations and qualitative LoRA-weight sweep disappear. The ranked image-pool gallery and LAN/statistics-matching analyses are retained in revised form.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix A.1 and Tables 5–6 newly report quantitative evaluation using ten sampling seeds. V1 illustrates multiple seeds qualitatively but does not document an equivalent repeated-seed benchmark. Neither version provides confidence intervals or significance tests; independent training-run counts remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Benchmark, ablation and personalization results are substantially replaced and expanded for the revised model and protocol. For example, v2 Table 2 reports FID values of 37.34 for the base model, 26.05 after the normal stage and 28.66 after the hard stage, alongside new quality/sharpness results. These are within-v2 findings, not same-setting improvements over v1's win-rate results.

M1.justification: V1 uses generated winning/losing pairs and a statistics-matching loss in a single DPO stage. V2 retains this as the easy stage, adds normal and hard stages using reconstructed real-image targets and filtered preference datasets, and introduces separate text-encoder training and selective LoRA application at inference. The default hard-stage winners are lightly reconstructed images, not unmodified photographs.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution framing and method narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before the method, the RLHF/DPO preliminaries disappear, and the appendices are reorganized around curriculum stages. The title and affiliation also change.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the single-column format with a two-column layout, rebuilds the opening visual presentation, adds a curriculum diagram and stage-specific detail comparisons, and expands table structures and highlighting. User-study displays also change. Some illustrations are retained and reformatted, including v1 Figure 6 becoming v2 Figure 14.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands curriculum-learning, GAN and newer DPO literature. Positioning shifts from applying Diffusion-DPO with AI-labeled synthetic preferences, presented as orthogonal to real-image dataset work in v1 Section 6, to a real-image curriculum approach explicitly contrasted with Curriculum-DPO in v2 Section 2.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions for intermediate-domain pools, timestep-constrained selection, filtering and hard-stage preference triplets (Eqs. 5–9). The statistics-matching objective and LAN transformation remain mathematically equivalent despite changed notation and placement. The formal additions concern these constructions; neither version contains theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for its realism claims: v1 mainly reported preference win rates, whereas v2 adds real-reference FID, quality/sharpness metrics, controlled stage and SFT comparisons, target-choice tests, and ten-seed baseline evaluation. Together with fuller implementation details, these make the method and its tradeoffs substantially easier to assess. Losing earlier sensitivity studies and replacing PartiPrompts with an internal benchmark reduce continuity and external comparability, while uncertainty intervals remain absent, but the methodological and evidential gains outweigh these drawbacks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HG-DPO and retain identifiable shared methods and experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons, curriculum-stage experiments, user studies and personalization results, including additional appendix evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark comparisons, ablations, user studies and InstantBooth personalization results.

results.title:
Boost Your Human Image Generation Model via Direct Preference
  Optimization

C1.justification: The central contribution and claim that synthetic-domain alignment improves diffusion-driven TTA remain intact. The abstract and conclusion now explicitly extend the demonstrated performance claim to segmenters and MLLMs, broadening the earlier classifier-centered evidence without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops the interpretation that visually faithful diffusion reconstructions can still be strongly misaligned with source models, separating this issue from target corruption in Section 3.2. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit discussion of slow inference, adaptation overhead and potentially missing task-relevant synthetic attributes, along with the specific contrast-corruption failure explanation. The general caveat that adapted images can be less recognizable remains.

D1.justification: v2 Table 12 adds CIFAR/VOC optimizers, learning rates, batch sizes, training budgets and diffusion settings; the supplement also documents the LLaVA task format and references its fine-tuning defaults. Some ImageNet details are relocated, but measured generation/alignment/fine-tuning times, the 80GB GPU specification and the ResNet decay factor are removed. The code-access link is unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained ImageNet-C/W classification coverage, v2 adds CIFAR-10-C, PASCAL VOC-C semantic segmentation and four-option language-based classification with LLaVA on ImageNet-C. Its UniTTA evaluation also extends the earlier stream tests to broader class/domain correlation and imbalance scenarios.

E2.justification: The stream comparison adds ROID, NOTE, CoTTA, TRIBE, BN, UnMIX, RoTTA, LAME and UniTTA alongside retained TENT and DDA, while dropping MEMO, DiffPure and GDA from that comparison. DiffPure also disappears from the four detailed classifier comparisons in v1 Figure 5 versus v2 Tables 13–16. The headline ImageNet comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The earlier batch-size 1/64 stream tests on three classifiers are replaced by averages over 12 UniTTA settings using ResNet-50. New protocols include source-image accuracy across diffusion timesteps, FID measurements, segmentation evaluated with mIoU, and four-option LLaVA evaluation with zero-shot and fine-tuned controls. The original ImageNet 50K-image, 15-epoch adaptation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds a source-image control examining diffusion-induced misalignment, timestep/FID analyses and substantially expanded stream robustness tests. It removes the timing comparison, classifier-free-guidance ablation, ImageNet-W portions of the component and data-volume ablations, and four supplementary Grad-CAM cases. The two main Grad-CAM examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The prediction confidence scores removed from the Grad-CAM displays are not estimates of experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: New experiments report SDA/DDA results of 72.4/65.3 accuracy on CIFAR-10-C, 39.8/38.6 mIoU on VOC-C and 93.6/91.2 accuracy for LLaVA. Original SDA ImageNet scores persist, but Swin-T Source changes from 33.1 to 33.5, and conditional-only Swin-T/ConvNeXt-T scores change from 39.2/44.2 to 40.1/44.6 without an explanation of reruns. The detailed ConvNeXt-B Source average changes from 45.6 to 46.1, although v2 Table 3 still reports 45.6. Stream results are replaced under different settings, and several ablation, timing and qualitative results disappear.

M1.justification: The SDA procedure remains conditional generation, unconditional diffusion alignment, synthetic-data fine-tuning, target-data adaptation and prediction ensembling. v2 names the existing generation/alignment process Mix of Diffusion and explicitly includes source pretraining in its diagram. These changes and the additional experimental instantiations do not establish a revised SDA algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Separate preliminaries and framework sections become an integrated Methodology section; experiments gain a scalability subsection, the Discussion section disappears, and the appendices are reorganized. Mix of Diffusion terminology is introduced, and the author list changes.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and substantially redraws the framework diagrams. The corruption bar charts become numerical tables, existing ablation tables lose their ImageNet-W columns, and the retained Grad-CAM display is reformatted without confidence scores. New control, scalability, stream and timestep displays appear, while timing, guidance-scale and supplementary visualization displays are removed.

R1.justification: The cited research context expands substantially around realistic continual TTA and the new task/model experiments, including UniTTA, additional traditional TTA methods, LLaVA, Dataset Diffusion, FLUX and EDM. Several earlier synthetic-data examples and generated-image-detection references are removed. The central positioning as complementary to DDA/GDA is retained.

T1.justification: v2 adds a KL-divergence contraction relation attributed to prior work, formal minimum-timestep reasoning and a noisy-distribution approximation for conditional-to-unconditional alignment. v1 provides mainly qualitative convergence motivation and includes a generic diffusion-training loss that v2 omits. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 gives the central alignment argument a more direct source-image control in Section 3.2/Table 2 and tests applicability beyond ImageNet classifiers through segmentation, LLaVA and broader stream comparisons. These address important limitations of v1's largely classification-based and indirect mechanistic evidence. Removed runtime/limitations disclosure, reduced ablation coverage and some numerical inconsistencies weaken transparency, but the stronger tests of the central explanation and applicability provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Synthetic-Domain Alignment (SDA) work and retain matching ImageNet experiments. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains original SDA experiments and adds source-image alignment tests, CIFAR-10-C, segmentation, LLaVA and expanded data-stream evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original SDA results on ImageNet-C and ImageNet-W, component and hyperparameter ablations, timing measurements, and appendix data-sensitivity experiments.

results.title:
Everything to the Synthetic: Diffusion-driven Test-time Adaptation via
  Synthetic-Domain Alignment

C1.justification: The central contribution remains the first human-annotated joint benchmark for prompt/query performance prediction. V2 updates its stated extent to 10,200 queries and over 1.6 million annotations, and explicitly claims utility for cross-model, cross-dataset, and cross-task evaluation in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of transfer failures involving dataset mismatch, limited DrawBench training data, and weak alignment between generation and retrieval. It also discusses practical uses and automatic-label predictability. V1's boxplot-based failure interpretations and natural-image-only limitation disappear, while the principal annotation limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds extensive dataset documentation covering formats, fields, directory structure, an example record, maintenance, support, licensing, and intended uses. It also supplies detailed annotation examples, graph-predictor construction, and the reformulation prompt. Most existing training hyperparameters and hardware specifications are retained or relocated; estimated fine-tuning time changes from 48 to 50 hours.

E1.justification: V2 adds 200 DrawBench prompts to v1's 10,000 MS COCO captions. This introduces generator-oriented prompts with substantially different retrieval difficulty: Appendix 12 reports that approximately half have no relevant MS COCO images. Separate-source and cross-dataset evaluations extend coverage beyond the original caption population.

E2.justification: V2 adds HPSv2 and removes Score Variance @100. Its Table 5 also expands individual-system comparisons beyond the six predictors in v1 Tables 4–6 to the wider linguistic and graph-based suite previously reported only against averaged performance. These are substantive changes in comparator coverage, beyond renamed predictors.

E3.justification: The training/validation/test split changes from 6,000/2,000/2,000 to 6,080/2,040/2,080. V2 additionally introduces cross-model, bidirectional cross-dataset, cross-task, and separate-source training/testing protocols, plus evaluation against HPSv2 and CLIP-derived relevance targets. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic generalization analyses, automatic-versus-human assessment experiments, and generator-selection and prompt-reformulation case studies. Conversely, v1's prediction-error boxplots and associated analyses in Appendix A.8 are removed. The generation-versus-retrieval analysis is retained and moved into the main text.

E5.justification: V1 Figures 7–8 report prediction dispersion through boxplots conditioned on ground-truth performance; v2 removes these distribution summaries. This concerns variation across predictions, not repeated-run uncertainty. Student's t-testing at the 0.01 and 0.001 thresholds remains, and neither version reports repeated-run confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Numerical results and rankings change, and numerous transfer and automatic-assessment results are added. For example, fine-tuned CLIP's GLIDE/HBPP Pearson correlation is 0.615 in v1 Table 4 and 0.649 in v2 Table 3; changed data and settings prevent interpreting this as an isolated same-setting gain. V1's averaged predictor-result tables are no longer reported.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction and principal predictor designs are retained. V2 specifies Long-CLIP/ViT-B/32 and per-system BERT fine-tuning, whereas v1 describes CLIP generically and task-specific tuning while already reporting per-system results. The PDFs do not clearly distinguish implementation changes from expanded documentation.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Generation-versus-retrieval analysis moves from Appendix A.6 to main Section 4, predictor implementation details move into Appendix 11, and the supplementary material is extensively reorganized. These structural changes go beyond simply inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the benchmark pipeline to include DrawBench, and consolidates per-system comparisons into wide tables. It adds transfer tables and application figures, updates the embedding visualizations, and removes the two prediction-error boxplots. Several retained displays are resized or relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds a focused human-feedback discussion covering Pick-a-Pic, ImageReward, and rich human feedback, alongside references supporting its new resources and predictors. It removes the QPP-evaluation discussion concerning correlation and alternative measures. Most QPP positioning, including the comparison with Bizzozzero and colleagues, remains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The substantive HBPP, precision, and reciprocal-rank definitions remain unchanged. V2's expanded explanation of existing graph-based predictors supplies implementation context rather than new mathematical results.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's restricted data coverage and lack of transfer validation through DrawBench and systematic cross-model, cross-dataset, and cross-task experiments. These reveal important generalization failures rather than merely adding favorable scores. The dataset documentation also materially improves reuse. Although error-distribution plots are lost and some implementation details remain ambiguous, the gains in empirical scrutiny and documentation support a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the PQPP benchmark. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original annotations and predictor evaluations, supplemented by cross-model, cross-dataset, cross-task, and application experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original human relevance annotations, predictor evaluations, generation-versus-retrieval correlations, and qualitative analyses, including appendix results.

results.title:
PQPP: A Joint Benchmark for Text-to-Image Prompt and Query Performance
  Prediction

C1.justification: The central contribution remains progressive simplification for compact, editable layered vectors. v2 presents two-stage reconstruction and superior semantic alignment as explicit contributions, while removing v1's claim that the optimization avoids local minima.

C2.justification: v2 Section 4.2 explicitly acknowledges shape distortion during ordinary SDS simplification and explains preserving macrostructure through unconditional noise. v1 instead emphasizes increased variation from reduced guidance. v2 also removes the concluding qualification that the method excludes stylization and leaves it to future work.

D1.justification: PyTorch, Adam, learning rates, and hardware disclosures remain. v2's supplement supplies Douglas–Peucker tolerance, filter parameters, and comparator initialization schedules. However, v1's explicit 100/500-iteration vector-optimization schedule and project-homepage link are no longer provided.

E1.justification: v2 explicitly includes emoji-style inputs alongside photos and clipart, modestly extending the reported image variety. v1 already covers flat illustrations and realistic images in Figures 10–11. The vectorization and recoloring tasks remain; the increase from ten to 100 evaluation images primarily changes sample size.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from LIVE and O&R in v1 to LIVE, O&R, DiffVG, and SGLIVE in v2. Bilateral filtering also joins Gaussian filtering and superpixel simplification in the simplification comparisons.

E3.justification: The principal evaluation changes from ten images at 256 primitives to 100 images with 64, 128, and 256 primitives. v2 adds VGG-based LPIPS and caption-based CLIP evaluation, changes VeC containment from over 90% to over 85%, and caps structural primitives at half the comparison budget.

E4.justification: v1 already compares SDS simplification with Gaussian filtering and superpixels. v2 extends this comparison to reconstructed vector layers and adds controlled tests without the simplification sequence, structural optimization, and overlap loss (Figures 9–10 and supplementary Figures 17–19). These directly examine previously untested component contributions.

E5.justification: v1 Table 2 reports cross-image standard deviations for both MSE and VeC. v2 retains VeC standard deviations in Table 1 but presents MSE curves without dispersion in Figure 12. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the ten-image numerical comparisons with broader aggregate results and adds LPIPS, CLIP, and ablation findings. Reported mean VeC changes from 43.9% to 73.8%, but the dataset and containment threshold differ, preventing a same-setting performance comparison. v1's per-image runtime results are removed.

M1.justification: v1 jointly optimizes structural and pixel-wise primitives at successive simplification levels using visual, structural, and length losses. v2 instead optimizes structural vectors with an overlap penalty, fits and freezes their colors, then performs separate visual refinement. SDS simplification also changes from reduced guidance with a text prompt to an empty prompt.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. The method is reorganized around two reconstruction stages, the earlier Results and Experiments organization becomes an integrated Evaluation section, and dedicated supplementary sections organize ablations and implementation details.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the pipeline and introductory illustrations, adds ablation displays and metric curves, restructures tables, and substantially reorganizes the galleries and page layout. Some examples are retained. Supplementary Figures 20–21 have mismatched captions describing simplification filters although their panels compare vectorization methods.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially recast around image vectorization and layer decomposition. v2 adds positioning against SAMVG, SuperSVG, SGLIVE, and texture-aware vectorization, alongside extensive layer-decomposition literature. v1's separate vector-generation and sketch-abstraction discussions, including several associated citations, are removed.

T1.justification: Mathematical changes are concentrated in the objective definitions: v1's length-regularized joint objective is replaced by an overlap-regularized structural objective and separate visual fidelity loss in v2. Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs; the rewritten SDS gradient alone does not establish new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central claims: comparisons include a relevant segmentation-guided baseline, multiple primitive budgets, perceptual and semantic measures, and controlled component ablations missing from v1. These address important weaknesses of the earlier ten-image evaluation. Runtime evidence and some reproducibility details are lost, and caption errors remain, but the stronger experimental validation provides a clear net improvement. The changed VeC settings do not establish a direct cross-version performance gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, tables, and figures are readable, including v1's post-reference galleries and v2's supplementary material.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on 100 images, perceptual and semantic comparisons, and ablations in Section 7 and supplementary Section 9.

before.justification: v1 reports original vectorization examples and quantitative comparisons on ten images, including runtime, reconstruction error, and vector compactness in Tables 1–2.

results.title: Layered Image Vectorization via Semantic Simplification

C1.justification: The central claim of grounding frozen LMMs while preserving conversational ability remains. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the application claims to reasoning segmentation and grounded-conversation generation, and the introduction adds learned keyword selection as a contribution. Hallucination-resistance claims remain in the experimental discussion.

C2.justification: v2 interprets weaker late-layer grounding through increased abstraction and strong long-query performance through preserved contextual understanding. It drops v1's VisualGenome-exclusion-based argument about the origin of grounding priors. The stated limitations concerning inherited biases, modality coverage, and F-LMM model size are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A1.3 newly documents dialogue formatting and concatenation of RES expressions; Table A4 summarizes training datasets by method. v2 specifies selector settings and describes code as available rather than promising a future release, while dropping the XTuner implementation disclosure. Main training budgets, optimizer settings, and hardware remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds reasoning-segmentation evaluation requiring knowledge or logical inference and GCG evaluation requiring generated text with interleaved masks (Tables 2–3). v1 includes grounded-conversation illustrations but lacks these benchmark evaluations. F-LMM's RefCOCO(+/g) and PNG training coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: v2 adds GSVA-7B to Table 1, GroundingSAM and OVSeg to the new reasoning-segmentation comparison, and OMG-LLaVA, BuboGPT, and KOSMOS-2 to GCG comparisons. Table 6 newly compares the selector against spaCy. Specialist segmentation comparisons omitted from the main table remain in Tables A2–A3.

E3.justification: Decoder ablations now explicitly exclude SAM refinement and expand input sizes from 32–128 to 16–256. Figure 5 labels their metric cIoU, leaving alignment with the surrounding PNG-recall description unclear. New task protocols introduce reasoning-segmentation gIoU and GCG METEOR/mIoU/recall. Table A1 adds 13B baseline configurations, while VisCoT/POPE comparisons retain only the 7B F-LMM configuration.

E4.justification: v2 adds attention-layer ablations, a no-refiner control, keyword-selection analysis, reasoning-segmentation examples, and cross-model attention-map comparisons (Figure 5, Tables 5–6, Figures A3 and A6). It removes v1's plain-CNN versus U-Net ablation and VisualGenome-exclusion training experiment (Tables 3a and 4).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The chat-versus-grounding rank analysis retains the same data and linear-fit reporting.

E6.justification: New results include F-LMM's 46.2 test gIoU for reasoning segmentation and selector F1 of 82.8 versus spaCy's 57.8, alongside GCG and additional baseline results. The mask-only refiner's Stuff score changes from 69.8 to 66.8 (v1 Table 3f; v2 Table 5a). The 1.3B VisCoT/POPE and VisualGenome-exclusion results disappear. Detailed RES/PNG and retained 7B VisCoT/POPE scores remain unchanged; decoder-only scores use different conditions.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 replaces spaCy phrase extraction with a trained linear keyword selector using sigmoid scores, BCE supervision, a 0.3 threshold, and adjacent-token grouping. This changes phrase selection while retaining the frozen backbone, attention processing, U-Net decoder, and SAM refiner.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes experiments around standard tasks and complex scenarios, rewrites the keyword-selection and ablation sections, and restructures the analysis narrative. Appendices move before the bibliography, with Broader Impact and Limitations integrated as appendix subsections and acknowledgements relocated. Introductory and concluding prose also receives editing.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout throughout. Figure 3 adds the selector, revised decoder ablations appear as multipanel plots, and new benchmark, selector, and dataset-usage tables are introduced. Existing visualizations are trimmed or relocated, and specialist comparison rows are consolidated in the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused citations including OPERA, OVSeg, Grounding DINO, OMG-LLaVA, PSALM, and BuboGPT, and removes XTuner. The positioning against fine-tuned segmentation-token models and the claimed novelty of grounding fully frozen LMMs remain substantially unchanged. GSVA and KOSMOS-2 were already cited in v1.

T1.justification: The vision-language embedding and attention equations in Section 3.1 remain mathematically unchanged despite removal of equation numbering. v2 adds no substantive theoretical assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important validation gap: v1 used spaCy without measuring selection quality and illustrated generated grounded conversations, whereas v2 evaluates the replacement selector, end-to-end GCG, and reasoning segmentation (Tables 2–3 and 6). Decoder-only controls and explicit training-data formats strengthen component analysis and reproducibility. Removing the VisualGenome-origin control and Figure 5's ambiguous metric labeling are drawbacks, but direct validation of the paper's central combined capabilities provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe F-LMM and provide readable methods, equations, experimental results, figures, and appendices. Relocated and reformatted material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original F-LMM results and adds reasoning-segmentation, grounded-conversation, keyword-selection, and component-analysis results.

before.justification: v1 reports original F-LMM evaluations across ten backbones, segmentation and question-answering benchmarks, VisCoT experiments, and ablations.

results.title: F-LMM: Grounding Frozen Large Multimodal Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the contribution from a benchmark with three training-free adaptations to include SUIT as a central training strategy. v3 additionally claims its effectiveness and transferability, while retaining the original benchmark novelty and multimodal-query feasibility claims.

C2.justification: v3 explains adaptation failures through generated-query distribution shift and interprets SUIT as reducing that mismatch. It also interprets the artifact experiment as supporting benchmark generalizability and discusses residual cross-modal semantic distortion. v1's explicit model-availability limitation and malicious-image safety/privacy caveat are dropped.

D1.justification: v3 Section 5.1, Appendix B.1, and Table 10 document pseudo-query construction, BLIP-2 caption generation, GPT-3.5 templates, and SUIT implementation. Added details include LoRA placement, rank 32, alpha 64, learning rate 0.0002, one epoch, and up to 16 hours on an NVIDIA A40. Existing code/data access statements remain.

E1.justification: v3 introduces Flickr30K and COCO image-caption data for surrogate training and evaluates retrieved reference images paired with generated images across four styles. The original ICQ-Highlight video coverage and four-style evaluation dataset are retained.

E2.justification: TimeChat and VTimeLLM join the MQ-Cap and MQ-Sum recall/mAP comparisons in v3 Table 1 and Appendix Table 7. TimeChat was previously cited but not evaluated. Existing comparators remain, making this a targeted expansion of the Video-LLM group.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce SUIT training with 89,420 training and 4,785 validation pseudo-queries for one epoch, plus an 84-pair generated/retrieved comparison selected for semantic and stylistic similarity. The original ICQ test coverage and recall/mAP evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds an artifact-control experiment, qualitative image/caption case studies, and a t-SNE analysis of query distributions (Figures 5, 6, and 11). v1's detailed per-prompt analyses and Figures 7–8 disappear. Refinement-text ablations and rank-correlation analyses are retained, partly relocated.

E5.justification: v3 adds averages with plus/minus values across training seeds for SUIT, without specifying the seed count. The original practice of reporting standard deviations across three prompts for captioning and summarization remains. These two sources of variability are different.

E6.justification: Matched original recall/mAP entries are unchanged. v3 adds SUIT results, TimeChat/VTimeLLM results, and artifact-control findings; for example, Table 1 newly reports TR-DETR with SUIT at 58.85 R1@0.5 on scribble. This is a new trained condition, not a correction to an earlier score. Detailed per-prompt results are removed.

M1.justification: v3 Section 4.2 adds SUIT: GPT-3.5 constructs pseudo-queries and forged target captions, then LoRA fine-tunes the multimodal summarizer using next-token prediction. This introduces a learned adaptation procedure. The original CAP, SUM, and VISENC methods remain as MQ-Cap, MQ-Sum, and VQ-Enc.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, adaptation becomes a standalone section, and results are reorganized around explicit research questions. Terminology changes throughout, and the appendix is restructured into dataset, implementation, and extended-results sections.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the overview and adaptation diagrams, and adds SUIT, artifact-control, embedding, and case-study figures. The mAP table and refinement-type plots move to the appendix. Tables are reorganized, and the old per-prompt plots are removed.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands composed image/video retrieval coverage, including Pic2Word, EgoCVR, and CoVR-2, and adds audio-visual localization and SUIT-related references. References supporting v1's episodic-memory motivation are removed. The claimed distinction between holistic retrieval and multimodal event localization remains.

T1.justification: The image-plus-refinement query definition and temporal-localization target retain their mathematical meaning. Neither version develops theoretical results or proofs; SUIT adds an algorithmic training procedure without a new formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses v1's explicitly unresolved training-data problem with a documented surrogate-training pipeline and substantial empirical evaluation of SUIT. Additional Video-LLM comparisons and the artifact-control study strengthen the benchmark's evidence. The artifact study remains small, seed variability does not directly establish prompt robustness, and detailed prompt plots and some caveats are lost. Nevertheless, the methodological and empirical gains substantially improve the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICQ/ICQ-Highlight research. Their main text, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching renamed methods and relocated analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark experiments and adds SUIT evaluations, additional backbone results, and generated-versus-retrieved image experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original ICQ-Highlight recall/mAP evaluations, refinement-text ablations, and prompt-sensitivity experiments in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Localizing Events in Videos with Multimodal Queries

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds a benchmark exposing perception and binding failures across contrastive and generative models. v2 makes StrictVLE a central contribution and focuses its primary evaluation on Video-LLMs. Its abstract and contributions also foreground action-versus-agent difficulty, shortcomings of ClassicVLE and multiple-choice evaluation, and the requirement for visual inputs spanning multiple frames.

C2.justification: v2 develops substantive explanations involving yes-response bias, nearly indistinguishable entailment scores, model-size effects and why simultaneous caption presentation makes multiple-choice evaluation easier. Appendix D explicitly limits StrictVLE's applicability to models supporting yes/no decisions. Human-centric scope and scaling limitations persist, while v1's discussion of societal stereotypes and the unexplored audio modality is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds model-specific evaluation prompts, input details and an OV-7B runtime of approximately 2.6 hours on one RTX 4090 (Appendices B.6–C). However, it removes v1's datasheet documenting JSON distribution, a loading notebook, licensing and maintenance, and omits the earlier explicit decoding settings. This changes reproducibility documentation without establishing that the underlying resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: The VidSitu movie domain and seven caption tests remain, including Agent Identification renamed Agent Random and Action Modifier renamed Action Manner. However, v2 removes the separate Intra-Video Association Test using two cropped video segments and the text-to-video control task. The new input ablations use the retained benchmark.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Qwen2-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, Gemini-1.5-Pro and GPT-4o models. Compared with v1 Tables 2–3, the ClassicVLE comparison in v2 Table 4 drops CLIP, EVA-CLIP, CLIP-ViP and mPLUG-Owl-Video rows while retaining several other comparators. Table 6 additionally evaluates a base language model and a single-image checkpoint.

E3.justification: v2 makes paired yes/no classification under StrictVLE primary, while retaining relative ranking as ClassicVLE and systematically testing both multiple-choice orders. Filtering changes the reported base from 900 videos and 4,500 event captions to 864 videos and 3,101 pairs. Human evaluation changes from five volunteers making retrieval judgments to three classifying individual video-caption pairs. Appendix B.3 also specifies subset selection through trials matching OV-72B performance, and new experiments vary prompts and frame sampling.

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive positive/negative decision analyses, quantified choice-order bias, blind-model and single-frame controls, chain-of-thought and frame-rate ablations, and scored success/failure cases (Sections 5.2–5.5 and Appendix A). These investigate response bias, dependence on visual and temporal inputs, and prompting sensitivity beyond v1's plausibility check and brief qualitative discussion of choice bias.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for model performance. v2's scatter plots display individual examples' entailment scores, not estimates of experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive StrictVLE and diagnostic results, including subset averages of 44.5% for OV-72B, 49.3% for Gemini-1.5-Pro and 93.0% for humans (Table 2). Retained relative-ranking results also change: PLLaVA averages 55.3% in v1 Table 3 and 59.5% in v2 Table 4. These concern revised data/settings, not demonstrated same-setting model improvements. IVAT results are removed.

M1.justification: The retained tests use the same basic construction procedures: LLaMA-3 converts SRL dictionaries into captions, entities or actions are substituted, and templates construct coreference and chronology examples. No predictive architecture or training objective is introduced. StrictVLE changes the evaluation criterion, assessed under E3 and T1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much of the explanatory narrative are rewritten. Tests are regrouped around agents, actions, multiple events and negation strategies; StrictVLE receives a dedicated section. The appendices are extensively reorganized around results, benchmark construction, prompts and limitations, replacing the earlier prompts/annotation/statistics/datasheet structure.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a predominantly single-column layout to two columns. v2 adds a Venn diagram, redraws the benchmark schematic, introduces extensive diagnostic tables and scatter plots, and presents scored qualitative examples. Appendix prompts are reformatted, dataset plots are revised, and a categorized action word cloud replaces the earlier frequency-chart presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through a comparative benchmark table and a dedicated entailment discussion. Newly discussed works include VITATECS, Vinoground, TVBench, TempCompass and NaturalBench. The distinction from prior work now emphasizes strict entailment and evaluation bias alongside in-video negation, rather than mainly contrasting perception with concept binding.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4 introduces the formal StrictVLE condition requiring positive-caption entailment above 0.5 and negative-caption entailment below 0.5, with 25% random accuracy. It adds a numerical counterexample demonstrating why relative ranking can accept incorrect yes/no responses. v1's IVAT matching and group-score definitions disappear; neither version contains substantial theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation validity and diagnostic value: StrictVLE and the score/choice-bias analyses expose errors hidden by v1's relative ranking, while blind and single-frame controls directly test the benchmark's dependence on video information. These gains outweigh reduced datasheet and access documentation. Important qualifications remain: Appendix B.3 conditions subset selection on OV-72B performance, and Table 9 labels its main-result OV-72B scores as 8fps despite the stated 1fps default, weakening the frame-rate interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VELOCITI, built from VidSitu movie clips and semantic role annotations. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations and appendices are readable. The substantial reframing and changed evaluation settings can be identified reliably.

after.justification: v2 reports original StrictVLE, ClassicVLE and multiple-choice evaluations, human results, and additional diagnostic experiments in the main text and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 Tables 2–3 report original evaluations of contrastive models, Video-LLMs, Gemini and humans on VELOCITI, supported by appendix annotation and dataset analyses.

results.title:
VELOCITI: Benchmarking Video-Language Compositional Reasoning with
  Strict Entailment

C1.justification: The central contributions remain video-to-document conversion and iterative retrieval/augmentation. v2 narrows headline superiority to existing LLM-based methods, replaces the LLaMA-Vid-QA performance claim with Video-MME and subtitle-assisted claims, and explicitly claims to be the first such document-retrieval system with a training-free, accessible implementation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of subtitle dominance, restricted subtitle coverage in VideoAgent, and information redundancy or loss across iteration and sampling settings. It replaces v1's proprietary-model transparency/end-to-end-training limitation with a limitation about balancing sufficient and irrelevant information. Component dependence and context-length limits remain, with new failure analysis illustrating the former.

D1.justification: Supplementary Section 7 adds full EgoSchema agent prompts, RTX 4090/24 GB hardware information, temperature settings, captioner specifications and checkpoint links, and detailed baseline reproduction procedures. These materially expand reproducibility information. The LaViLa training-overlap exclusion was already stated in v1; v2 documents it more fully rather than establishing newly changed training.

E1.justification: v1's constructed LLaMA-Vid-QA evaluation, comprising 400 questions over 23 movies lasting approximately 1–2 hours, is removed. v2 replaces it with multiple-choice evaluation on Video-MME's 30–60-minute long split, including conditions with and without subtitles. EgoSchema and MovieChat-1K remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership changes substantially within retained benchmarks. EgoSchema Table 1 adds Vamos, ProViQ and MVU while removing SeViLA, InternVideo, LongViViT and MC-ViT-L, among others. MovieChat-1K Table 2 adds MM-VID, LLoVi, VideoAgent, MovieChat+ and Jeoung et al.; Video-MME also introduces comparisons with newer proprietary and open-source multimodal models.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 changes the reported sampling rate from 2 FPS for all videos to 0.5 FPS for EgoSchema/MovieChat-1K and 0.2 FPS for Video-MME. v2 also introduces DeepSeek V2.5 evaluation and controlled comparisons across interaction counts, agent models and sampling rates. These establish reported protocol changes, but the unchanged retained DrVideo scores do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, augmentation-type, top-K and captioner ablations, v2 adds interaction-count comparisons with VideoAgent (Figure 3), agent-model comparisons (Table 7), sampling-rate sensitivity (Table 8), and a subtitle-only control (Table 3). New success and failure cases examine frame selection, long-video reasoning and captioning errors.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or empirical error bars. Agent-generated confidence outputs occur in both versions and are not statistical uncertainty estimates for the reported performance.

E6.justification: v2 removes the LLaMA-Vid-QA results and adds Video-MME accuracies of 51.7% without subtitles, 71.7% with subtitles and 68.5% using subtitles alone, plus numerous diagnostic results. MovieChat-1K baseline values also change, including MovieChat's global accuracy from 55.1% in v1's Gemini-Pro row to 68.3% in v2. DrVideo's reported EgoSchema and MovieChat-1K headline scores remain unchanged; these revisions do not demonstrate same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The five-component retrieval, augmentation and agent-loop procedure remains intact. However, v2 introduces subtitle-conditioned inference on Video-MME, feeding frame-aligned subtitles into the LLM, whereas v1 explicitly uses visual information without prior language information. This extends the inputs without redesigning the core algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, method exposition and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting, especially the explanation of prior-method limitations and the organization of comparisons. v2 adds a structured supplement covering implementation, ablations, the algorithm and case studies, and moves Algorithm 1 out of the main text.

P2.justification: v1's performance-summary plot and conversion/retrieval detail figure disappear; its overview is retained as v2 Figure 1, and the agent-loop illustration is redrawn. v2 adds an iteration plot and three case-study figures, restructures comparison tables, and introduces additional tables and boxed prompts in the supplement.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against the already-cited LLoVi and VideoAgent, contrasting holistic video documents and language-space augmentation with summarization and image-text retrieval. It adds references covering Video-MME, newer multimodal models and document reasoning, alongside an explicit claim to be the first document-retrieval-based system for this task.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 retain the document construction, cosine-similarity retrieval, augmentation and frame-selection conditions. Algorithm 1 is relocated and reformatted with the same substantive operations. Neither version adds theoretical guarantees, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves reproducibility and the evidence supporting the retrieval framework. Previously missing prompts, checkpoints and reproduction settings are supplied, while Video-MME comparisons, the subtitle-only control, sensitivity studies and failure analysis make the results easier to assess and qualify. Removing the 1–2-hour benchmark narrows duration coverage, and the changed sampling description remains unreconciled with unchanged scores, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in documentation and empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DrVideo and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. The retained method and experiments can be matched reliably, including the additional supplementary material in v2, Sections 7–10.

after.justification: v2 retains original EgoSchema and MovieChat-1K results and reports Video-MME evaluations, additional ablations and qualitative case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on EgoSchema, MovieChat-1K and its constructed LLaMA-Vid-QA benchmark, together with component and parameter ablations.

results.title: DrVideo: Document Retrieval Based Long Video Understanding

C1.justification: The claimed first comprehensive benchmark becomes a three-factor empirical analysis covering both DAM generations. v2 adds EPNL-based equatorial accuracy and synthetic indoor/outdoor joint training to its central contribution narrative, replacing v1's emphasis on metric-depth supervision and newly collected data. The broader SSL/MTSA generalization claim remains.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes disparity supervision and metric-head tradeoffs when explaining equatorial failures. v2 develops explanations involving global normalization, polar-region dominance and equator-focused supervision. Appendix E.6 newly acknowledges that visualization normalization can conceal DAM details; Appendix A identifies extremely dark scenes as problematic. Limited labeled-scene coverage remains a stated limitation.

D1.justification: v2 documents dataset-specific scaling/clipping, frame extraction and dark-scene filtering, sky masking, doubled-resolution pseudo-label generation, representation patch/FoV settings, EPNL sampling, LoRA rank, and inference hardware/timing. These substantially expand reproducibility information. v1's Diverse360 collection procedure and metric-head implementation details disappear with those components.

E1.justification: Teacher training moves from real indoor Matterport3D to synthetic indoor Structured3D and outdoor Deep360. The stated unlabeled training set replaces self-collected Diverse360 with 360+x while retaining ZInD. v2 adds Stanford2D3D evaluation and controlled camera-height/location scenarios (Sections 3.2 and 5; Appendix A).

E2.justification: The Matterport3D comparison drops OmniFusion and adds BiFuse, BiFuse++, HoHoNet, HRDFuse, S2Net, Elite360D and Depth Anywhere (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 5). v2 also introduces quantitative zero-shot comparisons against DAM v1, DAM v2 and Marigold, and evaluates RPNL against EPNL.

E3.justification: v2 separates aligned zero-shot PanDA evaluation from unaligned, 30-epoch dataset fine-tuning, adds threshold-accuracy metrics and evaluation resizing, and changes student training from 20/40 epochs to four. Default training zoom expands from 1–1.2 to 1–1.5. DAM robustness testing expands from three rotation/zoom settings each to ranges of −90°–90° and 0.4–4.0.

E4.justification: v2 adds local-output representation analysis, controlled camera placement, EPNL/RPNL and equator/pole comparisons, pseudo-label-only training, limited-label fine-tuning, LoRA-rank sensitivity, and pseudo-label-resolution analysis. Existing loss, data-volume and augmentation-range ablations use revised designs. The metric-head comparison in v1 Table 5 is removed.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix E.8 newly states that inference timings are averaged over 100 measurements; v1 has no corresponding procedure. Neither version reports repeated training runs, training seeds, or uncertainty intervals for depth-accuracy results.

E6.justification: DAM v1 representation RMSE values remain unchanged, but method results are substantially replaced and extended. v1 Table 3 reports student Matterport3D RMSE 0.3931; v2 Table 5 reports PanDA-S/L values 0.3950/0.3305, and Table 6 adds Stanford2D3D results, including PanDA-L RMSE 0.2540. Changed training and evaluation prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The teacher–student framework remains, but v1's DAM v1 adaptation with metric-depth heads and SILog-based objectives becomes DAM v2 adaptation producing normalized affine-invariant depths. v2 introduces equator-aware patch normalization loss, equator-biased sampling with boundary continuity, and gradient loss in supervised and pseudo-label training (Section 4).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, analysis and methodology are extensively rewritten. The five-aspect benchmark becomes a three-factor analysis, experiments are organized around zero-shot and dataset-specific evaluation, and appendices become separate supplementary sections A–F. Any360D is renamed PanDA, with accompanying terminology and author-header changes.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the opening demonstration and pipeline, introduces transformation curves, camera-position illustrations, error maps and point clouds, and restructures comparison tables by dataset and evaluation setting. Large appendix image galleries are removed. Retained Möbius geometry material moves into the supplement rather than constituting a new analysis.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes its approach from Depth Anywhere's unlabeled-panorama distillation and positions EPNL relative to Metric3D's random patch normalization. DAM v2 and synthetic-data training become central reference points, while Marigold and diffusion-based depth estimation enter the discussion. This substantially revises the closest-work positioning beyond citation updates.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal definitions of percentile depth normalization and the patch-normalized EPNL objective (Equations 1–3). The spherical projections, Möbius transformation and inverse-projection mathematics are retained from v1 Appendix C.1 in v2 Appendix D.3. No new theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's generalization evidence beyond Matterport3D is mainly qualitative. v2 substantially strengthens it through separate quantitative zero-shot and fine-tuned evaluations on two real datasets, plus EPNL/RPNL and equator/pole controls. Appendix E.6 also addresses a visualization confound. Outdoor accuracy and training variability remain unquantified, and zero-shot scores require scale/shift alignment, but the more diagnostic evidence and clearer protocols provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Despite renaming Any360D to PanDA and extensive revisions, both describe the same panoramic-depth research built around teacher–student learning, LoRA and Möbius augmentation. The text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original PanDA results on Matterport3D and Stanford2D3D, camera-position experiments, and extensive component and sensitivity analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original representation and transformation experiments, trained teacher/student results, and loss, architecture and augmentation ablations, including appendix experiments.

results.title:
PanDA: Towards Panoramic Depth Anything with Unlabeled Panoramas and
  Mobius Spatial Augmentation

C1.justification: V1 primarily claims a large in-the-wild dataset, challenging avatar benchmarks and improved generalization. V4 elevates the annotation/filtering pipeline to a central contribution and adds claims of superiority on EMDB and improved downstream reconstruction through better annotations. The dataset-scale and generalization claims remain.

C2.justification: V4 adds interpretations of filtering benefits, improved extremity alignment and high SSIOU arising from loose clothing rather than erroneous fitting. It removes v1's detailed annotation-noise, clothing and lighting challenge discussion, explicit limitations concerning backgrounds, static activities and human interactions, and specific portrait-rights and bias caveats.

D1.justification: The appendices newly document model variants, filtering thresholds, frame selection, loss weights, L-BFGS settings, pipeline runtime and evaluation details. V4 also supplies a project address and S-Lab License 1.0 statement. V1's per-baseline training-time and rendering-FPS entries are removed.

E1.justification: V4 adds quantitative SMPL annotation evaluation on EMDB and consistency and qualitative comparisons using 3DPW, extending evaluation beyond avatar rendering and dataset characterization. WildAvatar and the four laboratory datasets remain in generalization experiments; ZJU-Mocap's separate per-subject comparison disappears.

E2.justification: V4 Table 2 adds eight annotation comparators: SPIN, VIBE, PARE, TRACE, CLIFF, TCMR, HybrIK and HMR2.0. Table 4 additionally compares HMR2.0 annotations against the proposed annotations for downstream reconstruction. The seven avatar reconstruction methods and four generalization methods are retained.

E3.justification: Per-subject evaluation changes from 10 subjects with 10 training and 10 test frames each to 133 subjects with 100 training and 100 test frames each. V4 adds an annotation-source control and new protocols using EMDB-1, joint/vertex errors, PCK at threshold 0.1 and SOIOU. Cross-version reconstruction scores therefore are not directly comparable.

E4.justification: V4 adds sequential filtering/refinement analysis measuring consistency and retained clip counts in Table 3. Appendix figures examine unusual viewpoints, high-SSIOU clothing examples, coarse versus refined SMPL, and accepted/rejected masks. V1's detailed per-subject failure-case comparison is replaced by annotation-source comparisons.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for experimental results. V4's standard deviation across annotating experts is a filtering component, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V4 adds EMDB and filtering results and replaces the per-subject results under its revised protocol. Corresponding generalization entries also change: the first MPS-NeRF row's laboratory novel-view PSNR changes from 18.46 to 16.99, while WildAvatar generalization scores remain unchanged. The resolution chart corrects the 720×1280 label from 70.3% to 23.1%, and Appendix D adds population and scene statistics.

M1.justification: The four-stage annotation backbone remains, but v4 adds multi-expert prediction fusion and agreement-based filtering across detection, pose and SMPL models. Protocol III also introduces PCK-based consistency filtering between projected SMPL joints and estimated 2D keypoints. These materially extend the procedure described with YOLO and PARE in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the pipeline. Existing collection, processing and dataset-analysis material is reorganized into Methodology, WildAvatar and appendices, while the experimental narrative shifts from diagnosing reconstruction challenges to demonstrating annotation benefits.

P2.justification: V4 adopts a two-column layout, redesigns the opening overview and dataset graphics, expands the pipeline diagram, and adds filtering illustrations and annotation tables. It replaces the per-subject comparison display and adds six appendix figures. Retained generalization illustrations are reformatted and faces are blurred.

R1.justification: V4 substantially strengthens positioning around automatic SMPL annotation and filtering, including direct comparison with HMR2.0. It adds relevant references such as EMDB, HMR2.0, TCMR, Detectron2, HRNet and DWPose, and extends application positioning to human interactions and relightable avatars. The earlier dataset and avatar-method survey largely remains.

T1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies constant body shape across frames, temporal and alignment losses, GMM pose-prior regularization, and their weighted objective in Equations 1–4. V1 describes refinement verbally. This adds limited mathematical specification; neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens a central weakness of v1: annotation quality was asserted without direct quantitative validation. EMDB evaluation, staged filtering analysis and downstream annotation-source comparisons provide important supporting evidence, while the appendices make the pipeline substantially more reproducible. These gains outweigh the removal of useful failure and limitations discussion. A remaining documentation problem is the unexplained relationship between selecting 20 frames per clip and evaluating 200 frames per subject.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WildAvatar, retaining the 10,647-clip dataset and identifiable pipeline and avatar experiments. Text, tables, figures and equations support reliable comparison. V4 includes Appendices A–D; the supplied v1 ends with references.

after.justification: V4 reports original annotation evaluations, filtering analyses, avatar experiments and qualitative comparisons, including evidence in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original dataset analyses, per-subject reconstruction experiments in Table 2, and generalization experiments with and without WildAvatar training in Table 3.

results.title: WildAvatar: Learning In-the-wild 3D Avatars from the Web

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds hallucination mitigation across downstream tasks. V2 makes caption clarity and caption quality the central contribution, emphasizes training-free downstream integration, and explicitly claims CQA as a newly proposed benchmark. The underlying caption-to-QA evaluation already exists in v1, so its elevation to a named contribution changes the claims rather than establishing an entirely new procedure.

C2.justification: V2 adds an interpretation that stronger regional attention and more consistent answers indicate firmer visual understanding and greater confidence under element-focused prompts. V1 mainly explains improved completeness through explicit object separation. Dependence on human annotation and insufficient captioner grounding remain stated limitations.

D1.justification: V2 documents SAM-2 frame sampling and mask-ID merging, ECO-to-QA examples, and CLIP label matching for detection. It omits v1's maximum sequence length of 2048 and the planning evaluation's 1,000-image sample and matching thresholds. Most captioner hyperparameters, A100 hardware and approximately 100 GPU hours remain documented; these omissions do not establish changed training settings.

E1.justification: ECO retains the earlier BACON dataset, and CQA largely renames existing caption-based VQA coverage. However, v2 uses five additional caption-training datasets, adds MMVP evaluation, and introduces GQA, SQAI, POPE, MMB, MMBCN, SEED and MM-Vet evaluations in Table A2. The BACON/ECO scene-graph evaluation reported in v1 Table 2 is omitted.

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 adds comparisons with LLaVA captioners trained on DOCCI, IIW, DenseFusion, Recap and DCI. Table A2 adds a multimodal comparison including Qwen-VL, Qwen-VL-Chat and VILA-13B. Figure 7 also adds LLaVA to a qualitative detection comparison. The established quantitative detection and scene-graph comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: The scene-graph protocol changes substantially: v1 uses all Visual Genome annotations, separate subject/predicate/object CLIP matching at 0.85, and correct-triplet counts. V2 Appendix D.1 restricts evaluation to triplets outside common categories, matches concatenated triplets at 0.9, and reports recall in Figure 6. V2 also adds Qwen-14B as a fixed caption-QA evaluator and introduces new prompt-analysis protocols.

E4.justification: V2 Figure 2 and Appendix A.1.4 introduce a 1,000-image analysis comparing ordinary and element-focused prompts through spatial attention and answer consistency. Table 1 checks caption evaluation with another QA model, and Figure 7 adds qualitative grounding comparisons. The earlier CLIP/LLaVA grounding ablation is retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.1.4 newly specifies ten repetitions with different random seeds for each question in the prompt study. Existing plus/minus uncertainty reporting for detection and human evaluations remains. This does not establish increased run counts for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for caption-dataset comparisons, prompt analyses, another QA evaluator and seven multimodal benchmarks. All OK-VQA/OK-CQA scores are revised, including BACON from 32.1 to 56.8 in v1 Table 3 versus v2 Table 1; the reason is not explained. Scene-graph results are replaced under different conditions. Detection, region QA, user-preference win rates, image-generation and planning results remain unchanged apart from rounding.

M1.justification: The core prompting, graph construction, grounding pipeline and 13B LoRA captioner remain. The video extension switches from the Cheng et al. tracking method to SAM-2, with associated prompting and tracking procedures. Appendix D.6 also introduces LLaVA fine-tuning on automatically generated ECO question-answer pairs. These are bounded extensions to the retained framework.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much explanatory prose are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around caption quality followed by downstream assistance; related work moves into the main text, dataset construction joins the method section, and appendices are reorganized into A–D. BACON dataset and captioner terminology changes throughout.

P2.justification: Figures are extensively redrawn and rearranged, with new attention plots, a CQA schematic and comparison tables. The scene-graph table becomes a recall plot; planning results and the editing example move to the appendix. Several illustrations are consolidated or removed, and the document template, captions and table layouts change substantially.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantial positioning against DOCCI, IIW, DenseFusion, Recap and DCI, discussing bounding-box support and annotation costs in Section 2. It also adds SAM-2 and caption-evaluation references. V1's text-decomposition emphasis and Guo et al. ZS-VQA attribution are dropped as caption-based QA is presented as CQA.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A.1.4 introduces a formal symmetric semantic-consistency score using thresholded T5 sentence matching, including Equation A1. This mathematical definition is absent from v1. Neither version develops substantial theorem or proof content.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for the captioning contribution: Table 2 supplies direct comparisons with other dense-caption datasets using a shared LLaVA backbone, Table 1 checks another QA evaluator, and Figure 2 tests the prompting rationale. The clearer separation of caption quality from downstream applications also improves assessability. These gains outweigh the loss of some reproducibility details and unexplained OK-CQA score revisions, which remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BACON's structured captioning framework, captioner and downstream applications. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including image-based figures. Renamed datasets, models and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds prompt analyses, caption-dataset comparisons and ECO-derived QA fine-tuning results, including Figure 2 and Tables 2 and A2.

before.justification: V1 reports original detection, question-answering, scene-graph, image-generation, planning and human-evaluation results in Tables 1–6 and the appendices.

results.title: BACON: Improving Clarity of Image Captions via Bag-of-Concept Graphs

C1.justification: v1 presents downstream semantic applications mainly as future potential. v2 makes three implemented downstream tasks using shared latent representations central contributions and claims compression up to 1:16384 for these applications. The abstract retains the approximately 1:100–1:1000 reconstruction claim.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the UMAP-based semantic interpretation and VAE-versus-StyleGAN discussion with task-specific explanations of useful predictions despite degraded identity reconstruction, spatial feature requirements, and segmentation failures on details such as earrings. Appendix A adds conditions for extending LSI toward general vision and discusses nonlinear optical encoders. Existing domain restrictions and SPI motion limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds projector dimensions and feature-selection details, and replaces the promised code release with a statement of implementation availability and a repository URL. Most optimizer, hardware, batch-size, and fine-tuning details are retained. The explicit 98,000-image training total and separate dataset-access instructions in v1 are omitted.

E1.justification: FFHQ, CelebA-HQ, and AFHQ cat/dog reconstruction coverage are retained. v2 adds evaluated tasks involving 40 facial attributes, 18 segmentation classes, and 68 landmarks, substantially extending v1's reconstruction and identity focus. Appendix C.3 also evaluates faces with uncontrolled backgrounds.
