E2.justification: v2 retains FSI-DL and binary SAUNet but adds evaluated OCTUF, TCS-Net, CSGM, Non-Latent LSI, and an 8-bit SAUNet variant (Tables 2 and C.1). OCTUF was cited but not evaluated in v1. The earlier LSI-VAE comparison is removed.

E3.justification: The sampling sweep expands from 512–64 measurements to 512–16 for reconstruction and down to four for downstream tasks. CurricularFace feature similarity is replaced by reported VGGFace/DLib verification accuracy. New task protocols introduce attribute accuracy, segmentation F1, landmark NME, FaRL-derived references, and method-specific exclusion of failed downstream outputs.

E4.justification: v2 adds controls testing learned versus fixed random masks, latent versus direct reconstruction, uncontrolled backgrounds, and sensing-matrix quantization (Table 2 and Appendix C). It removes v1's UMAP analysis, VAE comparison, and explicit with/without-fine-tuning analysis. The energy-loss histogram is retained, while failure examples are revised.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The expanded results retain point estimates and qualitative displays without a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive task, compression, comparator, and ablation results. At 256 measurements, LSI's reported FID changes from 35.65 in v1 Table S1 to 26.62 in v2 Table C.1, alongside backbone and loss changes. The new Non-Latent baseline exceeds LSI's VGGFace accuracy at 1:128: 94.22% versus 91.97%. v2 also contains conflicting FSI-DL FIDs at 1:256: 123.5 in Table 2 versus 118.79 in Table C.1.

M1.justification: v2 switches the face generator from StyleGAN2 to StyleGANXL and introduces trained linear projectors for attribute classification, segmentation, and landmarks while freezing the optical and digital encoders. Segmentation and landmarks also use generator feature maps. The perceptual loss changes from LPIPS alone to reported DINO/LPIPS features.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized. v1 places Methods after Discussion and Future Potentials; v2 separates related work, method, downstream learning, hardware, training, simulations, prototype results, and comparisons. The supplement is reorganized into foundations, implementation, and results, while the abstract and introduction are rewritten around the expanded contribution.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the opening workflow around downstream branches, separates the hardware schematic, and adds a setup photograph and extensive task-comparison galleries. Tables gain new methods, metrics, and compression settings. The energy histogram and encoder diagram are retained in reorganized supplementary displays, while the UMAP figure disappears.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 substantially expands positioning against learned compressed sensing, generative-prior reconstruction, single-pixel methods, and minimalist/freeform-pixel cameras. New citations include generative-prior and minimalist-camera work. v2 develops distinctions involving physical feasibility, single-pass reconstruction, and shared masks supporting multiple tasks; this exceeds relocation or bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the stated optical-encoder dimensions from mn × d to d × mn, making the multiplication O·I dimensionally consistent with d measurements in Equation 1. The underlying mathematical formulation remains largely unchanged, with no new theorems or proofs. The added standard NME formula documents evaluation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for LSI's central premise: v1's largely prospective semantic applications become three implemented and evaluated tasks, including hardware demonstrations. Non-latent, random-mask, background, and quantization controls better test the design choices, while broader comparisons reveal meaningful limitations. These gains outweigh the removal of useful VAE and fine-tuning analyses. Reporting weaknesses remain, particularly the conflicting FSI-DL values in Tables 2 and C.1 and method-specific exclusion of failed downstream outputs, but the central claims are substantially better tested.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Latent Space Imaging by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete supplements support reliable comparison despite substantial scientific and structural revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction and downstream-task results from simulations and hardware experiments, including Figures 5–8 and Tables 1 and C.1.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated reconstruction results, physical single-pixel-camera experiments, and supplementary analyses, including Figure 3 and Table S1.

results.title: Latent Space Imaging

C1.justification: Both retain the same central contributions: an open-access, country-scale VHR canopy-height benchmark, a canopy-change benchmark, and evaluations of vision models. The conclusions about hierarchical-transformer performance and the difficulty of change detection remain. Added experiments support these contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 interprets field checks as supporting ALS reference reliability and distinguishes geographic transfer from strong SPOT-sensor dependence. It adds explanations concerning training from scratch, LoRA, and NIR initialization, plus limitations involving acquisition costs, cloud cover, and seasonal mismatch. The earlier limitation about canopy height being an imperfect biomass proxy is removed.

D1.justification: The detailed preparation and split instructions largely remain. v3 adds annotation-file instructions, LoRA implementation details, preprocessing compute estimates, updated GPU costs, and maintenance information. It reports training code and weights as available instead of promising later release. Prominent links become placeholders, but explicit project and dataset addresses remain in Appendix F.

E1.justification: The French benchmarks remain, but v3 adds a 30 km² Utah evaluation using NEON ground truth with SPOT and NAIP imagery (Table 5). It also evaluates heights against measurements from 135 field plots and 44 individual trees (Appendix A), substantially broadening geographic, sensor, and validation coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds SATLAS-pretrained SWIN to Table 2 and Pauls et al.’s canopy map to Table 3 and the 10 m comparison in Table B. LoRA is additionally compared with full fine-tuning in Tables 4 and D. These extend the retained comparison methods.

E3.justification: Change detection switches from 10 m/100 m² thresholds to 15 m/200 m², with expert review of 73 candidate areas and correction of false-positive reference labels. New protocols include maximum-height comparisons within field plots and tree neighborhoods, and resampling plus histogram matching for NAIP transfer. Existing French splits and standard training settings remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds ground-truth validation, geographic and sensor-transfer tests, NIR-removal ablations, initialization comparisons, LoRA-rank sensitivity, and model error-map comparisons. These investigate reliability, transferability, and design choices beyond v1’s analyses. The earlier height-bin and 10 m evaluations are retained, while change-threshold sensitivity results are revised.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Fixed-seed split sampling and prediction-error distributions remain documented; the new field-validation fit metrics do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing height-estimation scores remain, including PVTv2 MAE of 2.52 m. v3 adds substantial validation, transfer, baseline, and ablation results, including Utah PVTv2 MAEs of 2.08 m with SPOT and 4.38 m with NAIP. Change-detection IoU changes from 22.5% to 37.0%, but under revised thresholds and curated masks, not unchanged conditions.

M1.justification: Change-mask inference adopts 15 m/200 m² thresholds instead of 10 m/100 m². Section 3.2 also revises the stated output head from a simple linear layer to a transposed-convolution decoder, without establishing whether retained experiments were rerun. The RGB+NIR initialization scheme and L1 objective remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are rewritten, with greater emphasis on computer-vision challenges. Analysis and limitations passages are expanded or recast, comparison caveats are relocated, and the appendices are substantially reorganized into validation, results, ablations, dataset documentation, preparation, and a datasheet.

P2.justification: v3 switches to a two-column layout and extensively rearranges displays. Figure 1 is repacked and gains Pauls; Figure 4 replaces predicted-height illustrations with error maps. New validation, curation, transfer, and ablation displays are added, and Table 1 is restructured. Earlier appendix illustrations are retained as Figures B and E.

R1.justification: v3 adds literature on SATLAS, Pauls et al., LoRA, additional forest-change methods, alternative open data sources, and dataset documentation, while dropping some carbon-accounting references. The organizing framework and positioning around accessible VHR forestry benchmarks remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The regularized nMAE definition in v1 Equation A-1 is retained in v3 Equation A. Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs, and no substantive mathematical derivation or assumption is added.

improvement.justification: Field validation and expert label curation address previously unquantified reference-data reliability, while transfer and ablation studies expose important applicability limits and test design choices. These substantially strengthen the benchmark’s evidential foundation. Stricter change thresholds narrow the target, so higher IoU is not a demonstrated model improvement. Placeholder links and Figure 4 caption errors weaken presentation, but access addresses remain in Appendix F and the scientific gains outweigh these defects.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Open-Canopy and Open-Canopy-∆ research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite substantial reorganization and added studies.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark results and adds field validation, Utah transfer experiments, and initialization and infrared-channel ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, canopy-map comparisons, change-detection results, and supplementary sensitivity analyses in Tables 2–4 and A-1–A-3.

results.title: Open-Canopy: Towards Very High Resolution Forest Monitoring

C1.justification: The central grouped-scanning, CAM and distillation contributions and headline accuracy claims are retained. The conclusion extends the claimed efficiency advantage to measured throughput, beyond v1's concluding emphasis on fewer parameters.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of scale-dependent distillation gains and the four-group efficiency tradeoff. Its new limitations section acknowledges modest downstream gains over VMamba, discusses localization and task-specific requirements, and identifies reliance on external teachers. These materially qualify applicability and efficiency claims that v1 leaves largely unqualified.

D1.justification: v2 Table 6 supplies previously missing per-variant channel widths, block depths, convolution kernels and strides, substantially improving architectural documentation. Figure 4 specifies the throughput hardware and batch size. The code/model access link is unchanged, while the relationship between the newly specified depths and v1's schematic remains unexplained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same tasks on ImageNet-1K, COCO 2017 and ADE20K. Added ablations and qualitative examples remain within this coverage. Video recognition and time-series applications appear only as future work.

E2.justification: v2 removes EffNet-B6 from Table 1, PVTv2-B2 from the COCO comparison, and DeiT-S + MLN, ViM-S and EfficientVMamba-B from the ADE20K comparison. Figure 4 adds a separate VMamba-T V1 comparator alongside V2 and broadens the component comparison to other existing SSM baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces throughput evaluation using one NVIDIA A100 and batch size 128, with additional scanning/group-count controls and Small/Base distillation comparisons. The stated benchmark splits, training schedules and optimization settings remain unchanged. ADE20K parameter and FLOP metrics are no longer reported.

E4.justification: v1's Tiny-model CAM, distillation and parameter-matched tests are retained and reorganized. v2 substantially expands analysis through 4-D versus 1-D scanning, one/two/four-direction comparisons, two/four/eight-group sensitivity, Small/Base distillation ablations, training-loss curves and additional qualitative examples. The parameter-matched comparison in v2 Table 5 already existed in v1 Table 4.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 5 newly reports shaded standard-deviation bands for training loss, described in Section 8 as variability across training epochs. Neither version specifies independent-run counts or seeds, and v2 does not explain the band-estimation procedure sufficiently to infer repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial throughput, scanning/grouping and loss-curve results, including undistilled Small/Base accuracies of 83.0%/83.2%. Main classification, AP and mIoU scores remain unchanged. Tiny-model FLOPs change from 4.6G to 4.5G in Table 1; the matched 31M variant changes from 5.4G to 5.2G between v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5. Several baseline entries and ADE20K resource results disappear.

M1.justification: The VSSS, CAM and distillation equations remain unchanged. However, v1 Figure 2 specifies stage depths of 3/4/6/3, whereas v2 replaces these with symbols and Table 6 specifies 2/2/9/2 for Tiny and 2/2/20/2 for Small/Base. The PDFs do not establish whether this corrects the earlier diagram or reflects an actual architecture change.

P1.justification: Most introduction, related-work and method prose retains its wording and sequence. v2 revises the title and affiliations, expands selected explanations, rewrites the ablation narrative, extends the conclusion with future work, and organizes supplementary material into dedicated sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws Figure 2, merges the COCO/ADE20K tables, and introduces throughput and training-loss graphics plus an architecture table. The earlier qualitative grids move to supplementary Figures 6–7, while the main qualitative display includes additional examples. These are substantial display and layout revisions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks and explicitly discusses CAM's relationship to SE in Section 3.3.3, positioning CAM around inter-group communication in Mamba. The PVT v2 reference disappears with its comparison row. The broader related-work discussion remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 changes the stated dimensions of both SSM projection matrices B and C from N×1 to 1×N, a limited revision to the formal specification. The continuous/discrete SSM equations and model/loss equations otherwise remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for central efficiency and stabilization claims through measured throughput, scanning/grouping controls, and larger-model distillation analyses, beyond v1's Tiny-model component tests. Detailed architecture configurations and explicit limitations also improve reproducibility and interpretation. These gains outweigh removed comparator/resource entries, although unexplained stage-depth differences, inconsistent FLOP reporting and underspecified loss-variability bands remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GroupMamba, and their text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes readable supplementary Sections 7–11. Changes in title, layout and placement do not prevent matching content.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds throughput measurements, scanning and grouping ablations, larger-model distillation comparisons, and training-loss analysis.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.4 report original ImageNet-1K classification, COCO detection and instance segmentation, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and component-ablation results.

results.title: GroupMamba: Efficient Group-Based Visual State Space Model

C1.justification: The headline benchmark contribution increases from 700 to 1,400 prompts in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The central claims remain: the first systematic compositional T2V benchmark, seven categories, tailored metrics validated against humans, and substantial difficulties for existing generators.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations distinguishing successful object generation from relationship understanding and motion magnitude from directional control, alongside explanations of subgroup difficulty. Appendix G newly explains why fixed-frame evaluation may fail for longer videos and why longer duration can favor motion scores. The earlier limitation concerning the absence of a unified metric is retained.

D1.justification: v2 documents vocabulary-selection thresholds and word-list access, generated frame counts, MLLM repetition settings, and detailed AMT worker screening and quality-control rules. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit list of six human-study generators and six category-specific annotation interfaces. Reproducibility information is substantially expanded and revised, with some detail lost.

E1.justification: The seven compositional tasks remain, but v2 revises the represented prompt vocabulary using frequent nouns and verbs from VidProM's real-user prompts and TempCompass examples for attribute changes. These sources inform benchmark construction; they are not separately evaluated video-generation benchmarks. The increase in prompt count is assessed under E3.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Vico, T2V-Turbo-V2, CogVideoX-5B, and Mochi, replaces Open-Sora-Plan v1.1.0 with v1.3.0, and removes Dream Machine. Table 1 adds B-BLEU, ViCLIP, VPEval-S, and M-GDino. It also removes the LLaVA comparisons for dynamic attributes and motion, while retaining LLaVA in other categories.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from 100 to 200 prompts per category, revises subgroup allocations, and introduces matched quantity-group prompts and diagnostic measures. Reported generation settings also change: VideoCrafter2 moves from 2.7 seconds at 24 FPS to 2 seconds at 8 FPS. Human evaluation decreases from 656 to 651 videos, with interaction ground-truth videos reduced from 16 to 11. These are reported protocol changes, without independently establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds sample-count stability studies across all seven categories in Appendix A.4 and extensive diagnostic analyses in Appendix D. These separate object coexistence from spatial correctness, motion magnitude from direction accuracy, common from uncommon actions, and physical from social interactions. Table 4 and Figure 22 add subgroup and object-count analyses beyond v1's aggregate results and qualitative examples.

E5.justification: v1 reports three human raters but no MLLM seed-variability study. v2's Appendix C.2 reports eight seed-varied Grid-LLaVA evaluations, repeated sampling of two- and three-run averages, and correlation distributions in Figure 19. It adopts averaging three scores per video, adding an explicit statistical reliability study and aggregation practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 contain extensive numerical and ranking changes, and Table 4 adds subgroup results. For example, Grid-LLaVA's consistent-attribute Spearman correlation changes from 0.8679 to 0.7893, while v2's Table 2 places PixVerse-V3 first in six categories. Changed prompts, scoring procedures, and model versions prevent treating these revisions as matched-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: The MLLM evaluation procedures change substantively. v1's joint action and interaction scoring prompts become presence-conditioned, multi-stage queries in v2's Appendix C.1 and Figure 18. Dynamic-attribute grading adds an intermediate-frame option for both states. v2 also introduces frequency-based vocabulary selection into benchmark construction, beyond the category-based GPT-4 prompting documented in v1.

P1.justification: The benchmark-construction and experimental narratives are extensively rewritten and reorganized. Model descriptions move from the appendix into Section 5.1, related work gains numbered subsections, and the appendices are reorganized from A–D into A–H with a contents list. Prompt templates move to Appendix H, while limitations and societal impacts receive separate sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws overview and prompt-generation figures, replaces the word-cloud display with new statistics, and restructures comparison tables by metric family and model architecture. It adds stability plots, an MLLM query diagram, subgroup tables, and diagnostic visualizations. Seven human-evaluation interface figures are reduced to one.

R1.justification: Related work adds a substantive comparison with ChronoMagic-Bench concerning natural versus artificial attribute changes, alongside references supporting new data sources, evaluators, and generators. The model discussion shifts toward UNet versus DiT architectures. The central positioning relative to compositional image benchmarks and general video benchmarks remains.

T1.justification: Appendix D.3–D.4 adds quantitative definitions for coexistence, conditional spatial accuracy, correct-layout scores, and motion accuracy requiring at least five units of displacement after 100-by-100 normalization. These are limited additions to mathematical measurement definitions. The existing spatial and relative-motion formulations remain, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens benchmark validation through sample-size stability and seed-variability evidence absent from v1. Its subgroup analyses make aggregate scores more interpretable, while documented vocabulary selection, annotation controls, and long-video limitations improve assessability. These gains outweigh lost annotation details and localized reporting errors, including Appendix D.2 assigning the dynamic-attribute score 0.0687 to PixVerse-V3 although Table 2 assigns it to Gen-3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe T2V-CompBench, with the same authors, research objective, and seven compositional categories. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, figures, and mathematical content support reliable comparison despite extensive revision and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations, human correlations, prompt-distribution analyses, seed and sample-size studies, and category-specific results in Tables 1–4 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated-video evaluations and human-correlation experiments in Section 5 and Tables 1–2, with study details in the appendices.

results.title:
T2V-CompBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Compositional Text-to-video
  Generation

C1.justification: V2 reframes the contribution around joint semantic and instance guidance and better instance-level representations. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion add zero-shot discovery claims and a claimed first high-fidelity compositional generation capability for complex real-world scenes using slot attention. Property prediction changes from comparable or slightly worse performance in v1 to claimed superiority over StableLSD in v2.

C2.justification: V1 identifies grouping same-class instances as a limitation. V2 explains how semantic guidance causes this drift and how feature reconstruction counteracts it, supported by component analyses. It adds limitations concerning slot-count sensitivity, residual semantic grouping, and generation quality, discusses weaker FG-ARI results, and explicitly qualifies the comparability of image-based GLASS and text-based Composable Diffusion.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility information: explicit dataset splits, MLP architecture, per-module learning rates for both training phases, pseudo-mask thresholds and ignored regions, and property-prediction optimization details. Hardware reporting changes to an A6000 Ada GPU. V2 states that code is available and supplies access information, whereas v1 promises release upon acceptance.

E1.justification: V2 retains COCO and VOC experiments but adds zero-shot object discovery on CLEVRTex and Objects365 (Table 4), object-position prediction alongside label prediction (Table 8), and demonstrated object addition, removal, and cross-image composition (Figures 6, 9, 12, and 13). These substantially expand the evaluated tasks and environments.

E2.justification: V2 adds SPOT to OCL comparisons and DeepSpectral, COMUS, DiffCut, and EmerDiff to semantic segmentation comparisons. It also evaluates SAMv2-derived guidance, an adapted DatasetDiffusion control, and Composable Diffusion. V1's StableLSD-Mask and StableLSD-Box guidance comparators disappear; bounding-box initialization remains a separate retained comparator.

E3.justification: Reported generated training-set sizes change from approximately 118K/12K to 100K/10K images for COCO/VOC, GRU iterations from three to five, and VOC slots from six to seven. V2 adds instance mIoU, SO-PO-GO, FG-ARI, and additional reconstruction metrics while dropping CorLoc/DetRate. FID uses 512 COCO images instead of 1,024 images per dataset, and property-prediction training changes from 6K steps to epoch-based training with early stopping.

E4.justification: V2 adds loss-component ablations, encoder comparisons, SAMv2 guidance failure analysis, slot-count sensitivity, and caption-generator/template ablations (Table 6; supplement Sections 4 and 7). Zero-shot transfer and SO-PO-GO examine generalization and segmentation errors, while an adapted DatasetDiffusion control tests the source of gains. V1's stronger-guidance and guided-DINOSAUR analyses are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run or seed counts or reports standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The expanded result tables retain single-score reporting.

E6.justification: Results are extensively revised and expanded. V1 Table 2 reports GLASS semantic mIoU of 43.7/64.0 on COCO/VOC; v2 Table 9 reports 46.7/68.9 for the new GLASS-Sem variant. MaskCLIP's reported COCO score changes from 23.6 to 20.6. COCO FID for StableLSD/GLASS changes from 78.47/73.06 to 140.62/71.30, but model and sampling changes prevent a same-setting performance comparison. Zero-shot, ablation, position-prediction, and compositional results are newly reported.

M1.justification: V1 combines image reconstruction with semantic-mask guidance and keeps the diffusion decoder frozen. V2 adds an MLP feature decoder and instance-guidance loss, introduces weighted semantic/instance objectives, and uses two-phase training that includes training the diffusion decoder. It also introduces the semantic-focused GLASS-Sem variant (Section 4; supplement Section 2).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, experiments, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized into instance-aware discovery, generation, property prediction, and semantic discovery. Dataset and training documentation moves into a restructured supplement, limitations move into the main text, and the broader-impact statement is removed.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Architecture diagrams are redrawn to show instance guidance and the MLP decoder. Segmentation and reconstruction displays are reorganized, earlier bar/scatter presentations give way to tables, and new ablation, SAMv2, and compositional-generation displays are added. The guided-DINOSAUR and dedicated drawback figures are removed.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning toward instance-aware representations and real-world compositional generation. It incorporates work including SPOT, SAM 2, DiffCut, EmerDiff, and Composable Diffusion, while trimming Gestalt and general self-supervised-learning background. Section 2 and Table 1 now distinguish instance-level discovery, semantic discovery, and compositional capabilities, and novelty is framed around combining semantic and instance guidance.

T1.justification: The formally defined objective changes from reconstruction plus binary cross-entropy in v1 Equation 4 to weighted semantic guidance plus an additional feature-reconstruction term in v2 Equation 3. This extends the mathematical specification, while the slot-attention and Hungarian-matching formulations remain essentially unchanged. Neither version develops theorem or proof results.

improvement.justification: V2 directly addresses v1's important limitation of grouping same-class instances and tests the proposed remedy through controlled loss ablations. In v2 Table 6a, adding instance guidance to reconstruction plus semantic guidance raises COCO instance mIoU from 30.9 to 38.9. Stronger comparators, transfer tests, and substantially fuller implementation documentation strengthen the paper's evidence and reproducibility. Some earlier analyses are lost and changed protocols limit cross-version score comparisons, but the improved validation of the central mechanism provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GLASS by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material support a reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original segmentation, generation, property-prediction, zero-shot transfer, and ablation results in the main text and supplement.

before.justification: V1 reports original COCO and VOC experiments on object discovery, conditional generation, property prediction, and alternative guidance methods, including appendix results.

results.title: GLASS: Guided Latent Slot Diffusion for Object-Centric Learning

C1.justification: The central claims about mask-free pseudo-data training, wild augmentation and localization loss remain. However, v2 strengthens the input-efficiency claim from requiring a source pose image to requiring no additional parser during inference, explicitly reflected in its abstract and contribution list.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of distillation overfitting, the differing benefits of refined pseudo-data and augmentation, and attention behavior across denoising stages. It qualifies the StreetVTON KID comparison and introduces a concrete controllability limitation: replacing a dress with only a top reference leaves the lower garment uncontrolled (Section 6).

D1.justification: v2 discloses SDXL/IP-Adapter/Reference Net details, loss attachment locations, training time, inference hardware and sampling steps, and standardized evaluation resolution. Supplementary Section 1 and Tables 4–5 add augmentation image counts, resolutions, probabilities, transformations and full prompts. Conversely, v1's promised code-release URL is omitted.

E1.justification: The four datasets and the in-shop, wild, anime and multi-garment scenarios are retained. v2 adds prompt-controlled garment rendering and missing-reference-garment demonstrations (Figures 9–10). WildVTON's increased sample count changes the protocol rather than establishing a new domain.

E2.justification: v2 removes GP-VTON from the VITON-HD comparison and adds CAT-DM. Its wild-scene comparisons additionally evaluate DCI-VTON, LaDI-VTON and TPD alongside StableVITON, OOTD and IDM-VTON. TPD corresponds to the baseline mislabeled 'TBD' in v1's Table 2, rather than being an entirely new comparator.

E3.justification: v1 reports only unpaired FID/KID testing. v2 adds paired testing using generated pseudo-pairs, with LPIPS, SSIM, PSNR and paired FID/KID, and expands WildVTON from 200 to 1,224 images. The stated learning rate, batch size and 12,000-step training budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 extends v1's augmentation/localization ablations with a high-quality pseudo-data component and in-shop evaluation. Figures 8 and 18–20 add component comparisons and attention analyses across denoising steps and network blocks. Figure 10 supplies a concrete failure case involving an unspecified garment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Additional metric values and attention visualizations in v2 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 add paired results and expanded ablations, while revising numerous unpaired scores. Reported VITON-HD FID/KID changes from 9.474/0.871 to 8.809/0.8176. In v2, newly evaluated DCI-VTON beats BooW-VTON on StreetVTON KID, 3.470 versus 4.494. WildVTON scores use the enlarged test set and are not same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: v1 conditions the try-on network on DensePose; v2 removes that input, enabling parser-free inference. v2 also introduces two-stage pseudo-image generation using a coarse mask followed by the union of original and intermediate garment regions (Section 4.2, Figure 3). The underlying augmentation and localization-loss approach remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work argument and results discussion undergo substantial rewriting. v2 reorganizes the method into numbered subsections, adds dedicated application and limitations sections, and supplies a structured supplement. These changes substantially revise the narrative beyond merely inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the motivation and pipeline figures, reorganizes qualitative comparisons, and restructures quantitative tables to separate DressCode results and integrate ablations with paired metrics. New displays cover data generation, applications, failures, attention heatmaps, augmentation assets and dataset examples. v1's localization diagram is retained as Figure 5.

R1.justification: v1 motivates diffusion by characterizing earlier mask-free approaches as GAN-based. v2 acknowledges PFDM and repositions its contribution around overcoming errors transferred through teacher-student distillation. It also adds relevant architecture, try-on and attention-analysis literature, including SDXL, IP-Adapter, AnyFit and diffusion correspondence studies.

T1.justification: The conditioning definition accompanying Equation 4 changes from concatenated person and DensePose latents to the person latent alone. The remaining diffusion derivation and attention-regularization mathematics retain their substantive forms; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper's experimental support and reproducibility: paired fidelity measurements supplement v1's distribution metrics, broader wild-scene comparisons and component analyses improve validation, and the supplement supplies previously missing augmentation and inference details. Concrete limitations also clarify applicability. The paired tests use pseudo-pairs, expanded WildVTON scores are not directly comparable, and the code-release link disappears, but these qualifications do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BooW-VTON and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. The comparison includes all supplementary material in v2; v1 ends with references and has no supplementary section.

after.justification: v2 reports original paired and unpaired evaluations, component ablations, application examples and supplementary attention analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original qualitative comparisons, FID/KID results on four datasets, and component ablations.

results.title:
BooW-VTON: Boosting In-the-Wild Virtual Try-On via Mask-Free Pseudo Data
  Training

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims: text-based object localization through TMPS/PRS, coherent editing through PCD, and background preservation through ABP without reference style images or supplied segmentation masks. The new name and editing terminology do not materially expand these claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of the patch-size fidelity/stylization tradeoff, smooth boundaries versus binary segmentation, and the expanded evaluation's quality-speed balance and generalization implications. The existing limitation concerning CLIP's coverage of unfamiliar objects and styles is retained.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies PRS threshold tau = 2, documents the default 64–128 patch-size range, and explains foreground masking and cropping for evaluation in Appendix C. It also clarifies that optimization uses only the source image and texts. These disclosures do not demonstrate changes to previously run experiments.

E1.justification: The work retains text-guided object editing of natural images, COCO 2017 evaluation, and color, texture, artistic-style and complex-prompt scenarios. The expanded COCO sample and new application illustrations retain the existing task and input requirements.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the existing baselines and adds pix2pix-zero, LEDITS++, local-prompt-mixing and StylerDALLE. The user study adds FlexIT, LEDITS++ and Null-text inversion as competitors. Appendix B.5 also compares the proposed outputs with an ODISE-masked variant.

E3.justification: The original 16-image, 10-style evaluation remains. v3 adds a 50-image, 500-output evaluation with comparative timing, fixed and variable patch-size controls, and two user-study rounds involving different competitor sets. The reported participant count remains 50. These substantially extend evaluation design without establishing changes to the original training setup.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss ablations, training visualization, complex-prompt examples and failure cases, v3 adds fixed and adaptive patch-size sensitivity experiments in Tables 4–5. Appendix B.5 and Figure 11 add a boundary-artifact case comparing unmasked outputs with ODISE-masked outputs, extending analysis of the patch-based design.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Appendix B.3 retains the same 10-repeat timing procedure. The additional user-study round introduces different comparison conditions, rather than repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original values in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged, while v3 adds baseline, sensitivity and expanded-evaluation results. Table 7 reports SimF 0.31, ConF 3.09 and PSNRB 26.71 for the proposed method. User-study style/background/content preferences change from 65.1/65.7/82.2% to averages of 66/64.4/78.6%. Changed samples and comparison panels prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains or losses.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2, losses in Equations 1–6, StyleNet architecture and target-text construction remain unchanged. The TEXTOC-to-Style-Editor renaming and newly documented threshold and patch-size range do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v3 renames the paper and method, revises selected introductory and related-work passages, and retains most methodological prose. Complex-input experiments move to Appendix D, the mask-guided comparison moves into Section 4.5, and references move before the appendices. The overall narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the main comparison table and image grid, adds Tables 4–5 and 7, and introduces application, segmentation-comparison and metric-visualization figures. Existing appendix galleries are enlarged, detail crops are added, and several figures are relocated. These are substantive display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: Sections 2.1 and 2.3 update the discussion with attention-based style transfer and more detailed diffusion-editing context, including AdaAttN, Aespa-Net and newer editing methods. ArtFlow, VQGAN-CLIP and Generative Artisan are removed. The central positioning around content-preserving, mask-free object editing remains.

T1.justification: The mathematical method, loss definitions and algorithms are retained, with no new formal assumptions, proofs or derivations. Equation 7 replaces the abbreviated foreground-image notation with an explicit masked image in the cosine-similarity denominator, clarifying the existing definition.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the retained method: patch-size tests and the boundary comparison examine previously untested design choices, additional baselines broaden comparison, and the larger COCO evaluation tests whether findings persist across more images. Newly disclosed settings improve reproducibility. The user-study average across different panels is less directly interpretable, and generalization evidence remains COCO-based, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, renamed from TEXTOC to Style-Editor. All 18 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v3, including appendices, support comparison. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable, and relocated material can be matched.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds patch-size experiments, a segmentation-mask comparison, an expanded quantitative evaluation and another user-study comparison round.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative evaluations, loss ablations, timing measurements, qualitative editing results and a 50-participant user study.

results.title: Style-Editor: Text-driven object-centric style editing

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction redefine the central contributions around visual encoding and a novel deformation-based learning task. V1 instead emphasizes pixel-to-point aggregation, LG-Net, and geometrical similarity. V2 makes efficiency and preprocessing requirements explicit goals and broadens its practical applicability claims, while retaining annotation-free full/partial matching as the core problem.

C2.justification: V2 adds the interpretation that reconstruction objectives cause mode collapse and that deformation-based learning avoids it, supported by new ablation discussion. It qualifies the existing orientation limitation using bounded rotation tests and adds explicit limitations concerning non-real-time execution and the need for overlap prediction when training on raw scans.

D1.justification: V2 supplies detailed attention-block diagrams, dataset construction/splits, hardware and PyTorch information, and a hyperparameter table specifying neighborhood sizes, image resolution, epochs, learning-rate decay, and softmax scheduling. It also adds a code-repository URL. These substantially expand documentation beyond v1; newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to previously unspecified implementation choices.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained human, TOSCA, spleen, and real-scan coverage, v2 evaluates GarmCap garments, pancreas shapes, and SHREC’07-Fourleg/SHREC’20 quadrupeds. It also adds a SHREC’19 partial-view training/testing scenario and synthetic training evaluations using SURREAL and SMAL (Sections 4, B, and C).

E2.justification: V2 adds NDP, AMM, and PointSetReg to the full-shape comparison, and PointSetReg to partial matching. RMA-Net, HSTR, and Elementary participate in supplementary comparisons. Conversely, PN-AE and DG-AE disappear from the retained spleen comparison. These are changes in evaluated comparators, not merely citations.

E3.justification: The stated batch size changes from 6 to 2, while the principal SCAPE/FAUST splits remain unchanged. Added evaluation designs include training with one full reference and 516 partial scans, garment transfer experiments, and controlled noise/rotation tests. V2 also adds medical EMD measurements and correspondence accuracy at 1% tolerance in supplementary sparse-point evaluations.

E4.justification: V2 adds deformation-versus-reconstruction and loss-specific analyses, full/partial registration failure cases, and controlled noise/rotation robustness tests (Figure 4, Figures 13–15, and Table 11). Density generalization is retained. Ablations are substantially revised, while v1's cross-benchmark quantitative 'w/o LVM' rows disappear.

E5.justification: V1 reports no repeated-run uncertainty estimates. V2 Section C.3 first documents three testing rounds and reports means and standard deviations for noise and rotation perturbations in Table 11. This is limited to those tests and does not establish repeated training runs or uncertainty for the principal benchmark tables.

E6.justification: Reported results change extensively under the revised method/training: SCAPE-to-SCAPE error changes from 7.6 to 6.2, FAUST-to-FAUST from 4.6 to 5.4, and SHREC’16-CUTS from 21.2 to 16.9. Spleen CD changes from 2.9 to 2.3. V2 adds numerous application, robustness, and timing results. Some comparator values also change without explanation, including SE-ORNet's SCAPE-trained DT4D-H entry, from 15.5 to 27.7.

M1.justification: V2 adds a learned deformation graph whose graph-convolution and MLP components predict local rigid transformations. Its deformation, ARAP, and smoothness objectives replace v1's reconstruction/mapping objective combination. Correspondence estimation changes from cosine similarity to Euclidean-distance soft maps with top-10 selection. Visual encoding, LG-Net, geometrical similarity, and nearest-feature inference remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are extensively rewritten around DV-Matcher and four practical goals. Retained methodology explanations are condensed and reframed, dataset descriptions move into Appendix B, a Remarks subsection is introduced, and experiments are reorganized into standard benchmarks, applications, and robustness/ablation analysis.

P2.justification: V2 switches to a two-column layout, merges v1 Tables 1–2, transposes the density table, and restructures medical and ablation tables. The pipeline is redrawn; its existing visual-encoding/LG-Net subdiagrams move into the supplement. New deformer, registration, garment, and supplementary comparison displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work against iterative deformation methods, supervised deformation networks, and reconstruction-based correspondence learning. Section 3.4 explicitly distinguishes its use of visual features from I2P-MAE. References newly include RMA-Net, PointSetReg, ARAP-related work, and rotation representations; NDP and AMM were already cited in v1 despite becoming evaluated baselines only later.

T1.justification: V2 substantially expands the mathematical formulation with sampled deformation graphs, transformation prediction, and deformation/ARAP objectives (Section 3.3 and Appendix A), replacing the earlier reconstruction/mapping formulation. The geometrical similarity definition is retained. No theorems or proofs are added; the new ARAP description contains inconsistencies, including six-dimensional rotations in the main text versus axis-angle terminology in the supplement.

improvement.justification: Beyond v1's component ablations, v2 directly examines deformation versus reconstruction, quantifies noise/rotation robustness with variability, reports runtime limitations, and substantially documents implementation (Table 6, Table 11, Appendix A, and Table 12). These materially strengthen validation and reproducibility. The loss of cross-benchmark visual-feature ablations and new reporting inconsistencies, including ARAP notation and conflicting DiffFMaps categorization in Tables 1 and 11, weaken parts of the presentation but do not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Despite the new title, both PDFs describe the same research lineage, with matching authors, retained components, and overlapping experiments. All supplied pages are readable. V1 ends after its references; v2 includes supplementary Sections A–D.

after.justification: V2 reports original DV-Matcher experiments across human, animal, garment, and medical data, including additional ablations and controlled perturbation tests in its supplement.

before.justification: V1 reports original matching experiments, medical shape-analysis results, density generalization tests, and component ablations in Tables 1–6 and Figures 1–4.

results.title:
DV-Matcher: Deformation-based Non-Rigid Point Cloud Matching Guided by
  Pre-trained Visual Features

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: consistent open-world video depth without camera poses or optical flow, three-stage training supporting up to 110 frames, stitching for longer videos, zero-shot state-of-the-art performance, and downstream applications.

C2.justification: V2 expands the brief computational-cost caveat into a discussion of measured speed, memory requirements and shorter-segment mitigation. Appendix B argues that task determinism permits fewer denoising steps and explains guidance's tradeoff between sharper details, numerical accuracy and computation.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly documents disparity normalization, latent caching, EDM settings, memory-saving training techniques, per-stage memory consumption, exact ScanNet cropping, depth caps and least-squares alignment. V2 also identifies baseline variants and ensembling settings. These substantially extend reproducibility information without establishing that all newly disclosed settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same compiled realistic and synthetic training data, five quantitative benchmarks, and qualitative video/application domains. Appendix experiments reuse existing benchmarks. Revised illustrative clips do not establish distinct new task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains NVDS, ChronoDepth, Marigold, Depth-Anything and Depth-Anything-V2. However, Table S2 adds Marigold and Depth-Anything-V2 reference rows to the training-stage comparison, where v1 Table 2 compared only DepthCrafter stages. V2 also introduces runtime comparisons.

E3.justification: The reported main inference configuration changes from 25 denoising steps with guidance to five steps without guidance. V2 additionally introduces selected step budgets from 1 to 25, guidance controls, and timing measurements at 1024×576 on one A100. These substantially revise and extend evaluation settings; they do not establish changes to training budgets or benchmark metrics.

E4.justification: V2 retains the stitching ablation, extends training-stage analysis from Sintel to all four video benchmarks in Table S2, and adds denoising-step sensitivity and classifier-free-guidance analyses in Figures S1–S2 and Tables S1/S3. These examine substantial additional questions about efficiency, accuracy and visual detail.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. New results remain point estimates. The newly disclosed five-prediction Marigold ensemble describes inference configuration rather than statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: DepthCrafter's Table 1 values change, including Sintel AbsRel from 0.292 to 0.270 and KITTI AbsRel from 0.110 to 0.104, under revised inference settings; baseline values remain unchanged. Table 2 now shows consistent improvement across stages. Table 3 and Tables S1–S3 add substantial runtime, sensitivity and ablation results.

M1.justification: V1 explicitly adopts classifier-free guidance; v2 Appendix B.3 disables it for the main experiments while retaining it as an option. The conditioning architecture, three-stage training and long-video initialization/stitching procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 edits the abstract, introduction and related-work prose, renames Section 3.3, separates limitations into Section 4.5, and organizes new supplementary material into Appendices A–B. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation with Table 3, Figures S1–S2 and Tables S1–S3. It also revises Figure 4's example clips and temporal-profile panels, changes annotation colors, relocates existing displays, and places table captions above their tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including Depth Pro, Lotus, Metric3D v2, ViewCrafter and work on fine-tuning image-conditional diffusion models. It removes several video-generation references and the standalone classifier-free-guidance citation. The central positioning against image-only methods and ChronoDepth's short temporal context remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds explicit mathematical definitions of previously unspecified EDM preconditioning functions, loss weighting and the training noise distribution in Equations 5–7. These extend the mathematical specification without introducing a new theorem or proof; Equations 1–4 remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves important inference choices, practical costs and reproduction settings insufficiently documented. V2 addresses these gaps through controlled step/guidance experiments, training-stage ablations across four benchmarks, explicit implementation and preprocessing details, and measured speed/memory costs. This substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility while clarifying accuracy–detail–efficiency tradeoffs. The revised inference settings limit direct interpretation of the updated scores as performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DepthCrafter, with matching central methods and benchmarks. Text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains readable Appendices A–B.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results and additional runtime, denoising-step, training-stage and guidance evaluations in Table 3 and Tables S1–S3.

before.justification: Table 1 reports original depth-estimation results, while Table 2 and Figure 6 report training and inference ablations.

results.title:
DepthCrafter: Generating Consistent Long Depth Sequences for Open-world
  Videos

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on the egocentric dataset, annotation method, and pressure estimation with hand-pose inputs. V2's abstract and introduction additionally claim the first model jointly estimating hand pose, mesh, and pressure localized in 3D, and explicitly establish two benchmarks. This substantially broadens the claimed contribution beyond image-projected pressure estimation.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of how hand-centric UV pressure resolves spatial ambiguity, why coarse UV supervision matters, and how HaMeR features may support generalization. Section 10 expands the discussion of nonplanar pressure sensing, instrumentation constraints, and background replacement. V1's gesture-specific interpretation is removed, while the planar, indoor-capture, and single-hand limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands capture documentation with marker-identification pseudocode, tracking thresholds, interpolation, circuitry, and synchronization timing (Sections 9.3–9.4). It specifies the second training phase's 500k iterations and PressureFormer loss weights. However, v1's explicit input dimensions, crop/augmentation margins, GPU/runtime, and licensing/hosting/file-format disclosures disappear; v2 instead states release upon acceptance. These are documentation changes, not proof of changes to the capture pipeline.

E1.justification: The recorded EgoPressure corpus, participants, and gestures remain unchanged. V2 adds evaluation of pressure localized on hand meshes, supervised hand-pose estimation through HaMeR fine-tuning, and qualitative testing on unseen objects and scenes (Section 7.3, Figure 15, Table 8). These extend task and test-environment coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 adds PressureVisionNet with HaMeR-predicted poses to both existing exocentric comparisons: seen cameras and unseen cameras. V1 includes this comparator only in the egocentric comparison. The original RGB-only and ground-truth-pose comparators remain.

E3.justification: V1 states a seven-participant training and three-participant held-out split, despite Table 2 describing all 21 participants; v2 specifies 15 participants for training/validation and six for testing. This is a substantive reported protocol revision, without establishing reruns of retained scores. V2 also introduces all-camera PressureFormer comparisons, UV-map evaluation, and MPJPE/reconstruction-error evaluation for fine-tuned HaMeR.

E4.justification: V2 adds a PressureFormer ablation testing coarse UV supervision (Table 4, Figure 13) and qualitative generalization analysis on unseen objects and scenes (Figure 15). Conversely, v1's five-category gesture analysis and Table 3 disappear. The annotation-loss ablations and existing unseen-camera tests are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain demographic standard deviations and the same nail-tip error standard deviations: 4.9 mm for the annotation method and 6.3 mm for HaMeR (v1 Table 6; v2 Table 7). Neither introduces training-seed counts, repeated-model-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 scores and annotation-quality results remain, while v2 adds exocentric HaMeR-pose rows, PressureFormer results, and pose fine-tuning results; v1's gesture-category scores are removed. In v2 Table 4, UV contact IoU is 33.12 for PressureFormer versus 24.10 for pose-augmented PressureVisionNet. Table 8 reports MPJPE of 10.75 mm after HaMeR fine-tuning versus 18.58 mm for pretrained HaMeR. These are newly reported comparisons.

M1.justification: V2 retains the annotation pipeline and pose-augmented PressureVisionNet baseline but introduces PressureFormer (Section 5.2, Figure 9). Its transformer decoder combines HaMeR image features and mesh vertices, predicts pressure through UV projection and convolution, and uses differentiable rendering with UV and image-pressure losses. This adds a substantial prediction architecture.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and benchmark narrative, adds numbered contributions, and places the annotation method before the dataset description. The lettered appendices are reorganized into numbered supplementary sections, and several sections are removed. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond the new scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout and substantially rearranges retained displays. The opening montage is redesigned, v1 Figure 5 is split, and dataset-comparison tables distinguish surface and hand pressure. New architecture, UV-pressure, fine-tuning, marker, and synchronization figures and tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The related-work categories and most prior work remain. V2 adds focused references including EgoTouch, StegoType, TouchInsight, and newer tactile-sensing work, while removing references such as DEP-RL and Adam. It also explicitly positions PressureFormer against the image-plane pressure representations of PressureVision and PressureVision++.

T1.justification: V2 formally defines PressureFormer's weighted UV and image cross-entropy objective in Equation 4. The existing annotation, geometry, contact, and temporal-regularization equations are retained after renumbering. The mathematical addition is limited; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1 provides mesh-level annotations but primarily benchmarks image-projected pressure. V2 directly evaluates learned pressure on the hand mesh, tests the contribution of UV supervision, and demonstrates improved HaMeR accuracy after fine-tuning (Tables 4 and 8). This substantially strengthens evidence for the dataset's intended 3D uses, while detailed capture documentation improves reproducibility. Removing gesture-level analysis and some training and licensing disclosures is a material drawback, and unseen-object generalization remains qualitative, but the added validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EgoPressure and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The retained dataset and annotation pipeline can be matched reliably despite extensive reorganization and added experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds PressureFormer evaluations, a UV-loss ablation, unseen-object examples, and HaMeR fine-tuning results.

before.justification: V1 reports original pressure-estimation experiments, annotation-quality measurements, manual verification, and loss ablations, including Tables 2–6.

results.title:
EgoPressure: A Dataset for Hand Pressure and Pose Estimation in
  Egocentric Vision

C1.justification: Both versions claim that a small, bounded number of adaptively spaced mesh shells enables sorting-free rasterization, better fuzzy-object representation than single-surface approaches, and faster rendering than volumetric alternatives on modest hardware. V2 emphasizes smartphones more explicitly but retains the contribution's meaning and scope.

C2.justification: V2 revises the explanation for inward initialization: v1 emphasizes transparent outer layers losing gradients, whereas v2 emphasizes outward geometry expansion and poor test-view generalization. It also explains the baked-versus-implicit quality gap and adds grazing-angle limitations and the possible use of textured fins. Existing sparse-view, thin-structure, and solid-scene limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Section S1 supplies previously missing network widths, activations, encodings, density-schedule endpoints, finite-difference settings, ray-sample counts, batch limits, and data-loading information. V2 also identifies the 3DGS web viewer and its sorting behavior and explicitly states that its final quality metrics come from WebGL renders. These additions substantially improve implementation and evaluation reproducibility.

E1.justification: Both evaluate Shelly, the custom plushy and hairy-monkey scenes, DTU scans 83 and 105, and NeRF-Synthetic in the supplement. The smartphone and laptop environments also remain the same. Added comparisons use this existing coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds MobileNeRF to the speed/memory comparison in Table 2 and to the existing Custom image-quality comparison in Table 3 and Table S1. These comparisons were absent in v1. QuadFields' memory result remains available in the Table 3 caption rather than being removed.

E3.justification: V2 adds optimization conditions capping 3DGS at 50,000 and 75,000 Gaussians, introducing resource-budget controls in Table 2. The principal training budgets, image-quality metrics, cleaned Shelly evaluation, and stated 720p timing devices remain unchanged. Newly specified network and sampling settings primarily document existing experiments.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds an outside-versus-inside shell-initialization ablation: outside initialization yields 30.85 PSNR versus 34.25 for the full 5-Mesh model. Figures S5 and S6 add qualitative comparisons with capped 3DGS and MobileNeRF. The previous four ablations, texture-resolution study, and solid-scene generalization analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both primarily provide point estimates and averages across scenes; the discussed logistic-distribution standard deviation is a model parameter, not experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Reported quality, speed, and memory results change substantially across the main and supplementary tables. For example, 7-Mesh smartphone speed changes from 27.5 to 42 FPS under the stated 720p Samsung A52s setup, while Shelly PSNR changes from 34.331 to 34.50. V2 also adds comparison and ablation results and corrects 3DGS Shelly SSIM/LPIPS from 0.964/0.064 to 0.975/0.089, matching the retained per-scene values. The PDFs do not explain the causes of all numerical revisions.

M1.justification: Both versions use nested k-SDF shells, learned offsets, view-dependent appearance and transparency, fixed-order blending, and staged optimization followed by mixed-resolution texture baking. V2 supplies architectural details and clarifies sampling descriptions without establishing a change to the underlying procedure.

P1.justification: V2 extensively edits the abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, evaluation, and limitations. It consolidates v1 Sections 4.3–4.5 into Section 4.3 and reorganizes the supplement into S1–S4. The title terminology also changes from 'Multiple' to 'Layered' meshes.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn with an additional explanatory panel, and Figure 6 switches from laptop to smartphone results with expanded comparisons. The two ablation tables are merged, the resolution study is relocated, and supplementary displays are reorganized. Render-buffer figures gain blending-weight panels, and new Figures S5–S6 present qualitative comparisons.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly grounds the representation in classical textured-shell fur rendering, citing Kenwright and Lengyel, and distinguishes its learned shells from Gaussian Shell Maps and Gaussian Frosting. It also adds SuGaR and implementation references. This materially expands the discussion of closely related foundations and alternatives beyond v1's positioning.

T1.justification: The rendering equations, shell construction, blending formulation, and transparency attenuation remain mathematically equivalent. Distinguishing relative from cumulative offsets clarifies existing notation. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves substantial reproducibility omissions through Section S1 and strengthens evidence for its central mobile-rendering claim through MobileNeRF timings and Gaussian-count controls. The initialization ablation tests a previously unquantified design choice, and corrected 3DGS averages restore agreement with the appendix. Better treatment of prior shell methods and clearer limitations further improve the paper. Unexplained numerical revisions and the retained Shelly comparability caveat limit interpretation, but the documentation and evidential gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Volumetric Surfaces work, despite the title changing from 'Multiple Meshes' to 'Layered Meshes'. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, references, and supplementary material support comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional baseline comparisons and an initialization ablation in Table 4.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction-quality results, rendering-speed measurements, ablations, and supplementary experiments on fully solid scenes.

results.title: Volumetric Surfaces: Representing Fuzzy Geometries with Layered Meshes

C1.justification: The central claim of inexpensive, high-performance conversion of pretrained ANNs remains. v2 reframes it around inference-scale complexity, makes delay selection an explicit contribution, extends claimed applicability to video, and proposes online on-chip conversion. These refine and extend the existing thesis rather than replace it.

C2.justification: v2 explains how spike propagation delays motivate the evaluation window and why one-time threshold optimization differs from timestep-specific calibration. Appendix G acknowledges LCP's timing advantage at 32 steps. The integration claim is qualified from improvement at all timesteps to most timesteps; the broad performance/cost and architectural limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability URL, delay-estimation and inference pseudocode, explicit ResNet architecture distinctions, and timing hardware information. Video implementation details include 15 fps, five 16-frame clips per video, and 112×112 crops. These substantially expand the documented information needed to reproduce and interpret the experiments.

E1.justification: v2 retains ImageNet, Pascal VOC/SBD, and COCO coverage and adds video classification on a Kinetics-400 subset using MC3-18 and R3D-18 (Section 5.6, Table 3). This extends evaluation from still images to spatiotemporal inputs and action recognition.

E2.justification: v2 adds QCFS to the integration comparison and includes QCFS and ACP in the main ImageNet comparison; ACP previously appeared only in the integration experiment. The LCP/ACP integration comparisons remain. v1's Figure 1 comparison with direct and hybrid training methods is removed, substantially changing the comparison scope.

E3.justification: Appendix D changes VOC calibration from 5/6 to 4/5 dataset traversals for FCN/DeepLab and detection calibration from 1000 to 5000 iterations. Reported ImageNet and detection preprocessing also changes. New protocols include the 12000/7881-video calibration/test split, video-level clip aggregation, and conversion-time comparisons using the same 4090 GPU environment.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit delayed-evaluation ablation, a delay-length sensitivity study across four inference budgets, QCFS integration analysis, and conversion-time scaling analysis. v1's clipping-error convergence plot is removed. The iteration-count sensitivity study and appendix detection/segmentation example grids are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the empirical results. v2 continues reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Numerous scores change: ImageNet ResNet-34 accuracy at 32 steps changes from 59.03% to 64.88%, while ResNet-18 at 512 steps changes from 69.66% to 69.21%. These accompany method/protocol revisions, so they are not same-setting gains or losses. v2 adds QCFS, video, and timing results and removes the 512-step segmentation/detection columns. Existing LCP/ACP integration scores and energy estimates remain.

M1.justification: The core threshold-balancing, channel-wise threshold, and pre-neuron max-pooling procedures remain. v2 adds data-dependent delay selection using an estimated first-spike time and t0 = min(estimated delay, T - 4), extending v1's fixed-window evaluation. The written threshold update also drops the 1/N normalization. These are localized procedural revisions.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and methodological explanations receive extensive editing, with revised terminology and notation. Experiments are reorganized to lead with integration and separate ablation, iteration, and delay analyses. The appendices are presented as supplementary material and gain a training-cost discussion.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 1–2 are redesigned, Figure 3 is recomposed, and a delay-sensitivity figure and timing table are added. Comparison tables are restructured. The existing appendix example grids are relocated and relabeled as Figures S1–S2, with their image content unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 expands citations to recent calibration, conversion, and spiking-transformer work, including FTBC and unified optimization, and adds video-related references. It explicitly positions delay selection as building on Hwang et al.'s delayed evaluation. The underlying distinction between backpropagation-dependent learning and lightweight conversion remains.

T1.justification: The conversion-error bound, max-pooling theorem, and their proofs remain substantively intact. v2 adds the delayed-window relation and first-spike-time estimate in Equations 18–19, corrects the preceding-layer threshold index in Equation 2, and revises the update-rule normalization and summation in Appendix B.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central efficiency claim through measured same-hardware conversion times in Appendix G, replacing reliance on largely qualitative or estimated cost comparisons. Dedicated delay-selection tests, broader validation, and improved implementation documentation also strengthen the paper. These gains outweigh the removed convergence analysis, although changed protocols prevent interpreting revised headline scores as controlled performance improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ANN-SNN conversion work despite the changed title and presentation. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on those tasks, plus video classification, delayed-evaluation analyses, and measured conversion times.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, segmentation, and detection experiments, conversion ablations, and energy estimates.

results.title:
Inference-Scale Complexity in ANN-SNN Conversion for High-Performance
  and Low-Power Applications

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contributions: unified shape/texture/material representation, scalable primitive latent diffusion, high-quality asset extraction, and image/text-conditioned generation. Additional evaluations and applications do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of initialization failures, compression artifacts, extraction requirements and the distribution mismatch motivating channel-wise normalization. Its new benchmark discussion acknowledges stronger visual quality from some reconstruction baselines while arguing geometric advantages. The original limitations paragraph is retained in A.1.2.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly documents normalization statistics from 50k samples, 518×518 image conditioning, default materials for assets lacking PBR information, conversion pseudocode, and cuBVH/PyMCubes implementation references. User-study presentation and anonymization/randomization are also clarified. Earlier hardware, training and inference details are largely relocated unchanged.

E1.justification: Objaverse coverage is retained, while v2 adds evaluation on GSO scanned household objects, an explicitly documented casual-phone-input case, and mask-constrained 3D inpainting and interpolation demonstrations. These extend the evaluated data and task requirements beyond v1's fitting and image/text-to-3D generation.

E2.justification: v2 broadens comparisons at representation, compression and generation levels: Sparse Points is added qualitatively in Figure 4, Unique3D in Figure 10(c), and PCA/DCT in Figure 17. The original generation comparisons are retained. Sparse Points does not receive a numerical row in Table 1.

E3.justification: A.2.1 introduces evaluations using 600 Objaverse and 300 GSO objects, random environmental lighting, 4096 sampled mesh points, and KID, material KID, FPD, KPD, coverage and matching-distance metrics. New ablations introduce additional compression and extraction controls. Previously reported training budgets and default sampling settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds initialization comparisons (Table 8, Figure 16), PCA/DCT compression analyses (Figure 17), material/UV/inpainting extraction ablations (Figure 18), and differentiable-rendering refinement (Figure 19). Inner- and thin-structure cases are also added. Earlier scaling, diversity and compression-rate analyses are retained, often relocated.

E5.justification: The reporting practice remains aggregate scores, preference percentages and qualitative variation across random seeds. v2 introduces no repeated-run summaries, explicit experimental seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. Additional benchmark rows do not change uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original numerical entries are retained, while v2 adds benchmark results in Tables 5–6, initialization PSNRs in Table 8, latent-FID entries in Table 7 and qualitative findings. For example, GSO FPD is 16.16 for ours versus 21.54 for InstantMesh, whereas reported KID (×10^-2) is 1.38 versus 0.91. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over matched v1 evaluations.

M1.justification: The core PrimX fitting, patch VAE and diffusion model remain unchanged. v2 adds mask-guided inpainting (Figure 7) and optional refinement through image-reconstruction gradients (A.2.10, Figure 19), extending inference applications. Newly documented normalization and conversion details do not independently establish changes to the underlying training pipeline.

P1.justification: Implementation details, user study, scaling, diversity and limitations move into a structured appendix. The main experimental narrative is condensed and reorganized, related-work headings and passages are revised, and the discussion becomes a shorter conclusion. This is substantial restructuring of retained content.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and extensively resizes and relocates retained displays. It adds application and ablation figures, Tables 5–6 and 8, and a latent-FID column in Table 7. The earlier combined generation gallery is expanded into separate image- and text-conditioned galleries.

R1.justification: A.1.1 substantially expands positioning against implicit vector sets, PrimDiffusion, M-SDF and 3DGS, explaining template independence, material modeling, renderability and token efficiency. v2 removes the early GAN background and adds cited works including 3DQD, XCube, MeshFormer and Unique3D.

T1.justification: The opacity expression uses the RGB field in v1 Equation 6 but the SDF field in v2 Equation 8, correcting its mismatch with the accompanying explanation. v2 also reverses the written SDF sign convention in Equation 1. Most remaining mathematical formulations are equivalent; no substantial theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v1's image-to-3D comparisons rely primarily on qualitative examples and user preferences; v2 adds objective appearance, geometry and coverage evaluations on Objaverse and GSO. New controlled ablations and important normalization/conversion disclosures substantially strengthen validation and reproducibility. The mixed rankings still require qualification of broad superiority wording, but the expanded evidence resolves important evaluation and documentation gaps.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 3DTopia-XL work. Their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison, including the complete Appendix A in v2. v1 ends with references and has no separately labeled appendix.
