after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Objaverse/GSO generation benchmarks, component ablations and application demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original representation-fitting measurements, generation comparisons, a user study, and ablation and scaling results.

3DTopia-XL: Scaling High-quality 3D Asset Generation via Primitive
  Diffusion

C1.justification: The contribution expands from image-trained visual context summarization to dynamic compression, curriculum learning, and composite/VICO training. v4 adds claims of minimal loss at 16× compression and broader leadership among comparable-size models. Its headline long-context demonstration changes from 1024 frames at nearly 100% accuracy to 2048 frames at about 95%.

C2.justification: v4 introduces explanations of complementary image/video supervision, the need to train with dynamic compression, and attention savings versus additional VST computation. Supplement A newly acknowledges substantial training-memory costs and errors beyond 1000 frames. These substantially expand v1's limited discussion of mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v4 adds learning rates, batch sizes, training hardware, Adam/ZeRO-2-offload/bf16 settings, benchmark-specific frame budgets, and VICO construction details and prompts. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond v1. However, Section 4.1 specifies linear learning-rate decay while Supplement F specifies cosine decay.

E1.justification: Training expands from image-only data to single-image, multi-image, video, and synthetic action-order supervision. Evaluation adds VideoVista, VideoChatGPT Bench, MVBench, GQA, POPE, and SEEDBench. MME and MMBench were already evaluated in v1 and are retained.

E2.justification: v4's main comparisons add VideoLLaMA2, Video-CCAM, and PLLaVA, while dropping Claude3-Opus and InternVL-Chat-V1.5 from their corresponding benchmark comparisons. New controlled compression comparisons include pooling, Q-Former, LLaMA-Adapter, and C-Abstractor. Supplementary image comparisons additionally evaluate VoCo-LLaMA.

E3.justification: v4 adds MLVU-test evaluation, memory and FLOPs measurements, a retrieval grid extending to 2048 frames, matched 16× compression comparisons, and testing at an unseen 32× ratio. Supplement D introduces backbone and training-regime controls. The main LLaVA-Next-Video comparator also changes from 7B to 34B.

E4.justification: v1's compression-ratio ablation expands into studies of dynamic compression during training versus testing, interval size, curriculum learning, data mixtures, VICO scaling, backbone choice, and context length. Qualitative comparisons and appendix cases expand substantially. The advertisement example is retained with an added LLaMA-VID comparison; the earlier surveillance-anomaly example is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Under revised methods and training, v4 replaces MLVU-dev M-avg 57.0 with 64.9 and VideoMME without/with-subtitle scores 51.0/54.4 with 55.5/61.0. Numerous benchmark, efficiency, ablation, and image results are added. v1's VideoMME duration and VNBench task breakdowns disappear. These replacements do not establish isolated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The interleaved VST/KV compression mechanism remains, but fixed-size chunks become content-dependent intervals using CLIP similarities and depth scores. v4 also introduces progressive compression-ratio training and composite/VICO data curation, replacing v1's image-only training with randomly sampled ratios of 2, 4, and 8.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes a dedicated section, training is integrated into the method discussion, and detailed material is reorganized into supplementary Sections A–G. 'Visual Context Latent Summarization' is reframed as 'VST Compression.'

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. v4 adds a radar overview, redraws the architecture, combines retrieval heatmaps with resource plots, and adds data-generation diagrams. The original benchmark tables are consolidated and restructured, with numerous new ablation tables, plots, and qualitative displays.

R1.justification: A dedicated related-work section and Supplement B substantially expand positioning against LongVA and VoCo-LLaMA. New sparsity references motivate compression, and VideoLLaMB is credited for the segmentation approach. Conversely, v1's explicit attribution to Activation Beacon and its corresponding reference are removed.

T1.justification: v4 adds the depth-score definition governing adaptive interval boundaries and a detailed computational-cost derivation separating attention and other operations for compressed processing (Supplement D, Equations 7–10). The earlier VST attention formalization is also shortened and revised in Supplement C. The new cost analysis substantially extends the mathematical treatment.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses v1's limited validation of compression and efficiency through matched alternative-compressor comparisons, quantitative resource measurements, and systematic mechanism and training ablations. Expanded implementation details and explicit limitations further strengthen the paper. These gains are substantial, although conflicting learning-rate schedules and Supplement D's disagreement between training-ablation prose and Table 3 limit reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Video-XL and retain the same underlying VST compression approach. Text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v1 has no appendix; v4 includes readable supplementary Sections A–G.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark, efficiency, compression, training, and data experiments, with additional results throughout the supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, needle-in-a-haystack results, compression ablations, and qualitative demonstrations.

results.title:
Video-XL: Extra-Long Vision Language Model for Hour-Scale Video
  Understanding

C1.justification: The central claims about character, motion and scene control remain. V2 adds an explicit abstract claim of outperforming prior methods by a large margin and recasts the existing controllable-synthesis task as a new task contribution; v1 already described video character replacement as an application.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands component-specific explanations: background distortions are attributed to absent scene guidance, limitations of 3D maps to undefined dense body-part labels, and reduced hand/foot confusion to canonical appearance transfer improving motion learning. These interpretations accompany new comparator and ablation evidence beyond v1's general architectural rationale.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies PyTorch, 80 GB GPU memory and 6,890 SMPL-anchored codes, and describes obtaining and fine-tuning comparator implementations. Initialization, frozen components and eight A100 GPUs were already documented. The project URL remains unchanged.

E1.justification: HUD-7K training data, AMASS/Mixamo motions, arbitrary-character animation and interactive real-world video scenarios remain. The new 100-clip evaluation formalizes testing within this existing coverage rather than introducing a distinct task or domain.

E2.justification: V1 cites animation methods but reports no direct baseline evaluation. V2 Figure 6 and Table 1 add qualitative and quantitative comparisons against Animate Anyone, Mimic-Motion and Champ, with reported fine-tuning on the authors' training data.

E3.justification: V2 introduces evaluation on 100 collected videos randomly truncated to 150-frame clips, using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS and FVD, plus baseline fine-tuning. The reported training batch size also changes from 4 to 8, while approximately 50,000 iterations and 24-frame training clips remain; this does not establish whether earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 Section 4.3 adds tests removing spatial decomposition, independent occlusion encoding and canonical appearance transfer, and replacing structured motion codes with 2D skeletons or 3D maps. Table 2 and Figures 7–8 provide quantitative and visual evidence; the occlusion-removal variant is shown qualitatively. V1 contains no corresponding component ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's quantitative tables contain point estimates only.

E6.justification: V2 adds numerical results absent from v1. Table 1 reports MIMO at 25.210 PSNR, 0.883 SSIM, 0.125 LPIPS and 221.4 FVD, leading all three comparators on these metrics. Table 2 adds component results, including PSNR 22.148 without spatial decomposition. These are newly reported evaluations, not measured gains over v1 under matched settings.

M1.justification: The spatial decomposition, SMPL-anchored motion codes, canonical appearance transfer, scene/occlusion encoding, diffusion decoder and training objective are retained. Specifying 6,890 SMPL vertices adds implementation detail without establishing a changed method.

P1.justification: Most existing introduction and method prose is retained. V2 revises the abstract and contribution bullets, inserts Related Work before the method, groups implementation details, and converts the three numbered control subsections into paragraph headings. Much of the additional text documents new scientific comparisons rather than rewriting existing material.

P2.justification: The standalone diverse-character gallery in v1 Figure 5 is omitted, while selected motion and scene panels from v1 Figures 6–7 are condensed into v2 Figure 5. New baseline and ablation Figures 6–8 and Tables 1–2 substantially reorganize the experimental presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated Related Work section substantially expanding discussion of 3D human modeling and diffusion-based animation. Newly discussed works include NeuMan, HOSNeRF, AG3D and EVA3D, with fuller positioning around reconstruction costs, motion representation and human–scene interaction.

T1.justification: The spatial masking equation and diffusion noise-prediction loss remain equivalent. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs, and specifying the existing SMPL representation's vertex count introduces no new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V1 relies on selected visual demonstrations without comparative or component validation. V2 substantially addresses this deficiency through a defined evaluation protocol, three-baseline comparisons and targeted ablations in Tables 1–2 and Figures 6–8. These additions make the central design choices considerably more assessable. The compressed character gallery and unavailable supplementary comparisons limit some evidence, but the main-text validation provides a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIMO framework, and their text, equations and exhibits support reliable comparison. Neither contains an appendix. V2 references a separate supplement; its unavailable results are excluded from this assessment.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthesis examples, quantitative baseline comparisons and component ablations in Figures 5–8 and Tables 1–2.

before.justification: V1 reports original generated-video examples demonstrating character, motion and scene control, particularly in Figures 5–7.

results.title: MIMO: Controllable Character Video Synthesis with Spatial Decomposed Modeling

C1.justification: The central claims about open Molmo/PixMo models, avoiding proprietary-VLM distillation for the main models, and competitive benchmark/human performance persist. v2's introduction additionally presents overlapping cropping, efficient multi-annotation training, and systematic model/data design insights as contributions. The more explicit abstract comparisons largely repeat claims already present in v1's introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations and qualifications concerning crop-mismatch failures, weaker reasoning performance, text-only knowledge loss, caption-metric errors, and differences between its human evaluation and Chatbot Arena. It explicitly cautions that caption/downstream correlation does not establish causality. Appendix H also acknowledges that using closed text-only LLMs leaves the data-generation pipeline incompletely open.

D1.justification: v1 gives a high-level recipe and promises full data and training-code releases; v2 states that datasets and source code are available. Appendices A–C and Tables 6–8 add architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, sampling rates, prompts, preprocessing, precision and gradient handling, sequence limits, evaluation details, H100 hardware, and training times. Much of this is newly disclosed information about retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds text-only knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, and programming evaluations, plus experiments incorporating Tulu 3 training data. It also evaluates real-world clocks from COCO, OpenImages, and Clock Movies, and introduces dedicated captioning and pointing evaluation sets. The original Flickr Count benchmark is retained as PixMo-Count, rather than being a new benchmark.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Llama-3.2V-11B-Instruct and Llama-3.2V-90B-Instruct. The Chameleon-7B/30B human-evaluation entries in v1 Figure 4 are omitted from v2's reported comparison. Additional comparisons introduce a specialized clock-reading model, the underlying Qwen2-7B language model, and a broader externally reported Chatbot Arena comparator set in Tables 9, 10, and 13.

E3.justification: New studies introduce caption scoring, point-assignment evaluation, controlled crop configurations, high-resolution post-training, and a balanced 500-question human ablation study distinct from the retained main study. Reported PixMo-Points image counts also change from 428k to 223k, and point-explanation images from 29k to 14k. These count revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun; newly disclosed original settings belong under D1.

E4.justification: v1 lacks corresponding systematic ablations. v2 Tables 2–5 and 15 test encoders, crops, dropout, pooling, caption conditioning, data scale/composition, and counting representations. Appendix D additionally investigates crop-mismatch failures and recovery, text-only knowledge loss and mitigation, opaque AI2D boxes, human-evaluation ties, and the relationship between caption quality and downstream accuracy.

E5.justification: v2 adds explicit 95% confidence intervals for externally reported Arena scores in Table 9 and a Pearson correlation/least-squares analysis across 22 ablations in Figure 9. Conversely, the boxes and whiskers accompanying v1's own-study Elo scores in Figure 4 disappear when those results are tabulated. Neither version documents repeated training seeds.

E6.justification: All 25 retained Table 1 rows have unchanged academic scores, including Molmo-72B's 81.2 average. However, v2 adds extensive ablation and supplementary results, including Molmo-7B-D's 68.2% clock-reading accuracy, Molmo-72B's 75.2 pointing F1, and text-only performance losses and recovery experiments. The new Arena scores concern a different evaluation, not a same-setting performance change.

M1.justification: The specified connector order changes from MLP projection followed by pooling in v1 Section 2 to pooling followed by MLP projection in v2 Section 2. v2 also introduces an optional high-resolution post-training adaptation in Appendix D. The core model family and two-stage pipeline remain; expanded architectural descriptions do not establish wholesale changes to the released models.

P1.justification: The introduction and technical exposition are extensively rewritten and subdivided. Data and Training become separate sections, the Release Plan section disappears, and appendices organize model, training, evaluation, results, ablations, data, examples, and related work. Existing material, including annotator questions, is relocated. The title also changes 'Multimodal Models' to 'Vision-Language Models.'

P2.justification: v2 redraws the architecture figure and adds dataset-overview, cropping, tokenization, mixture, diagnostic, and example figures, alongside numerous experimental and implementation tables. Table 1 gains Elo score/rank columns while v1's benchmark-summary and Elo plots disappear. The openness comparison is retained and relocated from v1 Figure 3 to v2 Figure 11.

R1.justification: v2 adds an extensive related-work discussion in Appendix H, covering contrastive encoders, multimodal architectures, instruction data, synthetic documents, grounding, and dependence on closed LLMs. It substantively compares PixMo with approaches such as GRES/RefCOCO and ExpertQA and discusses alternative architectures. This substantially expands v1's brief introductory positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix C newly defines caption precision and recall through atomic-statement matching and consistency judgments, then defines cap F1 from their image-averaged values. Appendix D specifies assignment-based pointing precision/recall and no-target cases. These are new task-specific mathematical definitions, beyond merely restating the standard F1 formula; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of controlled ablation evidence and reproducibility detail through Section 6 and Appendices A–E. It also exposes important failures and applicability limits, including crop sensitivity, text-only degradation, and less favorable independent human rankings. These gains outweigh the lost own-study Elo uncertainty display and occasional overclaims, such as the RealWorldQA summary not matching Table 1. The improvement comes from stronger evidence and transparency, while retained benchmark scores remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Molmo/PixMo research. The complete text, tables, and figures support reliable matching. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 includes substantial appendices A–H, all inspected.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds model/data ablations, clock-reading, pointing, and text-only experiments in Section 6 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Molmo results on 11 benchmarks, a human preference study, and AndroidControl in Section 4, Table 1, and Figures 2 and 4.

results.title:
Molmo and PixMo: Open Weights and Open Data for State-of-the-Art
  Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion add Delfys75 as a central contribution and claim favorable performance in a structured real-world benchmark. V1 centers its contributions on decoder-free estimation, dynamics beyond motion, extrapolation, and initialization robustness; those claims are retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations relating real-world baseline weaknesses to single-video training and spatial-transformer reconstruction, discusses prior rescaling, and identifies Euler-step tradeoffs and sliding-block parameter ambiguity. The principal limitations concerning absolute scale, discretization, interacting-object masks, and autonomous dynamics remain.

D1.justification: V2 provides recording specifications, camera controls, SAM2 mask annotation information, ground-truth measurement procedures, and detailed per-experiment training settings. It also specifies the previously described default initialization more precisely. A concrete code-and-data link and availability statement replace v1's promise of a future GitHub release; external availability was not checked.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on Delfys75: real pendulum, draining-water, sliding-block, exponentially decaying LED, and apparent-scale free-fall videos. This substantially expands physical and environmental coverage. V1's linear LED and pendulum examples remain in v2 Appendix A.9, alongside the retained synthetic datasets.

E2.justification: V2 adds an evaluated MSE-only comparator against the full MSE-plus-KL model in Appendix A.4 and Table 3; v1 only discusses its potential collapse. PAIG, NIRPI, and the PAIG-without-U-Net cost comparison remain. Extending the retained baselines to Delfys75 does not itself change their membership.

E3.justification: Delfys75 introduces three settings per system, five videos per setting, individual-video training, a 500-epoch budget for the proposed model, and experiment-specific temporal sampling and batch settings. Separately, the reported synthetic pendulum angle range changes from [-90,90] degrees to [-180,180] degrees; the PDFs do not establish whether that experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a KL-loss ablation testing latent collapse and parameter accuracy (Appendix A.4, Table 3, Figure 9), plus an Euler-step sensitivity study across intensity, Torricelli, and pendulum experiments (Appendix A.8, Table 6). The original initialization-robustness analyses remain.

E5.justification: The original mean-and-standard-deviation reporting over seven initializations is retained. V2 additionally documents ground-truth measurement uncertainty, including instrument resolution and standard deviations calculated across five or fifteen recordings (Appendix A.6, Table 4). Table 2 reports variability across five videos per setting, rather than additional initialization runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive Delfys75 results and both ablation result sets. For example, Table 3 reports oscillator parameters of 3.99 and 0.08 with KL, versus 5.7 and 6.6 with MSE alone. These are newly reported comparisons. The original oscillator estimates survive with equivalent rounding, and the earlier pendulum estimate remains 1.22 m against 1.20 m.

M1.justification: The encoder, Euler physics block, and MSE-plus-KL loss remain. V2 Section 5.4 introduces a Torricelli-specific adaptation, changing the KL target prior from N(0,1) to N(1,0.2) to accommodate square-root dynamics.

P1.justification: V2 substantially edits the abstract, introduction, methodological explanations, and discussion. It introduces a dedicated dataset section, consolidates the synthetic experiments, and moves the original real-world examples into the appendix. The author header also changes.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the method diagrams, adds dataset and ablation displays, and extensively reorganizes tables and figures. V1 Table 1 becomes v2 Figure 4b, replacing the separate encoder-versus-ground-truth panel; the cost table is transposed. The original real-world displays move to the appendix, with the LED visualization reformatted.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a dataset discussion positioning Delfys75 against Physics101 and distinguishes the approach from latent-control and equation-learning methods, including NewtonianVAE and LaSDI. Additional citations support annotation and oscillation discussions. The central positioning against PAIG and NIRPI remains.

T1.justification: V2 Equation 1 adds an affine constant term to the general ODE formulation. Section 4.1 and Appendix A.6 add physical equations and parameter-calibration derivations. The central Euler and loss derivations remain, with no new theorem or proof. Some added formulas are inconsistent, notably the Torricelli sign across Equations 15 and 23.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens two weak points in v1: limited real-world validation and the absence of direct loss-ablation evidence. Delfys75 adds structured comparisons across five physical systems, while the appendices test the KL term and temporal-step sensitivity and document measurement and training procedures. Some new calibration formulas remain internally inconsistent, particularly the Torricelli sign, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 11 pages of v1 and 13 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds results on Delfys75, a loss ablation, and an Euler-step sensitivity study.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic parameter-estimation experiments, baseline comparisons, initialization tests, and real-world LED and pendulum results.

results.title:
Learning Physics From Video: Unsupervised Physical Parameter Estimation
  for Continuous Dynamical Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, three introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the central claims of training-free temporal improvement, flexible teacher guidance, and prior distillation. Sections 2–3 additionally present optimization-based video-consistency guidance as an explicit contribution and claim priority for that formulation, adding a specific novelty claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explicit consistency-versus-dynamic-degree trade-off, interprets filtering as accelerating convergence and preserving the student's domain, and connects excessive interpolation to SDS-related blurring. Supplement H newly states the shared-VAE-space requirement and discusses the computational and detail-loss risks of decoding and re-encoding across incompatible spaces.

D1.justification: v3 clarifies that the pseudocode uses CFG++ throughout for presentation, while the experimental implementation switches back to CFG. It documents settings for the new filter, Open-Sora, and UniCtrl experiments and changes the printed project-page address. Most original prompt-selection and hyperparameter information is retained.

E1.justification: Both versions specify text-to-video evaluation using 800 prompts from VBench categories. Open-Sora adds model and scheduler configurations, without documenting a new dataset, task, population, or input scenario. The personalized-model domains and original qualitative galleries are retained.

E2.justification: The original AnimateDiff/LaVie comparisons with FreeInit remain. v3 adds UniCtrl and the UniCtrl-plus-VideoGuide combination to the AnimateDiff comparison in Table 7. Table 2 also adds unguided baseline timings to the existing timing comparison.

E3.justification: v3 adds RAFT-based dynamic degree as a fifth evaluation metric. New experiments introduce Open-Sora DiT configurations with DDIM and rectified-flow schedulers, filter-versus-no-filter controls over a longer interpolation sweep, and UniCtrl with motion injection degree 0.2. The original 800-prompt, 50-step DDIM evaluation settings remain documented.

E4.justification: Supplement A and Figure 5 newly isolate the low-pass filter's effects on consistency, imaging quality, and efficiency, extending the no-filter sweep to 50 interpolation steps. Supplements F and G add architecture/scheduler robustness and UniCtrl composability analyses. The original parameter ablations and CFG-versus-CFG++ analysis are retained, although reorganized.

E5.justification: Shared-seed qualitative comparisons remain, and neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The new filter plots show averages across prompts without introducing uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes all four AnimateDiff self-guided scores, including subject consistency from 0.9596 to 0.9520, and adds dynamic-degree results. Table 2 revises existing timings and adds baseline times. Figure 5 and Tables 6–7 introduce filter, Open-Sora, and UniCtrl findings. The original parameter-ablation, CFG++, and user-study values remain unchanged; the PDFs do not explain the revised existing scores.

M1.justification: The original interpolation, renoising, filtering, and self/external guidance procedures remain; Algorithms 1 and 2 are unchanged. Supplement F adds a velocity-based rectified-flow adaptation, with a corresponding inference update in Equation 18. The rewritten main derivation does not establish a replacement of the original DDIM procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, mathematical exposition, and results discussion undergo substantial rewriting, including increased teacher/student terminology. CFG discussion moves into the supplement, Section 3.3 is refocused on prior distillation, and existing appendix material is extensively reordered within a new supplementary structure. These changes exceed ordinary copyediting.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. The original six-panel qualitative comparison is redistributed between main Figure 3 and supplementary Figure 11, and the guidance-scale illustration moves to the supplement. v3 also transposes the CFG comparison table, expands the main results table, and adds filter plots and Open-Sora/UniCtrl displays.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands the optimization-guidance positioning through diffusion posterior sampling, decomposed diffusion sampling, score distillation, and consistency models, while removing the earlier DreamSampler citation. It also adds discussion of UniCtrl and I4VGen and references supporting DiT, rectified flow, and Open-Sora. The explicit optimization-priority claim changes its stated relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: v1 derives interpolation from a quadratic proximal objective using a temporally consistent reference latent. v3 replaces this reasoning with a teacher-denoising loss, gradient-based guidance, a different derivation of the interpolation coefficient, and a consistency-model/PF-ODE approximation in Sections 2–3. Supplement F additionally derives the rectified-flow formulation. These are substantive mathematical revisions.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens assessment of the central consistency, quality, and efficiency claims. Dynamic-degree measurements expose a previously unquantified motion trade-off; the controlled filter ablation tests a key component; and Open-Sora and UniCtrl experiments broaden validation. The shared-VAE limitation makes applicability more explicit. These additions address important evidential gaps in v1, although repeated-run uncertainty and explanations for revised existing scores remain absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VideoGuide by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved into the reorganized supplement.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds low-pass-filter experiments, Open-Sora evaluations, and quantitative and qualitative UniCtrl comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation experiments, parameter and CFG++ ablations, inference timings, qualitative examples, and a 30-participant user study.

results.title:
VideoGuide: Improving Video Diffusion Models without Training Through a
  Teacher's Guide

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: training-free improvement of structural plausibility, temporal consistency, and motion through two attention-based components, with negligible additional cost and applicability across video-generation backbones.

C2.justification: V3 corrects v1 Appendix A.4's reversed alpha/beta advice and explains motion suppression from excessive alpha and artifacts from excessive beta. It adds interpretations involving the guidance bottleneck and early determination of motion during denoising. The backbone-imposed performance limitation is retained.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies tau=7 for both main backbones, AnimateDiff's Realistic Vision V5.1 LoRA, and the one-dimensional FFT axis. These are additional implementation disclosures; the PDFs do not establish corresponding changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate open-domain text-to-video generation and SparseCtrl image-to-video generation. VBench supplies additional metrics and CogVideoX adds a backbone within the retained task; no new dataset, domain, or task requirements are documented.

E2.justification: V1 compares enhanced backbones with their vanilla versions. V3 adds an evaluated competing enhancement method: FreeInit appears in the qualitative comparison in Figure 9 and as AnimateDiff+FreeInit in Table 2, substantially extending the comparative evidence.

E3.justification: V3 replaces the stated 1,000-video optical-flow evaluation with a 200-video evaluation using six VBench metrics. New experiments introduce parameter sweeps, guidance-anchor and intervention-window controls, fivefold sampling, and CogVideoX. Attention-map discrepancy is also described as L2 rather than MSE, although the retained plots do not establish that this analysis was rerun.

E4.justification: V3 replaces v1's dedicated TSG/FME component comparison with broader alpha/beta/tau sensitivity analyses. Supplementary Section 8 and Figures 14–16 additionally investigate guidance-anchor choice, intervention timing, and whether increasing ordinary sampling steps reproduces the benefit.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly identifies means and standard deviations in the 100-versus-100 attention-map analysis. V3 retains the shaded plots but omits that explanation, reducing uncertainty documentation. Matched-seed user-study information remains unchanged; no increased run count or new statistical testing is reported.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports six VBench measures; for example, AnimateDiff dynamic degree is 0.4073 for vanilla, 0.2941 with FreeInit, and 0.5245 with ByTheWay. V1's standalone optical-flow results are removed, while user-study and MLLM percentages are retained. New ablation findings and CogVideoX examples add further results.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 retain temporal-attention interpolation, Fourier frequency reweighting, and adaptive beta, with equivalent Eqs. 3–7. Renaming and the CogVideoX demonstration do not document a changed method component or procedure.

P1.justification: The method and title are renamed, selected explanations and experimental paragraphs are revised, and supplementary sections are reordered. Most of the abstract, introduction, method exposition, and concluding narrative remain closely aligned with v1.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the method diagram, combines statistical plots, regroups qualitative examples, and restructures the quantitative tables. New comparison and ablation figures substantially change the visual presentation, while many earlier appendix examples are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: V3 adds FreeInit, UniCtrl, I4VGEN, and VBench references. Section 2.2 adds focused comparisons concerning competing approaches' inference costs and motion limitations, while retaining the broader related-work organization and research positioning.

T1.justification: The energy and Fourier definitions, Theorems 1–2, and adaptive-beta derivation are retained from v1 Appendix A.1 in v3 Section 10. Repeating the adaptive formula and replacing its piecewise expression with an equivalent maximum do not introduce new mathematical content.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses v1's lack of an evaluated competing enhancement method through FreeInit comparisons and adds six VBench quality/motion measures. Parameter, anchor, and sampling controls substantially strengthen support for design choices. These gains outweigh the removal of standalone optical-flow results and the dedicated component ablation, together with reduced uncertainty documentation. The improvement primarily concerns empirical validation, while the method and theory remain stable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from BroadWay to ByTheWay. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial layout changes.

after.justification: V3 retains original experimental results and adds VBench comparisons, parameter and sampling analyses, and CogVideoX demonstrations.

before.justification: V1 reports original video-generation experiments, user-study and GPT-4o assessments, optical-flow measurements, and qualitative ablations.

results.title:
ByTheWay: Boost Your Text-to-Video Generation Model to Higher Quality in
  a Training-free Way

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a large multilingual event-centric benchmark, evidence that existing retrieval models struggle, and the partial usefulness of modality-specific pipelines. Abstract and conclusion edits preserve these claims.

C2.justification: The expanded Table 4 caption explicitly interprets Chinese/Korean difficulty and modality-specific performance. The appendix adds concrete qualifications about transcription and translation errors, incomplete OCR coverage, and posting dates differing from event dates.

D1.justification: New Sections 8–9 provide extensive annotation instructions, including Label Studio interfaces, sampling rounds, resolution-based selection, minimum language/type coverage, query constraints, relevance decision rules, and escalation procedures. The introduction also adds a data-access link. v1 supplied substantially less operational documentation.

E1.justification: The collection, six languages, event and video categories, and query tasks remain the same. MSR-VTT comparisons are retained. Removing the results paragraph's reference to VALOR-32k does not establish lost coverage: v1's corresponding table already contained no VALOR-32k results.

E2.justification: Table 3 removes the fine-tuned VAST comparison on MSR-VTT, which reported R@10 of 0.896. Pretrained VAST and all comparators reporting MultiVENT 2.0 results remain.

E3.justification: No protocol revision is reported for the retained experiments: collection splits, ten-keyframe extraction, retrieval metrics, and 0/1/3 relevance scoring remain unchanged. The appendix's sampling rounds and selection rules are newly disclosed construction details, not evidence of changed experiments.

E4.justification: The language, video-type, query-type, and event-type analyses are retained unchanged, moving from Figure 4 to Table 4. Appendix examples illustrate annotation instructions rather than adding evaluated case studies or robustness analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 introduces no uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the unknown MultiVENT 2.0 average clip length with 145 seconds. Table 3 deletes the fine-tuned VAST MSR-VTT score of 0.896. All 39 retained retrieval scores, 96 subgroup scores, and Table 2 relevance percentages are unchanged.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction framework and baseline retrieval pipelines remain unchanged. The supplement documents the existing annotation workflow rather than introducing a revised algorithm or model.

P1.justification: v2 substantially expands the exposition through two structured annotation manuals with detailed subsections, decision rules, and worked examples. The main section sequence remains intact, with smaller wording, terminology, and author/affiliation edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds three annotation-interface figures, including two multipanel displays. It also rearranges Figure 3 panels and legends, relocates Table 1, simplifies Table 3, and relabels the former Figure 4 as Table 4 with an expanded caption.

R1.justification: Section 2 changes its characterization of DiDeMo filtering from excluding edited videos generally to excluding non-professional edited videos. The 43 cited works and the paper's broader research positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: No mathematical definitions, derivations, assumptions, or proofs are added or revised. The appendix's event and relevance definitions are operational annotation guidance.

improvement.justification: For this benchmark paper, v2 substantially improves reproducibility and usability by supplying data-access instructions and detailed guidance for creating queries and judging relevance. These additions address important documentation gaps in v1's central human-annotation process. Core empirical evidence is preserved; removing one peripheral fine-tuned MSR-VTT comparison is a limited loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MultiVENT 2.0 and are readable throughout. Their main text, tables, figures, and references can be matched reliably. v2 adds supplementary annotation guidelines; v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains the original MultiVENT 2.0 retrieval evaluations, subgroup results, and relevance-annotation outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval evaluations on MultiVENT 2.0, subgroup performance breakdowns, and relevance-annotation outcomes.

results.title:
MultiVENT 2.0: A Massive Multilingual Benchmark for Event-Centric Video
  Retrieval

C1.justification: v3 adds CDTS and its perceptual regularization as explicit contributions in the abstract and introduction. The central claim of using video world-model priors to improve 4D driving reconstruction, its novelty positioning, and the supported maneuver scope remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 explains temporal pairing as mitigating the real/synthetic data gap and regularization as promoting perceptual coherence; Section 8 interprets CDTS as improving vehicle-edge reconstruction. The former mixing-ratio tradeoff discussion disappears. Explanations concerning incomplete LiDAR supervision and FID's limited usefulness for speed changes are retained.

D1.justification: The new supplement supplies SVD initialization, 798 training videos and approximately 64K clips, optimizer settings, batch size, generator training iterations, H20 hardware, exact evaluation scene IDs and frame ranges, and user-study presentation details. These substantially improve reproducibility. Conversely, v1's explicit 50,000-iteration 4DGS budget disappears; v3's supplementary 50K count describes generator training.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate eight Waymo scenes using forward-facing views and lane-change, acceleration, and deceleration trajectories. v3 documents the generator's training data more precisely without establishing expanded coverage. Its nuScenes discussion concerns the cited source model, not an additional dataset used by this work.

E2.justification: PVG, S3Gaussian, and Deformable-GS remain the comparators in Tables 1–3. Supplementary Section 6 explains these existing baselines. The new CDTS variants are component ablations rather than additional comparison methods.

E3.justification: The ablation design adds a regularization-weight sweep and controls separating temporal pairing from regularization. The beta sweep and the lambda_novel=0.7 setting disappear. The established evaluation metrics, image resolution, clip length, and camera selection remain. Newly documented generator and user-study settings do not establish changes to those existing experiments.

E4.justification: The analyses substantially refocus on the new CDTS mechanism: v3 Table 5 tests regularization strength, Table 6 separately enables temporal pairing and regularization, and supplementary Figure 4 provides a visual ablation. The earlier mixing-ratio analysis is removed, while depth-loss testing and most of the novel-view loss-weight analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and user-preference percentages without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The newly described random left/right assignment in the user study is an experimental control, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Primary results are extensively revised for the CDTS method. Table 2 FID scores change from 79.54/76.24/82.67 to 71.52/66.93/77.32 for PVG/S3Gaussian/Deformable-GS, while baseline scores remain fixed. Tables 1 and 3 also change; PVG's reported average preference rises from 88.6% to 93.2%. New CDTS ablation results replace mixing-ratio results. These are results for a revised training procedure.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.2 replaces beta-weighted mixing of original and generated data with the Cousin Data Training Strategy (CDTS): temporally aligned pairs enter each optimization step, and a new perceptual feature regularizer augments the loss. These change the training procedure substantively; the trajectory-generation algorithm and underlying 4DGS framework remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution discussion, Sections 3.2.2 and 4.3 receive targeted revisions. New supplementary sections explain baselines and implementation, and speed-change discussion moves there. Author and affiliation information also changes. Most introductory, related-work, preliminary, and evaluation prose retains its earlier structure.

P2.justification: Figure 2 gains paired-data markings and a regularization connection. v3 adds the CDTS visual comparison and scene-identification table, revises the ablation-table structures, and adds frame-direction arrows to qualitative panels. The lane-change comparison becomes Figure 3, while the earlier speed-change comparison moves to supplementary Figure 5. The overall layout remains similar.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to nuScenes, UC-NeRF, XLD, HO-Gaussian, and EgoVid-5M. These extend contextual coverage without substantially changing the positioning against earlier driving reconstruction and diffusion-prior methods. Existing references are retained, including bibliographic updates that do not constitute new works.

T1.justification: Section 3.2.2 removes the beta-weighted hybrid-dataset definition and introduces the aligned-batch formulation, perceptual regularizer, and expanded total objective in v3 Equations 8–11. The Gaussian, diffusion, trajectory-safety, and IoU formulations remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses reproducibility gaps in v1 by documenting the central video generator's training recipe and identifying the exact evaluation segments. It also supports the new CDTS mechanism with component ablations and visual evidence, making its contribution easier to assess. These gains outweigh the loss of the explicit 4DGS iteration count, although uncertainty reporting and user-study participant counts remain absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DriveDreamer4D and contain readable text, equations, figures, and tables supporting reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references; v3 additionally includes supplementary Sections 6–8.

after.justification: v3 reports original reconstruction experiments, updated user-study results, and additional quantitative and visual CDTS ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Waymo reconstruction experiments, quantitative comparisons, a user study, and ablations in Tables 1–6.

results.title:
DriveDreamer4D: World Models Are Effective Data Machines for 4D Driving
  Scene Representation

C1.justification: The largest-dataset and state-of-the-art segmentation claims remain. v2 recasts the contribution list by explicitly claiming a trade-off analysis of unsupervised, synthetic, and automatically labeled training, replacing the pipeline-improvement bullet. Its highlighted 2.1-point overall and 5.5-point tail-class gains quantify comparisons already present in v1's tables.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations about transferable features, log-linear mIoU scaling despite absent loss scaling, and differing tail-class benefits for PTv3 and MinkowskiNet. It explains NeuS geometry difficulties on inside-out scans. ScanNet++ discussion changes from test deterioration and limited benefits to validation gains qualified by baseline non-reproducibility and unequal training data.

D1.justification: Most preprocessing, hardware, and scheduling details survive in the reorganized appendices. However, v2 removes explicit training-repository links and the DOI from v1 Appendix A, the mobile coordinate/depth-rendering recipe, and the stated PTv3 pretraining learning rate of 0.0016. Project and dataset links remain, and v2 adds an estimated 12 GPU hours per scene for the omitted neural-rendering step.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot semantic evaluation on Matterport3D and instance segmentation on ScanNet and ScanNet200 (Section 4.6, Tables 7–8). These extend both target-domain and task coverage. ScanNet++ remains evaluated in Appendix B, and the self-captured scenes are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds reported comparisons with LabelMakerV1 and ScanNet's manual annotations in Table 5, and OpenScene and Matterport3D-supervised MinkowskiNet in Table 7. Table 2 also adds a PTv3-PPT ablation comparator. The original MinkowskiNet, PTv3, Mix3D, and PonderV2 comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include label-quality evaluation on five ScanNet and three ARKitScenes scenes, 10/20/50/100% pretraining subsets, size-matched Structured3D, Top-40/80/160 NYU label mappings, accuracy metrics, and instance-segmentation AP metrics. Table 1 also changes the reported ARKit validation/test split from 548/no test set to 274/274, although the caption and prose still state 548 validation scenes.

E4.justification: v2 adds Grounded-SAM/gravity-alignment ablations, direct annotation-quality checks, dataset-size sensitivity and a size-matched synthetic-data comparison (Tables 4–6). New figures analyze gravity-related errors, class frequencies, and individual tail-class detections. The earlier aggregate head/common/tail analysis is retained in the expanded main table.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for benchmark scores. The two Mask3D seeds used for test-time augmentation and the stored vote-count information are documented in both versions; v2 adds no uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Numerous validation scores change: joint PTv3-PPT ScanNet200 mIoU changes from 40.3 to 37.5, while its test score remains 41.4; fine-tuned MinkowskiNet ScanNet20 validation mIoU changes from 77.0 to 74.1. Reasons for these revisions are not stated. v2 adds scaling, annotation-quality, transfer, and instance results, but removes all ScanNet++ test top-1/top-3 scores while retaining its validation scores in Appendix B.

M1.justification: Grounded-SAM integration, gravity alignment, ensemble voting, point lifting, and mobile-scanner integration already appear in v1. v2's explicit NeuS-omission discussion elaborates the neural-rendering omission already documented in v1 Section 4.6 and Appendix C.1; it does not establish a changed annotation procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodological explanations, and conclusion receive extensive rewriting. Experiments are reorganized into thematic comparisons, ablations, and transferability sections; ScanNet++ moves to the supplement and references move before it. ALC/ALS200 terminology is replaced with descriptive ARKit LabelMaker names.

P2.justification: v2 adds dataset-size, gravity-alignment, annotation-comparison, class-distribution, tail-detection, and scaling figures, plus several experimental tables. It merges v1 Table 3 and Appendix Table B1 into a wide ScanNet200 table and relocates the ScanNet++ table. Existing pipeline and self-captured-scene figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 broadens introductory coverage to distillation, denoising, and additional open-vocabulary approaches, citing works such as OpenScene, OpenNeRF, Search3D, and P2P-Bridge. It also adds references supporting Matterport3D, PointGroup, and NeuS discussions. The central positioning as a LabelMaker extension addressing scarce annotated 3D data remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The gravity-alignment mathematical rule is unchanged, and neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. v2's log-linear scaling discussion describes empirical observations rather than a new mathematical derivation or formal result.

improvement.justification: Tables 4–6 address important gaps in v1 by directly evaluating annotation quality, isolating pipeline components, and testing dataset-size effects against size-matched synthetic data. Transfer experiments further strengthen the evidence for usefulness beyond the original evaluations. These gains substantially improve the paper's empirical foundation, despite removed ScanNet++ test results and reproducibility details, unexplained score revisions, and inconsistent split reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ARKit LabelMaker and the LabelMakerV2 annotation pipeline. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, references, and appendices support comparison, including content renamed or moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds annotation-quality evaluations, component ablations, data-scaling experiments, Matterport3D evaluation, and instance-segmentation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original semantic-segmentation training experiments on ScanNet, ScanNet200, and ScanNet++, plus qualitative results on self-captured scenes.

results.title: ARKit LabelMaker: A New Scale for Indoor 3D Scene Understanding

C1.justification: The core contributions and KITTI state-of-the-art claim without extra data remain. The introduction adds a specific claim that height-ratio mapping avoids cascaded uncertainty and offers efficiency and noise-robustness advantages over Deep3DBox/Shift R-CNN-style projection-alignment constraints.

C2.justification: Appendix A qualifies perspective invariance when camera and object heights differ. Other new discussions explain cyclist difficulties, coupled errors in height predictions, dependence on pretrained depth domains and failure under height occlusion. These substantially expand the mechanism explanations and applicability limitations beyond v1.

D1.justification: Appendix C explicitly documents focal, L1 and GIoU losses and the 2D/3D loss decomposition; the stated loss-weight vector expands from eight to nine coefficients. v2 also identifies pretrained-depth variants and timing conditions. These expand the documented specification without establishing that retained experiments were rerun; the main training schedule, hardware and code access remain.

E1.justification: Reported evaluation expands from KITTI cars to KITTI pedestrians and cyclists in Appendix D and Waymo vehicles in Appendix G. These additions substantially broaden the evaluated populations and dataset coverage.

E2.justification: KITTI car Table 1 adds MonoDDE and MonoUNI. The new Waymo comparison in Table 10 additionally introduces M3D-RPN, PatchNet and PCT alongside retained comparators. MonoDDE was discussed in v1 but did not participate in its Table 1 comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include Waymo training/validation sets of 52,386/39,848 images sampled every third frame, AP3D/APH3D evaluation across difficulty levels and distance ranges, and IoU thresholds of 0.5 and 0.7. Other additions include KITTI pedestrian/cyclist evaluation at IoU 0.5 and ground-truth height substitution controls. The original KITTI split and training budget remain.

E4.justification: Beyond retained ablations, v2 adds computational-cost analysis, independent removal of RSH and decoupled queries, and a projected-central-height prediction control. Appendices add other-category ablations, ground-truth height sensitivity tests, pretrained-depth variants and qualitative occlusion/failure cases (Tables 2, 4-6, 8-9 and Figure 10).

E5.justification: Both versions describe five training runs with median moderate AP3D reporting for validation/ablation results. v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests or repeated-run reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 MonoDGP scores remain unchanged, while v2 adds substantial category, Waymo, cost, sensitivity and depth-variant results. For example, Table 10 reports Waymo Level 1 overall AP3D of 4.28 at IoU 0.7. Adding MonoDDE reduces the reported KITTI hard-test AP3D lead from 1.18 to 0.87; MonoDGP's score remains 15.97.

M1.justification: The core RSH, decoupled decoders and geometric-depth correction remain. Appendix F adds an exploratory variant using pretrained Depth Anything V2 predictions as initial depth before learned error correction, extending the procedure beyond projection-based initialization.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose remain. v2 makes localized revisions to the abstract, introduction, decoder explanations and results discussion, standardizes terminology and organizes supplementary material into Appendices A-H. The existing narrative is not extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 redraws architecture, segmentation and distribution displays, expands comparison and ablation tables, and adds computational-cost, category, sensitivity, pretrained-depth and Waymo tables. New camera-height diagrams and qualitative detection panels substantially expand the visual evidence. v1 Tables 2-4 correspond to v2 Tables 3-5.

R1.justification: The introduction and new Appendix B expand positioning through a dedicated comparison of height-ratio and projection-alignment constraints, including stability, efficiency and occlusion arguments. Citations expand to new baselines, pretrained depth, datasets and loss components. v1's original Pseudo-LiDAR citation is removed; the main multi-depth comparison remains.

T1.justification: New Appendix A defines the camera/object height ratio and derives wheel-depth bias, corrected depth errors and bounds for cameras below or above object height (Equations 11-24). This substantially refines v1's geometric explanation by establishing additional dependence on camera height and distance.

improvement.justification: v1 left generalization beyond KITTI cars and important geometric assumptions insufficiently tested. v2 substantially strengthens validation through Waymo and other-category results, independent controls and sensitivity tests, while camera-height derivations and failure analysis clarify applicability. One new comparison remains unclear: Table 9's 'Direct Depth' row repeats Table 4's 'Depth Map' values without explaining different settings. This local reporting weakness does not outweigh the broader gains in evidence and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MonoDGP with matching core methods and KITTI experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends after its references; v2 additionally contains readable supplementary material, Appendices A-H.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds results for other KITTI categories, Waymo, computational costs, sensitivity tests and alternative depth initialization.

before.justification: v1 reports original KITTI car detection results in Table 1 and experimental ablations in Tables 2-4.

results.title:
MonoDGP: Monocular 3D Object Detection with Decoupled-Query and
  Geometry-Error Priors

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: high-quality, semantically decomposed characters from arbitrary-pose single images in approximately three minutes, using S-LRM and layered refinement. Additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix H adds substantive explanations for using shared semantic-equivalent SDFs instead of separate class decoders, including transfer and scalability arguments. It also discusses real-human stylistic bias, limited semantic categories, resolution constraints, speed-quality tradeoffs, and restricted applicability beyond human-centric inputs.

D1.justification: Appendices E–G substantially expand reproducibility information: data filtering and connectivity checks, camera and rendering settings, semantic-loss weights, diffusion conditioning, frozen/trainable components, the 100×100×150 extraction grid, and texture-projection weights. The original implementation settings are largely retained; these are primarily newly disclosed details.

E1.justification: Anime3D++ training and evaluation coverage is retained. Appendix H adds realistic-human reconstruction on THuman 2.0, real-human editing, and furry and 2.5D inputs, substantially broadening the demonstrated input domains. These additions are qualitative and do not involve newly reported real-human training.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. The supplement adds bounded qualitative comparisons against D-IF and HiLo on THuman 2.0 and against AvatarPopUp for real-human editing in Figures 11 and 13.

E3.justification: Appendix D adds substantial evaluation protocols: semantic-mask IoU across eight views, geometric Chamfer distance and F-score with a 0.01 threshold, and a quantitative control using S-LRM plus color back-projection without refinement. The original split and main evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: The original qualitative decomposition and refinement ablations move to Appendix A. New analyses quantify refinement's contribution in Table 5, profile processing stages in Table 3, and probe generalization beyond anime training data in Appendix H.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its experimental results. The additional measurements retain point-estimate reporting; the user-study participant and mesh counts are unchanged.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. New results include hair/clothing/body mask IoUs of 0.73/0.86/0.88, StdGEN Chamfer distance/F-score of 0.023/0.664 in Table 4, and SSIM of 0.912 without refinement versus the retained full-method value of 0.916 in Table 5. Runtime measurements and additional qualitative outputs also expand the evidence.

M1.justification: The canonicalization, multi-view diffusion, semantic-aware reconstruction, three-stage training, and layered refinement pipeline remain unchanged. Appendices F–G disclose additional conditioning, semantic weighting, trainable-layer, and projection details without establishing a revision to the underlying procedure.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: implementation details, mesh dilation, qualitative ablations, and animation demonstrations move into the supplement. Main-text method and dataset descriptions are condensed, while supplementary Sections A–I organize extensive technical explanations, analyses, and discussion.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3–5 and Figures 11–19, reformats Table 1, resizes the main qualitative comparison, and relocates the original ablation and animation figures. The visual presentation expands substantially, although most original illustrations are retained rather than replaced.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 and Appendix H substantially expand positioning against decomposition methods, adding GALA and Frankenstein and developing comparisons with the already-cited TELA. The discussion distinguishes inputs, representations, texture preservation, cost, and scalability, replacing v1's broad characterization of prior character methods as holistic. Reference deduplication alone is not counted.

T1.justification: Appendices F–G add explicit mathematical definitions for previously described operations, including the deviation loss in Equation 17 and color back-projection in Equation 19. The central semantic-equivalent NeRF/SDF mathematics remains unchanged, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's validation by adding quantitative semantic checks, direct 3D geometry metrics, and a controlled refinement comparison. Detailed implementation disclosures and substantive limitations also improve reproducibility and interpretation. Non-anime evidence remains qualitative, and Equation 19's printed projection normalization appears incorrect, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in support for the paper's central contributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe StdGEN and retain matching core methods and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary Sections A–I.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds semantic and geometric measurements, runtime profiling, a quantitative refinement ablation, and non-anime examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original Anime3D++ experiments, qualitative ablations, application demonstrations, and a user study involving 28 volunteers and 16 meshes.

results.title: StdGEN: Semantic-Decomposed 3D Character Generation from Single Images

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims about prototype-driven curricula improving MAE efficiency and representation quality. The transfer experiments provide additional support without redefining those claims.

The supplement interprets its visualizations as showing more consistent organization of prototypical views in DINO spaces than in MAE or SIFT spaces. Existing limitations and future-work discussion remain unchanged.

These are newly disclosed recipes, not demonstrated changes to the original experiments.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains standard MAE and the hard-sample curriculum adapted from Sorscher et al. The prototype-identification comparators also remain unchanged. The added transfer evaluation introduces no distinct competing algorithm.

Separately, the temperature-table caption changes the annealing range from 0.05–0.2 to 0.07–0.6, matching Section 4.1 in both versions. This is a reported-setting correction, without evidence that the retained experiment was rerun.

These extend the existing prototype-identification analysis; the quantitative temperature, architecture, feature-space, and cluster-count ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: New Table 3 reports means and standard deviations over three runs. This introduces uncertainty reporting for the added transfer evaluation, while the original ImageNet results retain point estimates. The PDFs do not establish increased repetition of existing experiments.

E6.justification: New Table 3 reports eight-dataset average five-shot accuracies of 41.77% for the 1600-epoch baseline, 42.18% for the 200-epoch curriculum, and 47.23% for the 400-epoch curriculum. These are newly reported comparisons at different training budgets, not revisions to earlier scores. Existing ImageNet numerical results are retained, and supplementary figures add qualitative findings.

M1.justification: The MAE objective, clustering procedure, normalized centroid distances, temperature-controlled sampling, and effective-dataset-size scheduling remain unchanged. The supplementary material documents and analyzes the existing method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely retained. Changes include a few-shot results paragraph, supplementary explanatory text, and limited caption editing. Section 4.4 retains stale references to Table 4a–c after the corresponding table becomes Table 5.

P2.justification: v2 adds the transfer-results table, two configuration tables, and three substantial multi-panel supplementary figures. It also relocates Figure 5 and rearranges the retained temperature and prototype-identification tables together on page 8. This substantially expands and reorganizes the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the eight transfer datasets and removes the DATA reference by Chang et al. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to MIM, dataset selection, and importance sampling remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6, including the sampling distribution, effective dataset size, and asymptotic limit, are unchanged. Neither version adds substantive proofs or formal theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidential gap in v1: evaluation was confined to ImageNet, whereas Table 3 tests transfer across eight datasets with three-run uncertainty reporting. Supplementary Tables 6–7 also fill substantial gaps in downstream reproducibility information. Together these strengthen validation and documentation of the central efficiency claim. Earlier prose/table inconsistencies persist, and table renumbering introduces stale references, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same prototype-driven curriculum for masked image modeling. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains readable supplementary material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds five-shot transfer results on eight datasets in Table 3 and supplementary qualitative analyses.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.4 report original ImageNet experiments comparing curricula, training durations, temperatures, and prototype-identification settings.

Section 4.1 additionally specifies caption-generation prompts and long-text similarity aggregation. Conversely, v3 removes several exact checkpoint links and Long-CLIP/DreamLIP code footnotes; FLAME's code URL remains.

These substantially broaden evaluated task requirements. CC3M/YFCC15M training and the original retrieval and classification coverage remain.

E2.justification: Table C4 introduces reported comparisons against Frozen, LQAE, V2L-Tokenizer, and SPAE for few-shot image comprehension, adding a distinct family of comparison methods. Existing comparator memberships remain unchanged; extending CLIP and Long-CLIP to DCI/DOCCI alone does not change that comparator set.

Appendix C.5 extends ViT-L/14 evaluation to YFCC15M and large-model multilingual comparisons. E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for the new benchmarks, semantic-level ablations, and larger models; Table C4 reports FLAME averages of 86.8% and 68.4% for 2-way and 5-way comprehension. P1.justification: Most main-text wording and narrative organization are retained. v3 adds a semantic-interpretability subsection and an organized A–D supplement, renumbers the ablation subsection, adds acknowledgements, updates contact information, and makes localized explanatory and shortening edits.

P2.justification: v3 adds interpretability and retrieval-example figures and multiple supplementary tables, expands Table 1, and substantially redistributes displays. The original multilingual Figure 4 is split between the main text and Figure C1. Figure 3 highlights extracted features, and the runtime plot's vertical scale changes.

R1.justification: The principal related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain stable. v3 adds focused references connecting semantic decomposition to scene-graph research and DOCCI, alongside citations for compositionality benchmarks, AdamW, and frozen-LLM visual-comprehension comparators.

T1.justification: Sections 4.4 and C.3 add mathematical definitions for patch-to-word mapping and the construction of in-context examples and predictions. The original contrastive objective and attention formulation remain unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves an important reproducibility deficiency by supplying the full prompts and training settings that the supplied v1 references but omits. Removed checkpoint links and the unexplained runtime revision are drawbacks, but the gains in reproducibility and evidential support outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FLAME, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. Corresponding methods and experiments can be reliably matched. v1 ends with references; v3 includes supplementary Sections A–D, including material relocated from the main text.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds retrieval benchmarks, compositionality and few-shot evaluations, semantic-level ablations, and scalability results.

before.justification: v1 reports original FLAME retrieval and classification results, prompt and backbone ablations, and computational-cost measurements in Tables 1–7 and Figures 4–5.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims: introducing EEG-based colored 3D decoding, the EEG-3D dataset, and the fusion encoder with a two-stage decoder. The additional evidence does not redefine or broaden these contributions.

The supplement adds interpretations of task-dependent individual differences and attributes reconstruction failures to EEG noise and limited spatial resolution. The existing texture-generation and cross-subject limitations remain.

The abstract replaces a future-release promise with a stated code/data repository; its availability was not checked externally.

Table 4 also extends the existing component ablations to geometric fidelity; the original ablations and brain-region analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report average and best performance over five generated samples. v3 adds no new run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Figure 6 shows differences between participants rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 and the original semantic-score columns of Table 4 are unchanged. v3 adds substantial evidence on geometry and variability: Full achieves CD 5.35 and F1 77.01, versus Static 6.75/67.61 and Dynamic 6.40/69.42, alongside individual-subject scores and additional successful and failed reconstructions. These are newly reported outcomes, not performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same attention-based dynamic–static EEG fusion, decoupled geometry and appearance features, training objectives, and two-stage shape/color decoder. The method text and Equations (1)–(12) are unchanged apart from citations and formatting.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose remain intact. Changes include local wording and paragraph adjustments, expanded Section 3.3, updated authors and affiliations, acknowledgments, and supplementary Sections 7–11. There is no extensive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adds individual-subject radar plots, a large reconstruction gallery and a failure-case figure (Figures 6–8), and expands Table 4 with geometric columns. C2.justification: The supplement adds a proposed explanation for tiny-VAE degradation through reduced depth and lack of a global receptive field, and discusses GAN fidelity versus diffusion perceptual quality. The existing limitations concerning fine textures and heavily degraded details remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promise of future code/model release with stated availability and a concrete repository link. It also adds training/inference pseudocode with discriminator-update details, specific compression-model resources, and mobile hardware, SDK and quantization information, substantially expanding reproducibility documentation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–7 retain their numerical values, while the supplement adds extensive benchmark, ablation and qualitative results. New findings include preference rates of 31% for AdcSR, 29% for OSEDiff and 33% for S3Diff, and mobile latencies of 65 ms versus 1647 ms for AdcSR and OSEDiff. These are newly reported evaluations, not improvements between versions under the original settings.

M1.justification: Structural compression, pruning ratios, two-stage training, feature-space distillation and inference remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 documents the existing procedure, including discriminator updates; mobile quantization is an additional evaluation setting.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely preserved, with limited wording edits, affiliation and corresponding-author updates, and a supplementary-material pointer. New material is organized into Sections A–D without extensively rewriting the existing exposition.

P2.justification: v2 adds Algorithm 1, Tables B.1–B.2 and C.1–C.3, and Figures C.1–C.4. These introduce a substantial three-dataset comparison table, additional image-comparison grids, study thumbnails and new experimental displays. Existing main figures and tables are retained with minor layout reflow.

Pseudocode and the stated code/model release also improve reproducibility information. The user study remains descriptive without uncertainty estimates, but the added evidence resolves important gaps in practical and comparative validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ADC framework and AdcSR model, with matching main experiments. The complete text, equations, tables and figures are readable, including v2's added supplementary Sections A–D; v1 contains no supplementary section.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by additional ablations, benchmark results, an expert preference study and mobile-device measurements.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.3 report original super-resolution comparisons, efficiency measurements and component ablations, including Tables 1–7.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same distance-dependent completion problem, Scan Module/Scan Loss contributions, synergy claim, and state-of-the-art claims with identical headline benchmark scores.

Table D.2 reports 17.12 mIoU for ScanSSC versus 16.50 and 16.74 for loss controls; Appendix E reports curved-road mIoU of 14.56 versus CGFormer's 13.77. P2.justification: The original figures and tables are retained.
