C2.justification: Section 3.3 changes the style-loss rationale from preventing excessive feature concentration or dispersion to preventing dependence on a single agent. It also more strongly describes adversarial training as excluding agent-specific semantics and preserving exclusively shared semantics, without changing the mathematical objective.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability statement and repository address in the abstract. Existing prompt dimensions, loss weights, resizer specifications and parameter counts remain unchanged. The PDFs establish the new access information, but do not establish repository completeness or usability.

E1.justification: V2 adds real-world DAIR-V2X evaluation and LiDAR–camera collaboration scenarios using ResNet and EfficientNet neighbors. These substantially extend the represented environments and input modalities. OPV2V and V2XSet were already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: PnPDA and MPDA remain the evaluated interpreter comparators, with F-cooper and CoBEVT as fusion choices. The added multimodal and DAIR-V2X comparisons extend this same set; existing comparisons retain their participants.

E3.justification: V2 specifies new multimodal training/evaluation configurations: pp8-pp4-EfficientNet followed by adaptation to ResNet, and pp8-vn4-ResNet followed by adaptation to EfficientNet. Existing LiDAR configurations, AP metrics, evaluation range and two-phase evaluation procedure remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Supplementary Table 2 adds a focused ablation removing style, adversarial and single-agent losses separately across three encoder pairings. This extends the existing module, prompt-initialization and rank analyses with direct checks of the auxiliary training objectives.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds multimodal, DAIR-V2X and loss-ablation result tables. For example, supplementary Table 5 reports DAIR-V2X pp8-pp4 AP@0.5/AP@0.7 with CoBEVT of 66.8/39.9 for PolyInter, 62.9/34.4 for PnPDA and 65.0/35.1 for MPDA. These are new evaluation results; matched pre-existing numerical results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same two-phase interpreter, channel selection, spatial attention, general and specific prompts, losses and low-rank adaptation. The camera experiments do not document a modification to PolyInter's procedure or architecture.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected method, experimental and qualitative paragraphs are tightened. The supplement is reorganized into more specific sections, and corresponding-author markers and a funding acknowledgement are added. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Three supplementary tables are added using the existing presentation style, while retained tables and the supplementary figure are rearranged. Figure 3 gains channel labels. Figure 6 is reduced from six panels to four feature panels; prompt visualizations remain in supplementary Figure 1.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for ResNet, EfficientNet and DAIR-V2X to support the new experiments. The related-work discussion and positioning against one-stage and two-stage interpreters remain substantively unchanged; most citation changes are renumbering.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(11), the mathematical loss definitions and the low-rank parameter-count derivations remain unchanged. No theorems, proofs or formal assumptions are added or revised.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation by addressing v1's restriction to simulated, LiDAR-only evaluations through real-world DAIR-V2X and LiDAR–camera tests. The loss ablations also test previously unisolated training terms, while prior evidence is retained. Sparse documentation of the added experiments and absent uncertainty estimates limit the conclusions, but the gains in evidence for practical applicability are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PolyInter research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and supplementary material. Retained content can be reliably matched across appendix reordering and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds DAIR-V2X evaluations, LiDAR–camera comparisons and loss-function ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original collaborative detection results on OPV2V and V2XSet, including baseline comparisons, component ablations, parameter-efficiency experiments and qualitative evaluations.

results.title:
One is Plenty: A Polymorphic Feature Interpreter for Immutable
  Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements retain the same claims: training-free segmentation, improved object-level coherence through spectral distillation, object-presence-guided refinement, and strong benchmark performance. The shortened conclusion preserves their scientific meaning.

C2.justification: Section 11 adds substantive limitations absent from v1: expensive eigendecomposition, CPU matching latency, insufficient real-time speed, weaker small-object performance, and missing temporal consistency. Supplementary analyses also introduce interpretations of feature choice, matching strategy, and adaptive rank selection, substantially expanding the discussion of mechanisms and applicability.

D1.justification: v2 adds rank-selection and clustering pseudocode, the eigenscaling parameter of 1.5, cosine-distance clustering with Ward linkage, averaging over 80 prompt templates, and dataset-specific alpha/gamma values in Table 11. It also identifies CPU matching and RTX A6000 hardware. These disclosures materially improve reproducibility without establishing changes to the original experiments.

E1.justification: The eight segmentation benchmark settings remain unchanged. Limited additional coverage includes using segmentation masks for image inpainting and object removal in Figure 9, and cartoon-character inputs among the open-vocabulary examples in Figure 15.

E2.justification: The main quantitative baseline roster is retained. Figures 11–14 add SCLIP to qualitative comparisons that used NACLIP and ProxyCLIP in v1 Figure 6. Supplementary experiments also introduce focused comparisons with already-present baselines, including CaR for encoder scaling and NACLIP for image editing.

E3.justification: The main resizing, 224-by-224 sliding window, stride, and evaluation metrics are retained. Supplementary experiments substantially extend the controlled settings: separate scaling of the CLIP global encoder, additional DINO backbones, alternative attention features, matching strategies, and rank-selection procedures. Figure 15 additionally uses PAMR refinement, unlike the unrefined benchmark comparisons.

E4.justification: Tables 6–9 add targeted tests of VFM backbone dependence, attention-feature selection, sequential versus similar versus complementary head matching, and fixed versus adaptive rank selection. Figure 10 and Section 11 add a small-object failure analysis, while Figure 9 examines consequences of incomplete masks for downstream editing.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v2 revises several Table 3 ablation values; for example, experiment 3 changes from 62.5/36.9/24.5 to 62.9/37.7/25.2 mIoU on V21/PC59/C-Stf. Tables 5–9 add substantial numerical results, alongside new qualitative and runtime findings. Headline Tables 1–2 remain unchanged, including CASS averages of 44.4 mIoU and 69.0 pAcc.

M1.justification: The proposed spectral matching, low-rank eigenscaling, text-embedding adjustment, and object-prior fusion remain unchanged in Sections 3.2–3.3. Section 7 supplies previously deferred specifications of these components. The additional backbone configurations and optional postprocessing are settings for supplementary evaluations.

P1.justification: Previously brief, deferred method descriptions receive substantial step-by-step explanation in a newly organized supplement, with separate implementation, applications, and discussion sections. The main narrative remains largely intact, with localized shortening in Section 4.2 and the conclusion, plus author contact information and acknowledgements.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–11, Figures 9–15, and two algorithm displays, substantially expanding the presentation of procedures, comparisons, applications, and failures. Existing illustrations are also revised, including the input example in Figure 2 and the attention visualization in Figure 3; the main pages reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including SAM, LaMa, and recent attention-grounding studies, and supplies the correct PnP-OVSS reference for the existing baseline row. Section 8.2.1 further contrasts CASS distillation with LaVG graph partitioning. The central research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly defines the retained-energy criterion in Equation 11 and the dynamic eigenscaling function in Equation 13, which v1 described without these formulas. These are localized additions to the mathematical specification of existing components; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: The supplement substantially improves methodological transparency by supplying important specifications missing from v1, and adds targeted validation and explicit computational and small-object limitations. These gains strengthen the paper despite unchanged headline scores. Some new prose overstates the evidence: Section 8.1.2 claims universal superiority over CaR, although Table 5 reports 91.4 for CaR versus 89.3 for CASS on V20 with the L/14 global encoder. This limited inconsistency does not outweigh the documentation and evaluation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CASS and retain matching main sections, equations, and experiments. The supplied v1 ends after the references; v2 includes supplementary Sections 6–11. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the complete supplied material.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds encoder-scaling results, further ablations, qualitative comparisons, and application demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation results across eight benchmark settings, component ablations, and backbone comparisons in Tables 1–4.

results.title:
Distilling Spectral Graph for Object-Context Aware Open-Vocabulary
  Semantic Segmentation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: one-step face restoration, VRE-based visual conditioning, identity and distribution alignment, and strong quality with efficient inference. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: Supplementary Section E adds specific limitations involving color shifts, skin textures and non-facial regions such as fingers, and minimally degraded inputs, including explanations tied to training coverage. Sections C–D also interpret VRE transfer and downstream recognition benefits. v1 lacks this substantive discussion of applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the recognition evaluator as the official ArcFace MS1MV3 R50 model, describes parallel execution, and clarifies that existing OSEDiff* retraining uses OSDFace's dataset and experimental settings. Core training details remain unchanged, and both versions still promise future code and model release.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot cartoon restoration using Anime Face Dataset (main Figure 6) and downstream LFW face recognition under previously unseen atmospheric turbulence (Supplementary Section D). These substantially extend the evaluated domain, task requirements, and degradation conditions beyond the retained restoration benchmarks.

E2.justification: The original restoration comparator set is retained. Supplementary Tables 2–3 add OSEDiff*+VRE to comparisons against OSDFace. The new recognition experiment also includes a no-restoration control alongside DAEFR, DiffBIR, and OSEDiff*.

E3.justification: The new recognition protocol evaluates 3,000 positive and 3,000 negative LFW pairs at turbulence propagation lengths of 20,000, 30,000, and 40,000, reporting PR, ROC, F1, and similarity-separation measurements. Supplementary Section B also compares serialized and parallel execution. Existing main-text training and restoration-evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds experiments testing whether VRE improves OSEDiff, recognition robustness across unseen turbulence severities, and the computational benefit of parallel execution. Supplementary Section F adds case analyses involving occlusions, profiles, multiple faces, accessories, and backgrounds. The original prompt and loss ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new recognition curves and mean-distance bars introduce evaluation measurements without adding uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The unstarred OSEDiff scores change throughout main Tables 1–2. For example, CelebA-Test LPIPS changes from 0.4708 to 0.3306, overtaking OSDFace's unchanged 0.3365; the reason for this revision is unspecified. v2 also adds VRE-transfer results, serialized/parallel timings, recognition curves, and qualitative outputs. The original OSDFace benchmark scores and main ablation results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core OSDFace architecture, two-stage training, and losses remain unchanged. Supplementary Sections B–C add an evaluated procedure that executes the prompt embedder and VAE encoder in parallel, and an OSEDiff*+VRE adaptation integrating VRE into another restoration model.

P1.justification: v2 lightly edits main-text wording, updates terminology, adds acknowledgments, and organizes additional material into Supplementary Sections A–F. The original section order, narrative, and method exposition are largely retained; there is no extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds a cartoon-restoration figure, supplementary comparison and timing tables, a multi-panel recognition figure, and extensive synthetic and real-world comparison grids. Main Figure 3 gains explicit component labels, and Table 1 is resized beside the cartoon examples. These substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Anime Face Dataset, DialogueNeRF, atmospheric-turbulence simulation, and AdaIN. The DFOSD-to-D3SR rename matches the same arXiv:2410.04224 reference. The main related-work discussion and positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Supplementary Figure 3 newly defines mean sample distance as the difference between average cosine similarities for predicted positive and negative pairs. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition associated with evaluation. The original diffusion and loss equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The supplement substantially strengthens validation by testing VRE in another model and evaluating downstream identity recognition under unseen degradation. Concrete failure conditions also make the paper's applicability clearer than in v1. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the OSEDiff score revisions are unexplained, and Section 4.2 retains an LPIPS-superiority statement inconsistent with revised Table 1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OSDFace, with matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 adds a separately numbered supplement, which was included in this assessment.

after.justification: v2 retains original restoration experiments and adds VRE-transfer experiments, parallel-inference measurements, recognition tests under atmospheric turbulence, and cartoon-restoration examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original face-restoration results on synthetic and real-world datasets, computational measurements, and component ablations in Tables 1–5.

results.title: OSDFace: One-Step Diffusion Model for Face Restoration

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about pose-free and 3D-prior-free reconstruction, reciprocal benefits of self-supervision and Gaussian splatting, and cross-dataset generalization. The supplement adds supporting evidence without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: The supplement adds interpretations of efficiency and multi-view scalability, and attributes Splatt3R's DTU scale inconsistencies to pretrained metric geometry and intrinsic-parameter differences. It also explains the choice of self-supervised initialization. The earlier limitations concerning wide-baseline reconstruction and dynamic scenes are retained in Appendix C.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly documents encoder initialization, frozen-backbone adapters and dimensions, spherical-harmonic order, optimizer settings, batch sizes, training budgets, hardware, frame sampling, and evaluation splits. It also explains baseline adaptations and DL3DV initialization. These substantially improve documentation without establishing changes to the underlying retained experiments.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained RE10k, ACID, and DL3DV evaluations, v4 adds out-of-distribution evaluation on DTU object scenes. Appendix B.2 also evaluates three and four context views over longer sequences and measures camera-trajectory reconstruction, substantially extending domain and test-scenario coverage.

E2.justification: Table 12 introduces evaluated comparisons with Splatt3R, pixelSplat, and MVSplat on DTU. Table 13 adds VAE and DBARF to cross-dataset comparisons that previously included only FlowCAM and CoPoNeRF. The original comparator sets remain present.

E3.justification: New protocols measure peak memory and inference time for 256-by-256 images on an RTX 4090, and evaluate three/four context views over 80/120 frames using Absolute Trajectory Error. Section 5.1 also changes overlap thresholds from percentage notation to fractions. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: The original component and loss ablations remain. Table 14 adds tests removing CroCo initialization, the monocular encoder, and the multi-view encoder. Additional analyses examine inference cost, scaling to more context views and longer trajectories, and rendered depth quality, substantially expanding the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars. The supplementary results continue point-estimate reporting; the retained pose-error means and medians are not run-to-run uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Main Tables 2-8 are unchanged, but v4 adds substantial numerical and qualitative evidence in Tables 10-14 and Figures 8-14. For example, DTU PSNR is 13.14 for SelfSplat, 10.24 for Splatt3R, 12.89 for pixelSplat, and 13.94 for MVSplat. These are new comparisons with differing training or pose requirements, not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The encoders, feature fusion, matching-aware pose network, depth refinement, and training objectives remain unchanged. Appendix A supplies implementation details, while the additional context-view experiments test the existing model without establishing an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain nearly identical. Changes include author and affiliation edits, limited related-work and evaluation wording revisions, an organized supplement, and relocation of the limitations and project link. There is little rewriting of the retained scientific exposition.

P2.justification: The original figures and tables remain with small layout adjustments. v4 adds Tables 9-14 and Figures 7-14, including a detailed architecture diagram, trajectory plots, DTU and depth comparisons, and extensive qualitative galleries. This substantially expands the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds PF3plat and No Pose, No Problem alongside GGRT and revises discussion of pretrained-model dependencies. Appendix B.3 positions SelfSplat against Splatt3R and pose-required Gaussian methods. Additional supporting references broaden coverage while preserving the original research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an explicit first-order spherical-harmonic expression and permutation matrix for color-coordinate warping. The original mathematical definitions, objectives, and pose-gradient expression in Equations 1-11 remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v4 fills substantial reproducibility gaps through its training, implementation, and sampling details. New encoder ablations, measured efficiency, trajectory tests, and DTU comparisons make important aspects of the unchanged method more assessable. DTU comparisons remain qualified by differing training and pose requirements, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the gains in documentation and empirical scrutiny substantially improve the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SelfSplat and provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends after its references; v4 includes supplementary Sections A-D. The retained material and additions support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds efficiency measurements, multiple-context-view experiments, DTU evaluation, additional baseline comparisons, and encoder ablations.

before.justification: Tables 2-8 report original novel-view synthesis, pose estimation, cross-dataset generalization, and ablation results on RE10k, ACID, and DL3DV.

results.title:
SelfSplat: Pose-Free and 3D Prior-Free Generalizable 3D Gaussian
  Splatting

C1.justification: The central claims remain tuning-free identity-preserving generation through frequency-aware DiT control and hierarchical training. The contribution bullets and conclusion retain their scientific scope, including the claimed optimality of the control scheme; the shortened abstract does not redefine them.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations for tuning-based methods' identity weaknesses and I2V methods' temporal identity decay, and interprets the distinct roles of CLIP, face recognition and loss components. It expands applicability discussions to stylization and still images, identifies the 8-fps output limitation, and explicitly cautions interpretation of quantitative results following metric validation.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents the 130K-clip curation pipeline, YOLO filtering and identity tracking, SAM2 masks, Qwen2-VL captioning, hardware, comparator configurations and questionnaire quality controls. It adds a direct repository link and prospective release information for a CC BY 4.0 data subset. These disclosures do not establish that existing experiments changed or that the promised resources are available.

E1.justification: The human-identity generation task and original benchmark remain. Supplementary Section 2.8 and Figure 8 add demonstrated zero-shot generation with animated identities and stylized prompts. The expanded description of the in-house dataset does not establish changed training-data coverage.

E2.justification: v1's reported external comparison uses ID-Animator. v3 retains it and adds Vidu 1.5, DreamVideo, MotionBooth, Magic-Me, and PhotoMakerV2-based pipelines using CogVideoX-5B-I2V, EasyAnimate v4, OpenSora-Plan v1.3 and DynamiCrafter512 (supplementary Tables 1–3).

E3.justification: The original main experimental settings remain. Added experiments introduce a 60-video Vidu comparison, approximately 30K training clips with batch size 16 and one epoch for finer ablations, and automatic-metric agreement evaluation against human responses. The tuning-based comparison's sample count is unresolved: supplementary Section 2.2 specifies 1,350 videos per method, whereas Section 3.5 specifies 60.

E4.justification: v3 adds separate CLIP and face-extractor ablations, reference-noise removal, loss-mixture sensitivity, metric–human agreement analysis, and caching/interpolation tests. The existing inference-step study is retained in supplementary Section 2.5, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify a fixed random seed for the inference-step study. Neither reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests; v3 does not introduce such reporting.

E6.justification: Substantial comparison, ablation, runtime and qualitative results are added. Examples include Vidu's FaceSim-Arc score of 0.36 and A100 TeaCache timings of approximately 137 and 103 seconds versus 214 seconds without caching. Main Tables 1–3 and the relocated inference-step table retain their numerical values; these additions do not demonstrate a cross-version performance gain.

M1.justification: The core facial extractors, attention integration, losses and hierarchical training remain unchanged. Supplementary Sections 2.6–2.7 add optional inference extensions using TeaCache and frame interpolation from 8 to 16 fps.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. v3 shortens the abstract, rewrites the local-extractor explanation, clarifies terminology, adds appendix navigation and acknowledgments, and relocates the inference-step study and limitations to the supplement.

P2.justification: v3 adds dataset diagrams and statistics, an injection-scheme schematic, metric-validation and questionnaire displays, new tables, and extensive comparison and generation grids. It also clarifies the architecture diagram, revises the Fourier plot's legend and vertical-axis display, and relocates existing figures and tables.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands cited context for dataset construction, I2V alternatives, acceleration, interpolation and misuse, including Vidu, DynamiCrafter, TeaCache, SAM2 and Qwen2-VL. It also explicitly credits UniPortrait for feature choices and supplies source-specific support for the frequency arguments, while retaining the central novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(7) and their mathematical construction are retained. The supplement expands conceptual support for the frequency arguments but introduces no substantive formal derivation, theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 combines a single external comparator with sparse documentation of its in-house data. v3 substantially strengthens evaluation through broader comparisons, finer ablations and metric validation, while making data preparation and experimental implementation much more transparent. The new 1,350-versus-60 sample-count contradiction limits reproducibility of one comparison, but the broader evidence and documentation provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ConsisID and contain readable text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends after its references; v3 includes a complete supplement. Retained and relocated content can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, finer ablations, runtime measurements, metric validation and qualitative experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation comparisons, component and inference-step ablations, and a user study with 103 valid questionnaires.

results.title: Identity-Preserving Text-to-Video Generation by Frequency Decomposition

C1.justification: The central claims about training-free Self-Cross regularization, reduced subject mixing, and multi-patch aggregation remain. The introduction expands the stated benchmark contribution to include both two-subject and three-subject prompts.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies the attention-separation rationale to selected timesteps and layers and explains why relationship tokens remain unconstrained. It acknowledges dependence on Attend-and-Excite's effectiveness on SD2.1 and warns that missing subjects can inflate no-mixing scores (Section 5.2 and Table 5). Appendix B adds a background-separation explanation for Self-Self concatenation artifacts.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly documents SD2.1's 24-by-24 attention maps, normalization for larger maps, and SD3 attention extraction and fusion. Several existing sampling details are relocated there. Conversely, v1's disclosure of a single RTX4090 with 24 GB memory and batch size one is omitted.

E1.justification: The original datasets remain, with the 31-prompt Similar Subjects Dataset renamed SSD-2. V2 adds SSD-3 with 21 three-subject prompts and evaluates T2I-CompBench's 2D-Spatial and 3D-Spatial subsets. These introduce additional subjects and explicit spatial-relation requirements.

E2.justification: V1's SD2.1 comparison includes vanilla SD2.1 and Self-Cross only. V2 Tables 3 and 5 additionally evaluate INITNO and CONFORM in that setting, alongside CONFORM+Ours. The original SD1.4 comparator set and supplementary Attention Refocusing comparison remain.

E3.justification: Added evaluations introduce SD3-medium, quantitative SD2.1 comparisons, the spatial-relation metric Rel, and an SSD-3 evaluation comprising 21 prompts and 1,365 images per method. The retained sampling description still specifies 50 steps with Self-Cross guidance during the first 25; the additions do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B and Figure 9 add a Self-Self alternative-loss case study examining image concatenation and its attention maps. The existing one-patch/16-patch/masked-patch ablation, CLIP-score reliability checks, and failure examples are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report 65 images per prompt and matched random seeds across methods. V2 introduces no new repeated-run procedure, confidence intervals, variance estimates, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial SD3 and SD2.1/spatial results in Tables 1, 3, and 5. For example, SSD-3 existence scores are 33.54 for SD3-medium and 57.92 for Self-Cross; no-mixing scores are 70.08 and 77.15. These are new comparisons, while the original SD1.4 and Attention Refocusing numerical results remain unchanged. Figure 4 drops the bear/elephant and bus/truck example rows.

M1.justification: The core aggregation and overlap loss remain, but v2 adds an SD3 adaptation using image-image and image-text attention with maximum fusion of CLIP/T5 attention maps (Appendix A). It also introduces CONFORM+Ours, applying CONFORM early and Self-Cross later during SD2.1 generation (Section 5.2). These extend the actual inference procedure.

P1.justification: V2 extensively edits the abstract, introduction, method explanation, and experimental discussion. It reorganizes the formulation around pairs and multiple subjects, consolidates implementation details and CLIP discussion in the appendix, and integrates the former supplementary SD2.1 material into the main narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds three tables and figures covering SD3 examples, multimodal attention, and Self-Self artifacts. It reduces Figure 4 from four prompt rows to two, moves the existing SD2.1 gallery into the main paper, relocates CLIP displays to the appendix, and substantially resizes and rearranges displays.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to T2I-CompBench, T2I-CompBench++, pseudo-numerical diffusion sampling, and Enhancing MMDiT-Based Text-to-Image Models for Similar Subject Generation. The central related-work positioning and novelty argument remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 adds Equation 9 defining SD3 cross-attention through the elementwise maximum of CLIP and T5 attention maps. The original aggregation and pairwise overlap mathematics remain; replacing the generic pair count with an explicit binomial count clarifies the existing formulation. No new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: V1's broad applicability claims relied mainly on SD1.4 quantitative results and selected SD2.1 examples. V2 substantially strengthens their assessment through SD2.1/SD3 comparisons and three-subject/spatial tests, while exposing backbone-dependent weaknesses and explaining an alternative loss's failure. These gains improve both support and qualification of the central claims. Missing evaluation prompts for the new spatial/three-subject settings and removal of hardware details limit reproducibility but do not outweigh those improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Self-Cross diffusion-guidance research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary materials are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds SD2.1 and SD3 quantitative evaluations, three-subject synthesis, spatial-relation tests, and an alternative-loss case study.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation comparisons, quantitative SD1.4 results, a patch-aggregation ablation, and supplementary SD2.1 examples.

results.title:
Self-Cross Diffusion Guidance for Text-to-Image Synthesis of Similar
  Subjects

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding contribution statements retain the same three contributions and state-of-the-art segmentation claims. Terminology refinements and additional supporting experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit limitations concerning MLP-related computational cost, frequent SAM errors, and large-object fragmentation. Appendix E explains how incomplete object observations undermine feature consistency and aggregation. Appendix C also interprets robustness results and justifies prioritizing mIoU despite the newly disclosed accuracy tradeoffs.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 revises reported ScanNet training time from approximately 35 to 30 minutes and adds a timing comparison reporting 1847 seconds for InstanceGaussian. Appendix C adds merging-time measurements. Hardware, scene lists, preprocessing, densification settings, smoothing details, and the project-page disclosure remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use ScanNet, LeRF, and GraspNet for the same segmentation, querying, rendering, and qualitative generalization pipeline. v2 adds LeRF object renders and failure examples within this coverage, without establishing new datasets, task requirements, or altered input conditions.

E2.justification: The original comparators are retained, while Table 7 adds GAGA to instance segmentation and SAGA to instance and semantic segmentation. SAGA was previously only discussed as related work. Table 13 additionally compares aggregation against HDBSCAN, substantially extending the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: The original scenes, preprocessing, training schedule, and benchmark metrics are retained. Appendix C adds targeted protocols: mA50/mA25 reporting for existing ablations, FPS point-count sweeps from 200 to 1000, voxel-size and connectivity-threshold sweeps, and runtime measurements across point counts.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained representation/training and connectivity ablations, v2 adds hyperparameter sensitivity, random FPS initialization, aggregation runtime, and HDBSCAN substitution studies. Appendix E and Figures 12–13 add concrete analyses of incorrect SAM masks and unsuccessful aggregation of large, partially observed objects.

E5.justification: v1 contains no comparable variability reporting. v2 Tables 10–11 introduce ± summaries and explicitly report five different FPS starting-point samples. The meaning of ± is not defined, and these samples should not be interpreted as five complete training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain their numerical results, but Tables 6–13 add substantial comparative, accuracy, sensitivity, variability, and timing evidence. For example, HDBSCAN reports semantic/instance mIoU of 31.84/44.76 versus 40.66/50.27 for the proposed aggregation. Table 8 reveals that joint representation alone achieves higher mA25 than the full configuration, 84.42 versus 80.22. New renders and failure cases also extend the qualitative findings.

M1.justification: The shared-feature Gaussian representation, three training stages, truncated contrastive loss, FPS clustering, and graph aggregation remain unchanged in Section 3 and Algorithm 1. The ScanNet smoothing MLP was already documented in v1 Appendix A.3; the semantic-to-instance terminology clarification does not introduce a component.

P1.justification: Edits clarify semantic versus instance features, refine wording and headings, and add a funding acknowledgment. The conclusion gains a limitations paragraph, and the appendices gain dedicated comparison, ablation, and failure-analysis sections. The existing main narrative is largely retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is reorganized into scene rows and method columns and gains ground-truth panels. v2 adds structured experimental tables, a LeRF rendering montage, and two failure-case figures. Existing figures are relocated or resized; the GraspNet and feature-map figures are retained under new numbers.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for GAGA and HDBSCAN, associated with the new comparisons. The main related-work discussion and positioning remain substantially unchanged. Several other references receive publication or bibliographic updates rather than representing newly cited research.

T1.justification: Appendix C.3 newly states an O(K²) complexity bound for merging. This is a limited mathematical addition; Equations 1–6 and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged, and no new proof or theorem is supplied.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe InstanceGaussian. Their complete main texts, equations, algorithms, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, sensitivity and runtime experiments, sampling-variability results, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original ScanNet and LeRF evaluations, representation and aggregation ablations, and qualitative GraspNet results.

  3D Instance-Level Perception

It explains the bypass decoder's identity-preservation role and adds discussion of long-range lighting failures. Seed-selection use remains ambiguous: Section 5.5 excludes MIIW post-processing, but Table 1 distinguishes results without seed selection.

Figure 6 adds a same-scene, multiple-lighting demonstration. The earlier component ablation and 30-seed illustration remain, with the latter relocated to Figure S.1.

Seed-search and gallery figures move into the supplement, with gallery imagery and crops also revised.

R1.justification: v3 adds relevant literature on compositing, ScribbleLight, Spotlight, perceptual lighting evaluation, bypass decoding and shadow-geometry failures, while removing the standalone NeRF reference. It also distinguishes specialist and generalist competitors. The central positioning as latent-intrinsic control combined with diffusion remains.

T1.justification: The relighting formulation and losses in Equations 1–3 remain mathematically unchanged. Neither version introduces formal theorems or proofs. Revised conceptual grounding and decoder explanations do not constitute new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges an evaluation-code bug, corrects Table 1 and withdraws the central claim of over 20% MIIW superiority, substantially improving evidential reliability. after.justification: v3 reports corrected relighting results, decoder and seed-selection comparisons, data-generation ablations, and retained geometry and user-study results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MIIW relighting experiments, geometry-consistency measurements, a 31-participant user study and qualitative ablations.

P1.justification: The main section order and narrative are retained, with localized wording refinements in the introduction, method descriptions, and conclusion. The supplement organizes the added material into setup, ablation, and qualitative-results sections; the main paper is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–7 and Figures 8–11, including a gMAD comparison panel and extensive GradCAM grids. Original Figures 1–7 remain visually equivalent, with minor formatting changes. The new displays substantially expand the paper's visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds MM-PCQA and LMM-PCQA citations when discussing future point-cloud extensions. The related-work sections and positioning against existing mesh-quality approaches otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–11 are retained. The supplement introduces experimental configurations and implementation information, without new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies essential implementation details and supplementary evidence that v1 references but does not include. after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and additionally reports fusion, augmentation, and viewpoint/batch-size ablations, gMAD comparisons, and further GradCAM examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, cross-dataset generalization tests, component ablations, and GradCAM analyses in Tables 1–4 and Figures 5–7.

Appendix G.4.2 interprets faster watermark loss without DreamBooth preservation alongside loss of generative diversity. Appendix I.2 further explains hyperparameter trade-offs and possible causes of greater artifacts with pixel-space extraction.

Table 6 and Figures 18–19 also supply sampling, hyperparameter and extraction-space analyses that v1 referenced without providing their detailed evidence.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 9–21 and Table 6, including architecture and pixel-pipeline diagrams, diagnostic plots, ablation curves and full-page image comparisons. This substantially expands the visual presentation, while the main figures and table structures remain largely unchanged.

Although the explicit VAE downsampling/channel-count sentence is removed from Section 3.4, reproducibility documentation expands substantially.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds DynamiCrafter, PerVFI, InterpAny-Clearer, EMA-VFI and GIMM-VFI-R-P while retaining Time Reversal, RIFE and CBMNet-Large. This substantially broadens the evaluated frame-only and video-diffusion comparisons. Several qualitative comparisons also replace or supplement RIFE with these methods.

E3.justification: The main benchmark metrics, skip counts, VAE processing and dataset-specific upsampling factors remain unchanged. New experiments compare endpoint availability and upsampling factors of 1, 1.5 and 2. Section 14 introduces efficiency measurements on one RTX 4090, using 1024 × 576 outputs and runtime averaged over 16 frames.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained VAE illustration in Figure 5, v2 adds quantitative and qualitative tests of Two-side Fusion and input upsampling (Tables 3 and 5; Figures 9, 10 and 13). It also adds hallucination/error-accumulation case studies and computational analysis in Table 6, substantially strengthening component validation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new runtime averaging over 16 frames describes the evaluation procedure, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All existing Table 2 scores are unchanged, but v2 adds five baselines' scores, ablation results, efficiency measurements and revised qualitative comparisons. New BS-ERGB results include generation/interpolation PSNR of 25.79/27.74 in Table 3 and 1×/2× upsampling PSNR of 24.82/27.74 in Table 5; these compare experimental conditions rather than version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.5 retain the frozen video diffusion model, trainable event-conditioning components, multi-stack event representation, tiled denoising and Two-side Fusion. The supplementary implementation disclosures do not establish a changed algorithm or training objective.

P1.justification: v2 revises the evaluation discussion, adds an ablation subsection and a structured supplement, and moves training details into that supplement. The main section order and most abstract, introduction, method and conclusion wording remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains substantial comparator rows and ranking colors, and Tables 3–6 add ablation, dataset and efficiency displays. New figures illustrate generation failures, capture hardware and upsampling. The teaser and several comparison panels change, while matched qualitative examples are reorganized between the main paper and supplement.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the new baselines, TimeRewind, HR-INR, AdamW and additional event-camera research, while removing the EV-IMO and 0-MMS references. These broaden supporting literature without substantially changing the related-work narrative or central novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3 retain the same diffusion formulation, tile accumulation and temporal fusion mathematics. No new formal assumptions, propositions, proofs or derivations appear in the supplement.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation and reporting gaps: broader baseline comparisons test competitiveness, Tables 3 and 5 directly evaluate key design choices, and Sections 10 and 13 substantially improve reproducibility information. Table 6 and the expanded limitations also expose the considerable runtime cost. Together these substantially strengthen the evidence and transparency of the unchanged method; original benchmark scores remain unchanged and uncertainty estimates remain absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RE-VDM with matching authors, method and principal experiments. All supplied pages, including v2's supplementary Sections 8–14, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline results, component ablations, generation results and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative interpolation results on BS-ERGB, HQF and Clear-Motion in Table 2, alongside qualitative results and a VAE reconstruction experiment.

results.title:
Repurposing Pre-trained Video Diffusion Models for Event-based Video
  Interpolation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: two physics-based priors for joint inverse rendering, improved material estimation, and competitive novel view synthesis. The expanded evaluation supports these retained claims without redefining the principal contribution.

C2.justification: V2 explains SG-Env's advantage under environment lighting and weakness under mixed lighting, acknowledges inferior metallicness SSIM, and explains why clipping and unknown tone mapping prevent reliable DTU lighting estimation. New Appendix C discusses mechanisms of BRDF energy creation and loss. Existing reflective-surface and fine-detail limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 specifies an 8192-ray batch and 5K/1K/30K iterations for the geometry/material/joint phases, replacing v1's less specific 30K-iteration description. Reported hardware and runtime change from an RTX 4090 and 1–3 hours to an A6000 and 3–7.5 hours. Appendix D.2 additionally explains the two SDF uses during joint training; the code link and loss-weight tables remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same six NeILF++ illumination conditions and 15 DTU scans for reconstruction and novel view synthesis. The added geometry measurements assess an existing model output on retained data; the broader ablation uses conditions already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: Table 2 removes Neural-PIL from the DTU RGB comparison and introduces VolSDF and NeuS for geometry comparison. Table 1 retains PhySG, SG-ENV, NeILF, and NeILF++ as comparators.

E3.justification: V2 extends SSIM reporting to the main NeILF++ comparison and adds DTU Chamfer Distance evaluation against reference point clouds. Table 3 changes from City-only scores to averages over all six illumination conditions. Appendix A also changes the ablation sampling from 128 incident directions to the full method's 256.

E4.justification: Table 3 expands the three-variant ablation into all four combinations of the two losses, adding the previously missing specular-loss-only test and evaluating their contributions across six conditions. Appendix A and Figure 6 provide corresponding qualitative evidence. The DTU case studies add normal comparisons and replace scan 40 with scan 105.

E5.justification: Table 2 adds standard deviations to the DTU summary scores for PBR-NeRF and NeILF++. Both versions already report averaging three training runs, so this establishes additional uncertainty reporting rather than an increase in run count.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 contain substantial replacements and additions. Reported PBR-NeRF mean albedo PSNR changes from 19.09 to 20.08 in Table 1, and DTU RGB PSNR from 28.22 to 28.63 in Table 2. Baseline scores also change, SSIM and Chamfer results are added, and qualitative outputs are updated. The ablation results use different aggregation and sampling, and the PDFs do not establish a controlled version-to-version performance gain.

M1.justification: The BRDF, incident-light, and NeRF/SDF fields, two proposed physics-based losses, and three optimization phases remain unchanged. The expanded diagram and explanation of the SDF's two uses clarify the existing procedure.

P1.justification: There are localized rewrites in the related-work, method, and experimental discussions, plus terminology and affiliation edits. A short new Appendix C shifts the existing background appendix to D. The main section sequence and most explanatory text remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are rearranged or redrawn, Table 1 gains PSNR/SSIM subcolumns, and Table 2 adds geometry rows and uncertainty reporting while moving earlier. Figure 5 adds reference columns and a normals row; Figure 6 gains an ablation column. Figure 7 is relocated and its qualitative outputs are updated.

R1.justification: Section 4.2 adds a substantive comparison between SG-Env's explicit lighting representation and PBR-NeRF's more flexible implicit representation. The same 55 works remain cited, and the principal related-work positioning is retained; bibliographic metadata changes do not introduce new works.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations and appendix derivations are retained. Equation (9) gains the reflection-loss weight already specified in v1 Equation (21) and Table 5, harmonizing existing mathematics. New Appendix C supplies qualitative intuition about energy violations rather than a new formal result or derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central contributions: the complete six-condition ablation isolates both losses, and quantitative geometry comparisons directly test a reconstruction capability previously lacking numerical evaluation. Added uncertainty reporting, SSIM comparisons, and training details improve transparency. A small inconsistency remains—Appendix A claims an energy-only metallicness PSNR improvement although Table 3 shows 21.35 decreasing to 21.30—but it does not outweigh the stronger empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PBR-NeRF and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite revised experiments and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original reconstruction experiments, revised benchmark results, geometry measurements, and expanded loss ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original PBR-NeRF experiments on NeILF++ and DTU, including quantitative comparisons, qualitative reconstructions, and loss ablations.

results.title: PBR-NeRF: Inverse Rendering with Physics-Based Neural Fields

C1.justification: Both versions claim a fixed-size holistic identity representation learned through few-to-many reconstruction and complementary decoders, improving identity preservation in two generative tasks. v2's conclusion reiterates input-count scaling and representation structure already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific limitations concerning lighting injection and skin-tone predominance, with proposed remedies involving more diverse data or lighting augmentation. Section 4.2 replaces the claim of better pose accuracy with an interpretation of similar pose errors as evidence of convergence. Section 4.4 also explains the restricted ablation input counts through diminishing returns.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies extensive previously unavailable details: feature extraction and aggregation, decoder configurations, optimizers, learning rates, batch sizes, GPU hardware, training resolutions, downstream schedules, and initialization. Figure I documents MFHQ filtering and pose-based sampling. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although conflicting training-step counts and main-text versus appendix ArcFace dimensions leave some settings ambiguous.

E1.justification: v2 adds filtered WebFace21M identities as a controllable-generation test set; v1 used WebFace21M as alternative pretraining data in an ablation. The two downstream tasks, MFHQ coverage, and licensed personalized-generation training data remain. Additional generator backbones extend model settings rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: The supplied personalized-generation comparisons expand substantially beyond v1's displayed CLIP comparison. Table I evaluates IPA-FaceID, IPA-FaceIDPlusV2, IPA-Full, and PuLID; Figure IV also evaluates IPA-Plus and displays InstantID and PhotoMakerV2 comparisons previously only alluded to in v1. Table 1 retains the same controllable-generation comparators.

E3.justification: v2 extends MFHQ testing to seven inputs, specifies WebFace selection conditions, and supplies FLUX Schnell and SD1.5 evaluation settings. Section 4.1 changes MTD training from 250K to 200K steps and replaces the explicit ArcFace evaluation-feature description with features citing facenet-pytorch. However, Appendix A.2 reports 250K MTD and 5K flow-matching steps, conflicting with v2's main-text 200K and 10K. These are reported setting differences; actual reruns and exact budgets remain unresolved.

E4.justification: Tables 2–3, the pretraining-duration analysis in Figure 9, and the attention visualization are retained. Appendix A adds qualitative findings about token counts, feature aggregation, and injection locations. Appendix B adds template-driven examples and demonstrates transfer of the FLUX-dev-trained representation to Schnell and SD1.5.

E5.justification: Table I newly reports means and standard deviations across identities for personalized generation. v1 provides no corresponding uncertainty reporting. These describe variation across identities, not repeated training runs; neither PDF establishes additional runs or seed-based uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds seven-input MFHQ results, WebFace results, and quantitative personalized-generation comparisons. Examples include Omni-ID's seven-input MFHQ similarity of 0.742 and Table I's 0.8026 ± 0.0421 versus PuLID's 0.7289 ± 0.0572. Previously reported MFHQ entries and Tables 2–3 retain their numbers. WebFace has five values under four input-count labels, preventing reliable assignment of each value to an input count. These additions do not establish same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the fixed-query encoder, few-to-many reconstruction procedure, masked transformer decoder, flow-matching decoder, and both training objectives. Appendix A expands implementation documentation without establishing a revision to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose are retained. Local revisions condense the introduction and experimental overview, clarify explanations, and revise the conclusion. Appendices A–B organize the newly supplied documentation and supplementary experiments.

P2.justification: The full-page gallery becomes a smaller Figure 8, and the personalized-generation comparison is reduced and relocated as Figure 7. Table 1 becomes a full-width two-dataset display. v2 adds the dataset-construction diagram, expanded qualitative comparison grids, and Table I, substantially changing the visual organization while retaining the main ablation displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds Information Bottleneck literature, additional 3D face-model references, and technical citations including InsightFace, facenet-pytorch, BLIP-2, SDXL, and FLUX-ControlNet. The central positioning against discriminative representations and alongside personalization approaches remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–7 remain unchanged. The added Information Bottleneck reference supplies conceptual motivation, without introducing a formal assumption, derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies quantitative support for the personalized-generation claim that v1 deferred to an absent appendix, adds evaluation beyond MFHQ, and substantially documents training and dataset construction. This makes central claims more assessable and the implementation more transparent. Conflicting training settings, unexplained metric attribution changes, and the WebFace label mismatch remain material reporting flaws, but the gains in available evidence and documentation are substantial overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of Omni-ID, with matching core equations, methods, and experiments. v1 ends after the references despite appendix cross-references; v2 includes Appendices A–B. Appendix additions therefore mean newly supplied evidence or documentation, without establishing that those experiments were newly performed.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and supplies additional WebFace evaluation, personalized-generation results in Table I, and qualitative comparisons in the appendix.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original controllable face-generation and personalized-generation experiments, including quantitative comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–3.

results.title: Omni-ID: Holistic Identity Representation Designed for Generative Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a human-annotated grounded-caption dataset, a two-task benchmark, user-study-validated caption scoring and an end-to-end model for both tasks. Expanded data and revised experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the frame-count ablations as evidence that the benchmark requires temporal context and adds explanations of the newer comparisons. It retains the interpretation that captioning helps segmentation. However, deleting supplementary Section E removes v1's explicit qualification that automatic mask propagation introduces annotation errors.

D1.justification: Training-budget documentation changes, while preprocessing, token counts, learning rates, hardware and project access information largely remain. v3 introduces a reproducibility inconsistency: its prose describes segmentation training using only ViCaS, but supplementary Table 5 still lists MeViS and Ref-YTVOS. Their actual removal from training cannot be established.

E1.justification: Section 3.1 expands ViCaS from Oops fail videos alone to Oops, UVO and Kinetics-700, broadening coverage beyond accidental events. Both captioning and language-guided instance segmentation remain. The dataset grows from 7,331 to 20,416 videos.

E2.justification: The benchmark adds VideoLISA and replaces standalone LLaVA-NeXT captioning comparisons with LLaVA-OneVision and MiniCPM-o 2.6; LMPM and DsHmp remain. A revised LLaVA-NeXT segmentation comparison appears in Table 3. The scoring study's Table 2 removes Distiluse-B, BCE Rerank.-B, MiniLM and QNLI Electra-B.

E3.justification: Train/validation/test sizes change from 5,131/1,100/1,100 to 14,516/2,950/2,950. Supplementary training tables change the reported stage-3 batch size from 64 to 128 and iterations from 15,718 to 10,752. Captioning comparisons introduce off-the-shelf zero-shot models, and ablations introduce different frame-count settings. CA and segmentation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 3 extends temporal-context analysis to one-, two- and four-frame inputs, replacing v1's direct slow-fast pooling toggle. Single-task versus joint-training ablations remain, and the LLaVA-NeXT comparison is incorporated into this table. The caption-scoring robustness study retains its procedure with fewer comparison methods.

E5.justification: Human-score filtering, Pearson-correlation calculations and pooling across reference captions are unchanged. Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The reported Llama3-based model changes from 22.0 validation and 13.5 test mAP in v1 to 20.5 and 16.5 in v3; changed datasets and settings prevent interpreting these as direct performance gains or losses. Dataset statistics and ablation scores are extensively revised. v3 supplies LMPM and DsHmp test scores where v1 had blank cells. Retained Table 2 scores match.

M1.justification: The architecture and procedure remain the same: slow-fast video features, an MLLM generating per-object SEG tokens, a SAM2-initialized segmentation network, and three-stage training. Llama3-8B, emphasized in v3, was already evaluated in v1.

P1.justification: The introduction and acknowledgements are shortened, selected related-work and experimental paragraphs are rewritten, and supplementary Section E is deleted. Appendix citation placeholders are resolved. The main section sequence and most methodological explanations remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 3's word cloud and histograms are redrawn with revised axes. Table 3 gains explicit configuration columns, benchmark tables lose the LLM column, and several tables change row membership. Appendix review headers and line numbers disappear. Core illustrative figures remain; v3 also incorrectly labels the supplementary test-results table as validation results.

R1.justification: Sections 2.2 and 5.1 add focused discussion of recent LLM-based video segmentation, including VideoLISA and more detailed treatment of the already-cited VISA. New references include LLaVA-OneVision and MiniCPM, while several audio and multimodal references are removed. The overall holistic-versus-pixel-level research framing remains.

T1.justification: The feature-shape definitions, slow-fast token-count expression and caption-scoring calculations are retained. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs that are added, removed or revised.

improvement.justification: Broadening the Oops-only benchmark with UVO and Kinetics-700 addresses a substantial coverage limitation. Newer comparison models, temporal-context ablations and more complete test comparisons strengthen the paper's central dataset and benchmark contribution. The contradictory training-data descriptions, incorrect Table 7 caption and removed mask-error caveat weaken reporting, but the broader coverage and stronger benchmark validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ViCaS and Video-LLaVA-Seg. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and included supplementary sections support reliable comparison, including identification of incomplete tables and internal inconsistencies.

after.justification: v3 retains the original user study and reports revised dataset statistics, ablations and benchmark results, including supplementary test results.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset statistics, a caption-scoring user study, model ablations, and validation and test results.

C1.justification: Both versions claim efficient, globally and locally consistent indoor texturing through zero-shot MVIS, MVRS and related-view attention. V2 explicitly mentions occlusion handling in the abstract, but this contribution was already stated in v1's introduction and contribution list.

C2.justification: Appendix A.3–A.4 newly explains the staged sampling schedules as accelerating generation while maintaining texture quality. The introduction also attributes optimization overhead to numerous learnable parameters. Existing interpretations concerning consistency and occlusion remain, without new substantive limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies previously unspecified prompt rules, a 0.01 visibility threshold, camera counts and placement, timestep schedules, guidance scales and merge-exponent settings. Appendix B and Algorithm 2 further document instance repainting. These substantially expand reproducibility information rather than demonstrate changed experimental settings.

E1.justification: V2 extends coverage beyond synthetic 3D-FRONT bedrooms and living rooms to real scanned offices and computer rooms from ScanNet++ (Section E.2, Figure 9). This substantively broadens the input domain and scene types, although the added evaluation is qualitative.

E2.justification: Text2Tex-H, Text2Tex-C and SceneTex remain the evaluated comparators. The new user study uses this same set. Newly cited RoomTex is not added to the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix D adds a human-evaluation protocol using four rendered views and 1–5 ratings for prompt fidelity, visual quality and texture–geometry alignment, reporting 25 participants and 450 ratings. The existing 3D-FRONT evaluation, CLIP/AS metrics and timing protocol are retained.

E4.justification: Figure 7 adds a visual stage-two ablation to the existing quantitative MVRS ablation, showing how repainting fills occluded regions. Figure 10 adds intermediate denoising examples. These supplement existing component analyses without introducing a broad new robustness or sensitivity study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new user study reports mean ratings and participant counts, without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All Table 1 values remain unchanged. New Table 2 reports RoomPainter scores of 4.00 for prompt fidelity, 4.13 for visual quality and 4.31 for texture–geometry alignment, leading all three categories. V2 also adds stage-two, style-variation, ScanNet++ and intermediate-denoising visual results.

M1.justification: The MVIS/MVRS pipeline, view-weighted texture merging and related-view attention are retained. Appendix A and Algorithm 2 newly document sampling schedules and implementation choices; they do not establish a revision to the proposed method.

P1.justification: V2 edits wording and terminology across the abstract, introduction and methods, clarifies that Figure 5 shows final-step raw samples, and organizes the supplementary explanations into Sections A–E. The main section order and narrative remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 2, Figures 6–10 and a full-page Algorithm 2, substantially expanding the visual presentation. It also updates Figure 2 and its caption and relocates Algorithm 1. The original comparison and ablation images in Figures 4–5 are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations including RoomTex, ScanNet++, Align Your Latents and Tune-A-Video, while dropping Progressive3D, Showroom3D and Cycle3D. The related-work taxonomy and RoomPainter's positioning relative to inpainting and optimization approaches remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain the same diffusion, texture-merging and attention mathematics, with equivalent notation changes. Algorithm 2 elaborates the implementation of MVRS; no new theoretical assumptions, guarantees, proofs or derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses substantial reporting and validation gaps in the supplied v1: detailed implementation specifications improve reproducibility, while the user study adds human assessments beyond CLIP/AS and the ScanNet++ examples extend qualitative coverage to real scans. These materially strengthen the paper despite unchanged main results. User-study uncertainty and quantitative evaluation on ScanNet++ remain absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RoomPainter and contain readable text, equations, tables and figures. V1 ends with references; v2 retains the main paper and adds supplementary Sections A–E and Algorithm 2. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains these experiments and adds original user-study scores in Table 2, ScanNet++ examples and supplementary visual analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original scene-texturing experiments, including quantitative comparisons and ablations in Table 1 and qualitative results in Figures 4–5.
