  Texturing

C1.justification: The abstract, three principal contributions and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: a cloud dataset, a monoplanar representation and parametric posterior sampling coupled to physical volume rendering. Introducing the PDPS abbreviation and adding evidence do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 adds a specific rationale for concentrating refinement near the middle of optimization: avoiding early local minima and late overfitting artifacts. The existing limitations concerning density–lighting ambiguity, computational cost and transfer to other volumetric phenomena remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v1 promises code and dataset release upon acceptance; v3 states that both are publicly available and supplies a repository link. Section 5.2 also newly documents comparator latent dimensions and upsampling arrangements, while Section 4.5 supplies refinement timing. The parameter details clarify the existing representation experiment rather than establish that it was changed.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 1,000-cloud training dataset and the same applications: generation, single-view and sparse-view reconstruction, lighting recovery, transmittance reconstruction, super-resolution, interpolation and inpainting. The expanded evaluation samples retained cloud-reconstruction coverage; super-resolution is relocated, not newly introduced.

E2.justification: The representation comparison retains triplanar and dense-grid alternatives, and reconstruction comparisons retain DRT and SPS. Their additional single-view evaluations change settings, rather than introducing different comparison methods.

E3.justification: v1 evaluates DRT and SPS using three views and illustrates two reconstruction configurations. v3 evaluates both using one and three views and adds a 32-case aggregate evaluation sampled from 16 unseen clouds, three materials, seven environments and five camera-pose sets. This substantially expands the reported evaluation design.

E4.justification: The guidance-strength analysis changes from five settings ending at zeta=0.8 in v1 Figure 14 to six settings including 0.6 and 1.0 in v3 Figure 13, with revised examples and measurements. Figure 10 also removes the fully known-parameters control from the lighting-recovery comparison. The representation and latent-enhancement analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new Table 2 averages across test cases, continuing the case-averaging practice already used in Table 1; the restyled convergence plot does not specify a new uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: v3 adds aggregate LPIPS and runtime results in Table 2 and extended comparisons in supplementary Figure 16. For example, the new mean novel-view LPIPS values are 0.1126 for DPS1 and 0.2937 for DRT1. Reconstruction, lighting and sensitivity examples and scores are also replaced. Table 1 remains numerically unchanged. The replaced examples do not establish performance gains under identical settings across versions.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 now restricts latent refinement to selected passes through S_refine, with Section 4.5 specifying application around the middle of optimization. v1's displayed loop refined every pass, although its prose already called refinement optional. This is a limited revision to the specified procedure; the decoder, regularized loss and DPS updates remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the monoplanar explanation, clarifies gradient and optimization terminology, and revises algorithm presentation. It moves super-resolution from Section 5.6 to 5.3 and adds an extended-comparisons appendix section. Most prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The visual presentation is extensively revised: Figures 1 and 3 are redrawn, dataset and generated examples are combined in Figure 2, convergence plotting is restyled, and numerous result panels are replaced or reorganized. v3 also adds the aggregate comparison table and a full supplementary comparison figure. These changes extend well beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same works. Section 4.2 newly acknowledges that jointly training shared decoder components is common in triplanar generative models, citing existing references 6, 14 and 54. This modestly clarifies the relationship to prior work.

T1.justification: Sections 4.2–4.3 correct the stated transformation property from invariance to equivariance. This is a limited correction to the mathematical characterization. The rewritten interpolation description represents the same construction, while the posterior objective and supplementary rendering derivations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central reconstruction evaluation beyond v1's two illustrated comparisons: Table 2 reports 32-case aggregates on unseen clouds and includes DRT/SPS comparisons using the same numbers of input views as DPS. Together with newly documented experimental controls and reported code/data access, this materially improves evidential support and reproducibility. Run-to-run uncertainty remains unreported, but the stronger validation provides a clear overall benefit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cloudy dataset, monoplanar representation and light transport-aware reconstruction method. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and supplementary material support comparison, including the additional comparisons in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds aggregate reconstruction results over 32 test cases in Table 2, with further examples in supplementary Figure 16.

before.justification: v1 reports original representation-quality measurements in Table 1, reconstruction comparisons in Figure 9, and supplementary sensitivity and application results.

results.title:
Light Transport-aware Diffusion Posterior Sampling for Single-View
  Reconstruction of 3D Volumes

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: occlusion-aware synthetic pretraining improves real-world recognition, and DuoMamba provides an efficient alternative to Transformer encoders. The supplement supplies additional support without redefining those contributions.

C2.justification: New discussion interprets the larger-pretraining comparisons as evidence of data and parameter efficiency and characterizes complete-object performance as competitive. It also explains differences from Vim and identifies partial-cloud training fluctuations as motivation for EMA. The existing limitation concerning unavailable resources for Objaverse pretraining is retained.

D1.justification: Section 9 supplies previously absent reproduction details: 512-by-512 rendering, transparent backgrounds, batch size 32, color replacement rules, cached CLIP features, EMA decay 0.9995, and a cosine schedule with base learning rate 7e-4. The abstract replaces a future release promise with a project link and reported code/data availability.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation of OccTIP/DuoMamba on complete ModelNet40 objects, extending its partial-object ModelNet40-P evaluation. v1 already displayed complete-ModelNet40 baseline scores as motivation in Figure 1. The proposed method's ShapeNetCore training coverage and existing real-world evaluation datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 6 introduces evaluated Vim and Vim-plus-Hilbert comparators. Figure 5 adds an actual comparison with Uni3D-giant, previously only cited, and Figure 6 includes OpenDlign in few-shot probing, where it was absent from v1's Table 2. These substantially broaden architectural and large-scale comparisons.

E3.justification: Added evaluation conditions include 12-view voting on complete ModelNet40 objects and comparisons against encoders pretrained on 880K objects, including the much larger Uni3D-giant. Existing main-text training settings and evaluation metrics remain unchanged. Section 9's additional hyperparameters are disclosures, without evidence that existing experiments were rerun under revised settings.

E4.justification: The supplement extends analysis to Vim versus Hilbert-adapted Vim, complete versus partial pretraining for DuoMamba, and the encoder's contribution to detection performance (Tables 6, 9, and 10). Table 9 also redisplays existing SparseConv and PointBERT results. These additions strengthen analysis of the central contributions beyond the retained component and scanning-order ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The supplementary results retain the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain their scores, while v2 adds Vim comparisons, larger-pretraining comparisons, 71.6% accuracy for complete-ModelNet40 voting, a 57.5% complete-pretraining DuoMamba control, and additional detection results. Tables 7–8 newly provide class-level AP; their aggregate mAP values match Table 4 after rounding. The introduction also corrects the SparseConv gain from 3.5 to 3.8 percentage points, consistent with the unchanged 61.7 and 57.9 scores.

M1.justification: The OccTIP objectives and DuoMamba architecture remain unchanged. Section 11 adds a limited inference adaptation for complete objects: generate 12 partial views and majority-vote their predictions. Newly disclosed training details do not establish changes to the original training method.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording edits, corrects references to the pretraining section, updates acknowledgments, and organizes supplementary material into Sections 8–11. Most main-text prose and section ordering remain unchanged; the existing limitations paragraph moves without substantive revision.

P2.justification: v2 adds detailed detection tables and architectural/pretraining comparison tables (Tables 6–10), plus parameter-versus-accuracy, few-shot, and complete-object plots (Figures 5–7). Figure 7 reuses Figure 1's baseline bars with added OccTIP reference lines. Main-text displays are retained, with more compact captions and resulting layout reflow.

R1.justification: Section 8 adds targeted positioning against corruption-based occlusion handling, MVTN, and Vision Mamba. Six references are added, covering these works, ABO, 3D-FUTURE, and Mean Teacher. The main related-work narrative and broader research positioning remain stable.

T1.justification: The state-space and space-filling-curve definitions, contrastive objectives, and DuoMamba equations remain unchanged. The supplement introduces no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 refers to supplementary implementation and detection details absent from its supplied PDF. v2 fills those reporting gaps and adds relevant tests of the closest two-stream alternative, pretraining data choice, and encoder contributions to detection (Tables 6, 9, and 10). Together, these substantially strengthen reproducibility and support for the central contributions. The retained headline scores are unchanged, and the larger-data and voting comparisons remain conditional on their disclosed settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OccTIP/DuoMamba work, and their text, equations, figures, and tables support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends after references; v2 additionally includes Supplementary Material, Sections 8–11.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds results including Vision Mamba comparisons, complete-object evaluation, and further pretraining and encoder analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot classification, few-shot probing, instance recognition, object detection, and architectural ablation results in Tables 1–5.

results.title:
Occlusion-aware Text-Image-Point Cloud Pretraining for Open-World 3D
  Object Recognition

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain TRG, the two curricula and the same benchmark claims, including approximately 1.0% improvement on VidSTG-Declarative and 3.0% on HCSTVG-v1. The supplementary evidence does not redefine the principal contributions.

C2.justification: New discussion addresses tracking and label-switching ambiguity, harmful temporal trimming on VidSTG, missing LLM-generated action combinations, and loss of action-based identifiers during POS extraction. The supplement also explains curriculum-order and cumulative-training effects and acknowledges that combining both curricula does not improve over CG-SCL alone on HCSTVG-v2.

D1.justification: V2 supplies prompt templates and examples, detailed SLF label-selection rules, interpolation and filtering procedures, inference thresholds, and stage-wise sample counts. These fill substantial documentation gaps in the supplied v1. A project-page link is also added, although the PDFs alone do not establish code availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use VidSTG declarative/interrogative queries, HCSTVG-v1 and HCSTVG-v2 for weakly supervised spatio-temporal grounding. The supplementary experiments reuse this coverage without introducing another dataset, domain or distinct task scenario.

E2.justification: Supplementary Tables 8–9 add substantial quantitative comparisons with fully supervised methods, including TubeDETR, STCAT, CSDVL, CG-STVG and VGDINO. These contextual comparisons explicitly involve different supervision. The weakly supervised comparator sets in main Tables 1–2 are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce oracle proposal-selection controls and vary curriculum direction, stage counts, cumulative training, denoising and inference filtering/trimming. Section 4 also changes the stated CG-SCL schedule from increasing IoU bounds to decreasing IoU. V1 Figure 4 already suggested the latter, so this correction does not establish that benchmark experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The supplement adds extensive investigations of tracking noise and performance ceilings, extracted versus original captions, reversed and cumulative curricula, HCSTVG-v2 components, inference thresholds, and LLM extraction failures. V1's HCSTVG-v1 stage-performance plot and W-GDINO qualitative example are omitted, while its principal ablation tables remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. The added experimental tables and performance plots continue to report point estimates.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–5 retain their numerical entries, but the supplement adds many results. For example, denoising yields 9.74 m_vIoU for Switch-Addition and 10.81 for Switch-Dropping against a 10.40 baseline. Supplementary Table 7 reports 19.82 for both curricula on HCSTVG-v2 and 19.99 for CG-SCL alone, creating configuration ambiguity around the retained 19.99 headline result.

M1.justification: Supplementary Section A.3 introduces two proposed and tested preprocessing variants: Switch-Addition splits label-switched segments into separate tubelets, while Switch-Dropping removes non-dominant-label detections. These are limited procedural additions; the central TRG architecture, losses and two curricula are retained.

P1.justification: Sections 2–5 undergo broad paragraph rewriting and compression, covering related work, baseline motivation, method explanations, implementation and experimental discussion. The new supplement provides an organized A–H narrative with detailed procedures, supporting explanations and failure cases.

P2.justification: V1 Figure 2 is separated into v2 Figures 2–3, and v1 Figure 4 becomes dedicated SA-TCL and CG-SCL Figures 5–6, with enlarged diagrams and revised captions. V1 Figures 6–7 are omitted. The supplement adds numerous histograms, performance plots, qualitative examples and expanded comparison tables.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds brief positioning against unimodal semi-supervised and active-learning work and acknowledges concurrent Contextual Self-Paced Learning for Weakly Supervised Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding. A foundation-model survey is also cited. The principal research positioning remains stable; publication-metadata updates do not constitute additional works.

T1.justification: The grounding definitions and losses are retained. V2 explicitly writes the already-described average pairwise temporal IoU and clarifies feature indexing and tubelet durations. These elaborate existing mathematics; no substantive theoretical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: V1 refers to supplementary implementation details that are unavailable in the supplied PDF. V2 fills important prompting, curriculum-construction and inference gaps, directly tests central design choices, and documents concrete failure conditions. This substantially improves reproducibility and evidential support. Reporting problems remain: Section A.3 incorrectly says both denoising variants improve performance, and the HCSTVG-v2 appendix creates ambiguity about the headline model configuration. These limit some conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial gains in transparency and validation.

A1.justification: Both readable PDFs describe the same STPro work, with matching core methods and experiments. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary Sections A–H. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains these experiments and adds original tracking, denoising, curriculum and inference analyses in the supplement.

before.justification: Tables 1–5 report original benchmark experiments, component ablations and curriculum comparisons on VidSTG and HCSTVG.

results.title:
STPro: Spatial and Temporal Progressive Learning for Weakly Supervised
  Spatio-Temporal Grounding

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: Bayesian prompt distributions, ISD/IAD modeling, RCA alignment, and superior zero-shot performance across 15 datasets. Additional supporting evidence does not materially alter these claims.

C2.justification: The supplement adds substantive interpretations of distribution flexibility, hyperparameter complexity, overfitting trajectories, and embedding clusters. It also discusses speed–accuracy and memory tradeoffs against baselines. Appendix E explicitly identifies sampling overhead and CLIP's limited textual and fine-grained visual capabilities as limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices A and C supply previously unavailable sampling pseudocode, architecture details, random prompt selection during training, cosine scheduling, warm-up, early stopping, focal-loss settings, baseline code provenance, and dataset construction details such as RSDD cropping and DAGM reannotation. The abstract adds a code-access link. These are documented disclosures, not evidence that all underlying procedures changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same seven industrial and eight medical datasets for the same classification and segmentation tasks. Appendix C adds dataset descriptions and preparation details, without establishing changed dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The five external comparators remain WinCLIP, APRIL-GAN, CLIP-AD, AnomalyCLIP, and AdaCLIP. Appendix B.2 adds an explicitly evaluated Gaussian-distribution alternative to the proposed prompt-flow model in Figure 7, extending the methodological comparison.

E3.justification: The main training-transfer protocol and default settings are retained. The supplement substantially expands evaluated configurations through separate training/inference prompt controls, B/K/P/Q sweeps, three CLIP backbone variants, and input resolutions of 336, 518, and 700 pixels. Table 7 also introduces comparative GPU-memory measurement.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds single-prompt versus ensemble controls, Gaussian versus flow modeling, hyperparameter and backbone/resolution ablations, and embedding visualizations. Figure 9 expands the existing test-AP comparison with training AP and training/test-loss trajectories, providing additional evidence about overfitting.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five random seeds and retain Table 3's mean±standard-deviation reporting. Appendix A.1 additionally states that five experimental rounds are averaged, clarifying aggregation across runs beyond v1's statement about category averaging. An increase in run count is not reported.

E6.justification: The supplement adds substantial numerical and qualitative results, including category-level scores, configuration comparisons, and baseline runtime/memory measurements. For example, new Table 5 reports APRIL-GAN pixel AP of 37.4 with single prompts at both stages versus 40.8 with ensembles. Main Tables 1–4 retain their results apart from equivalent rounding.

M1.justification: Section 3.5 corrects the stated text-branch anomaly score to use the original text embeddings Z^t instead of RCA-refined F^t, bringing the formula into agreement with Figure 2. This is a localized revision of the written inference rule; the prompt banks, ISD/IAD flows, RCA architecture, and overall loss are retained.

P1.justification: The main section order and narrative are retained, with grammatical corrections, clearer notation, revised cross-references, and acknowledgments. The added material is organized into Appendices A–E; the existing main text is not extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: v3 adds Algorithm 1, Tables 5–13, and Figures 7–40, including sensitivity plots, diagnostic trajectories, embedding visualizations, category-level tables, and extensive segmentation galleries. Existing main figures and tables largely retain their designs, with limited annotation and layout adjustments.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Kanade and Gumaste's BrainMRI work, Qu et al.'s shift-equivalence study, and YOLOv10. It expands baseline descriptions and explains dataset-processing differences from VCP-CLIP. The principal positioning relative to existing prompt-based anomaly detectors remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 corrects the marginal likelihood from 'tractable' to 'intractable' in the variational-inference justification. Appendix B.2 adds the Gaussian alternative's KL-divergence objective in Equation 19. The principal Bayesian and normalizing-flow derivations remain.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves an important deficiency of the supplied v1: implementation, dataset preparation, and supplementary analyses were referenced but unavailable. The added details substantially improve reproducibility, while controlled Gaussian/flow comparisons, sensitivity studies, category-level results, and explicit limitations make the central claims more assessable. Headline performance remains unchanged. Some protocol ambiguity persists, particularly the unspecified validation split for early stopping, but the overall gains in documentation and evidential support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bayes-PFL work and support reliable text, equation, table, and figure comparison. The supplied v1 ends after its references despite referring to appendices; v3 includes Appendices A–E. Their contents can therefore be assessed as newly documented material.

after.justification: The original experiments are retained, and the appendices report additional controlled comparisons, sensitivity studies, efficiency measurements, and category-level results.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original anomaly-detection experiments across 15 industrial and medical datasets, including benchmark comparisons and ablations.

results.title: Bayesian Prompt Flow Learning for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: generative latent enhancement for SAM/SAM2, FDA and CRE, LQSeg, and robustness across degraded, clear, and unseen-degradation images. The additional experiments support these existing claims without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: Section 7.3 newly attributes noisy-box robustness to enhanced latent representations reducing noise-induced ambiguity. Section 7.4 connects increasing point counts with reduced prompt ambiguity and performance gains. These extend the interpretation to prompt conditions, although Figure 8 does not support the accompanying claim of superiority at every point count. No substantive limitations discussion is added.

D1.justification: Sections 8–9 add degradation-generation settings, including kernel choices, parameter ranges, noise probabilities, and JPEG quality factors. They also disclose T=1000, prompt-generation procedures, and training/inference pseudocode. The abstract adds a code/dataset release link. These substantially fill documentation gaps; they do not establish changes to the previously used method or data-generation procedure.

E1.justification: V3 adds evaluation on real driving imagery from BDD-100K, extending coverage beyond the synthetic degradation benchmarks in v1. It also evaluates ground-truth and perturbed bounding-box prompts, broadening input conditions beyond the earlier point-prompt experiments. The original training and evaluation datasets remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the original comparisons remains unchanged: SAM, SAM2, RobustSAM, and the PromptIR/DiffBIR restoration pipelines. Added experiments use existing comparator families. The ViT and Hiera variants are model configurations, while newly cited DN-DETR supplies a box-noise convention rather than an evaluated segmentation baseline.

E3.justification: Sections 7.2–7.4 add systematic evaluations across ViT-B/L/H and Hiera-T/S/B/L, point counts from 1 to 10, and ground-truth versus noisy boxes with noise scale 0.2. The original three-click default, metrics, optimizer, batch size, and training budgets remain unchanged. These are substantial additional protocols.

E4.justification: V3 retains the original component, decoder, channel-expansion, gamma, LoRA-rank, and degradation-level analyses. It adds backbone and prompt sensitivity studies in Tables 11–13 and Figure 8, further feature-reconstruction comparisons, and extensive qualitative cases under unseen degradations and on COCO. These broaden the evidence about robustness and generalization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, performance error bars, or significance tests. The added tables and curves continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice. Noise standard deviations in v3 describe degradation generation, not uncertainty in experimental results.

E6.justification: Tables 1–9 retain their numerical results. New Table 10 reports BDD-100K IoU of 0.8775 for GleSAM versus 0.8650 for SAM, and 0.9087 for GleSAM2 versus 0.8891 for SAM2. Tables 11–13 and Figure 8 add backbone and prompt results; Figure 8 includes a one-point case where GleSAM2 trails SAM2. These are additional evaluations, not improved scores for the original experiments.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 retain the same single-step latent denoising, FDA scaling, CRE weight replication, LoRA adaptation, and two-stage training with unchanged losses. Algorithms 1–2 document the existing procedure; the additional backbone evaluations do not establish a method change.

P1.justification: The retained abstract, introduction, method, experimental discussion, and conclusion are largely unchanged in wording and organization. Sections 7–10 organize the additional experiments and documentation, alongside affiliation, release, and acknowledgement additions. There is limited rewriting of the original narrative.

P2.justification: V3 adds Tables 10–13, Figures 8–15, and Algorithms 1–2, including prompt-count plots, backbone comparisons, feature maps, and several full-page qualitative displays. Figure 3 is simplified by removing displayed loss branches. These constitute substantial visual additions beyond the accompanying text reflow.

R1.justification: V3 adds eight supporting references, including ViT, Hiera, BDD-100K, DN-DETR, and corruption or degradation-generation research. The related-work discussion and positioning against robust segmentation and diffusion-based perception remain essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, reconstruction objective, segmentation objective, and underlying assumptions are retained. New Equation 7 expresses the already described blur/resize/noise/JPEG degradation composition symbolically. It adds no substantive mathematical assumption, derivation, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility: BDD-100K addresses v1's reliance on synthetic degradation evaluations, the backbone and prompt studies test broader applicability, and Sections 8–9 supply important missing construction and implementation details. New reporting problems qualify these gains: Figure 8 contradicts blanket prompt-superiority wording, and Table 12's GleSAM2-L average pixel accuracy exceeds every contributing score. These localized issues do not outweigh the substantial improvements to the evidence and documentation supporting the central contributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GleSAM/LQSeg work. The supplied text, equations, tables, figures, and supplemental material are readable. The original sections and experiments can be matched reliably against v3's expanded content.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds BDD-100K evaluation, backbone comparisons, prompt experiments, and qualitative results in Sections 7–10.

before.justification: V1 reports original segmentation experiments on ThinObject-5K, LVIS, ECSSD, and COCO, together with component ablations and sensitivity analyses in Tables 1–9.

results.title: Segment Any-Quality Images with Generative Latent Space Enhancement

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add explicit headline claims of superiority over modern vision encoders, including SigLIP2 and Perception Encoder, and update the MLLM comparisons to Qwen2.5-VL. The central contributions—efficient 4K pre-training, VILA-HD scaling and 4KPro—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 interprets weaker MME-RealWorld results as reflecting requirements such as counting beyond basic high-resolution recognition. It also argues that LLM alignment mainly improves language-centric capabilities. These interpretations are new; the existing limitations and future directions in Section 9 are retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the 4,000,000-pixel cap for Qwen models in Table 2 and specifies the per-scale patch allocation for the previously reported 35% 4KPro setting in Appendix C. Core pre-training hyperparameters, data-curation instructions and project-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation coverage with HRBench4K/8K, MME-RealWorld, CharXiV, SEEDBench-2-Plus, BLINK, MME, MMStar and MMVet, alongside Chinese MMBench evaluations (Tables 3–4). The curated PS3 training corpus and 4KPro construction remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Beyond v1’s SigLIP/C-RADIO comparisons, v2 evaluates SigLIP2, PECore, PELang, AIMv2 and InternViT2.5 in Table 3. Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, InternVL2.5 and PLM enter the MLLM comparisons in Tables 2 and 4. The original token-pruning comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The main state-of-the-art VILA-HD comparisons switch to SigLIP2-initialized PS3. New experiments match downstream training recipes, approximate encoder sizes and resolutions (Table 3), or visual-token budgets (Table 4). Appendix C also revises benchmark-specific patch allocations, including removing the special 6% V* allocation.

E4.justification: Table 3 newly examines LLM alignment through PS3 versus PS3Lang results and analyzes which task families benefit. The existing architecture, patch-selection, scale-allocation and high-resolution SFT-data ablations, along with appendix qualitative examples, are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark point estimates without repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added evaluations do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial result matrices in Tables 3–4 and replaces the main VILA-HD results with SigLIP2-based variants. In Table 2, 4KPro accuracy changes from 74.2% to 75.8% at 35% selection, but from 72.6% to 71.0% at 18%. These are results for changed model configurations, not isolated same-setting gains. Original scaling and ablation results remain.

M1.justification: Sections 2–3 retain the PS3 architecture, contrastive and box-supervision objectives, patch selection and VILA-HD procedure. PS3Lang uses the encoder after VILA-HD joint training, which already existed in v1 Appendix C. SigLIP2 initialization and separate evaluation of that checkpoint change experimental configurations without establishing a new underlying algorithm.

P1.justification: Section 6 gains a dedicated encoder-comparison subsection and reorganizes experiment settings and results within individual comparisons. Model names, the abstract and conclusion are revised, while most method, analysis and appendix prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds a substantial encoder-comparison matrix organized by task family and alignment status (Table 3), a dedicated token-matched high-resolution comparison (Table 4), and expands Table 2. Figure 1 updates its comparator and performance graphics. Existing method diagrams, scaling plots and appendix qualitative figures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion covering newer encoders, MLLMs and benchmarks, and adopts Perception Encoder’s distinction between encoders with and without LLM alignment. The established research positioning and Section 8 related-work discussion remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The saliency-score formula in Appendix A, minimum recognizable resolution definition and mathematical descriptions of training and selection are retained. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The controlled encoder comparisons and token-matched tests on independent high-resolution benchmarks substantially strengthen validation beyond v1’s narrower encoder comparisons and 4KPro-centered evidence. The added MME-RealWorld failures also clarify applicability limits. Changed initialization prevents treating updated VILA-HD scores as direct gains over v1, but the stronger controls and independent validation provide a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PS3, VILA-HD and 4KPro research. Their text, figures, tables and Appendices A–H support comparison; relocated and renumbered content can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds vision-encoder comparisons, additional benchmark evaluations and comparisons under matched visual-token budgets.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, resolution-scaling results, ablations, latency measurements and evaluations on the authors’ 4KPro benchmark.

results.title: Scaling Vision Pre-Training to 4K Resolution

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about balancing label relationships, parameter-efficient adaptation and group-aware MoE representations.

C2.justification: v2 hypothesizes that random grouping partially balances correlation and discrimination, and interprets conditional-error results as stronger correlation capture with reduced over-inference. These refine the existing explanation without changing its central rationale.

D1.justification: The supplement supplies clustering steps, explicit group assignments, pseudocode, ASL parameters λ0=2 and λ1=0, dataset splits and VG256 processing details. These substantially expand reproducibility information previously absent from the supplied v1, without demonstrating changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds Objects365, covering 365 everyday-object categories, while retaining VOC07, COCO, NUS-WIDE and VG256. This extends benchmark coverage within the existing natural-image multi-label classification task.

E2.justification: The original comparison methods remain, and Objects365 uses the same VPT, GateVPT and E2VPT baselines. New COCO comparisons evaluate random grouping in Table 8 and group-level gating against label-level gating in Table 7.

E3.justification: New protocols include conditional TPR/FPR evaluation on COCO label pairs with co-occurrence probability above 0.2, and Objects365 evaluation at 224×224 using validation images as the test set. Existing training settings remain unchanged; newly specified splits for retained datasets are disclosures.

E4.justification: v2 adds conditional-error analysis, per-class grouping and MoE effects, random-grouping and gating ablations, group heatmaps and expert-weight examples. Figures 10–11 also extend existing group/expert sensitivity analyses with CF1 and OF1 results.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or error bars. The averages in supplementary Tables 7–8 aggregate pretrained models rather than report replication or uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Original results remain unchanged, but substantial additional results appear. Table 6 reports Objects365 mAP of 52.2 for ML-VPT versus 49.3 for VPT with DINOv2/B at 224×224. Figure 12 reports higher conditional TPR for 88.4% and lower conditional FPR for 85.3% of selected label pairs; further ablation and per-class results are added.

M1.justification: CO/DC grouping, masked group prompts, label-specific MoE gating, dual ASL classifiers and averaged predictions are retained. The supplementary descriptions elaborate this procedure without establishing an implemented method change.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are nearly unchanged. v2 appends organized supplementary method and experiment explanations, with limited citation-related reflow rather than extensive rewriting of the existing paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–9, Figures 8–14 and Algorithm 1, substantially expanding the visual presentation. Figures 10–11 repeat existing mAP panels alongside new CF1/OF1 panels; the original tables and figures retain their displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds Han et al. on VPT versus full fine-tuning, Shao et al. on Objects365, and von Luxburg on spectral clustering. All 58 earlier references remain; the central research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Section 7.1 adds the normalized-Laplacian definition and constrained trace-minimization formulation of spectral clustering; Section 7.2 supplies explicit loss expressions. The main mathematical development is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The supplement substantially strengthens the central grouping rationale through random-grouping controls, conditional-error analysis and per-class ablations, while supplying previously absent reproducibility details. Objects365 broadens supporting evidence. Local errors temper these gains: Algorithm 1 partitions G+ for both branches, and Section 8.3 claims an 8.7-point maximum Objects365 mAP gap although Table 6 gives 7.7. These documentation problems do not outweigh the stronger empirical scrutiny and methodological transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ML-VPT work and are fully readable. v1 ends after the references; v2 adds supplementary Sections 7–8. The main text, equations, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds Objects365 results, further ablations, conditional-error analyses and visualizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on four datasets, component ablations, computational comparisons and prediction case studies.
